Please prepare an idea development worksheet for one campaign for this brand on this topic. The worksheet has these sections:

1. task_understanding: the problem or opportunity the campaign focuses on, and the assumptions about the brand, topic and audience.
2. candidates: exactly 4 candidate campaign directions whose core ideas differ from each other (not just different executions of one idea). For each: the core idea, how it connects to the brand, expected strengths and main concerns.

task_understanding.focus: Loneliness is rising, and payments technology has quietly helped design out small human moments (self-checkout, tap-and-go, delivery, no-contact everything). The opportunity is for Mastercard to move from being a tool that removes human contact from commerce to a brand that puts it back, using what it owns: the moment of paying, the Priceless platform, and a network that connects billions of people to local businesses.
assumptions: Mastercard's Priceless platform (what money can't buy: moments, connection, belonging) gives it a credible, long-standing right to talk about human connection without sounding opportunistic.

The audience is broad but the sharpest tension is among adults 25-45 with wide but shallow social lives, and adults 65+ living alone. They are not short of contacts; they are short of easy reasons to meet.

The main barrier to connection is not wanting company but the awkwardness and perceived imposition of reaching out first. People will accept an excuse, a structure or a small ritual more readily than a direct appeal.
Loneliness is stigmatised, so people will not self-identify as lonely. The campaign must invite everyone and avoid labelling or targeting 'lonely people'.
Mastercard must not infer or use sensitive emotional data. Trust and privacy are core to a financial brand, so any mechanic must be opt-in and transparent.
A financial brand earns credibility on this topic only if the idea involves real money, a real product behaviour or real merchants, not just a sentimental film.

candidates.title: The Loneliness Tax
candidates.core_idea: Expose the literal price of being alone: single supplements on holidays, solo-diner minimums, bulk-size packaging, rent for one. Mastercard partners with hotels, restaurants and travel brands to waive these 'solo penalties' for cardholders and publishes a 'Solo Surcharge Index' showing what going it alone costs per year.
candidates.brand_connection: A finance brand talking about the economics of living alone. It is a product-led, price-led way into the topic that turns Priceless into a commercial benefit.
expected_strengths: Revealing, shareable insight: loneliness and solo living have a measurable price.
Strong earned-media potential through the index and a clear commercial offer.
Directly tied to the card's core role in money and pricing.
main_concerns: Addresses solo living more than loneliness; people can be alone and happy, or lonely in a couple.
Risks stigmatising solo people as victims.
Depends on many merchants to be meaningful.

candidates.title: Priceless Regulars
candidates.core_idea: Celebrate and fund the 'weak ties' of daily life: the barista who knows your order, the shopkeeper who asks about your week. Mastercard backs local merchants who are good at recognition, with a 'Regulars' programme that rewards businesses for staying human-paced (a slow checkout lane, a chat bench, name-known loyalty).
candidates.brand_connection: Mastercard serves small businesses and everyday transactions, so it can reframe the commercial moment as the last remaining social infrastructure.
expected_strengths: Warm and culturally resonant; the 'third place' conversation is well established.
Supports Mastercard's small-business commitments.
Easy to localise across markets.
main_concerns: Close to existing ideas (Jumbo's chat checkout), so originality is limited.
Passive for the consumer: they receive an experience rather than do something.
'Known by name' can feel like surveillance if tied to data.

candidates.title: Two-Tap Treat
candidates.core_idea: A gift that only works together. You send someone a small treat (a coffee, a pastry, a cinema ticket) as a prepaid token at a participating local venue. It cannot be redeemed by one person alone: it unlocks only when both cards or phones tap at the same place at the same time. Money becomes the excuse to reach out, and the 'imposition' of inviting someone is replaced by a gift with a built-in plan.
candidates.brand_connection: Turns the act of paying into the act of meeting. It is Priceless inverted: money that is only worth something when shared. It uses Mastercard's tap technology, tokenisation and merchant network in a way no other payment brand has a reason to own.
expected_strengths: Behaviourally sharp: it lowers the hardest barrier, which is making the first move.
Platformable: it works as a product, a ritual, local-merchant partnerships, physical cards, gifting campaigns and seasonal moments.
A tangible, demonstrable mechanic that makes a strong film and PR story without saying the word 'lonely'.
main_concerns: If the recipient doesn't redeem, the sender may feel rejected.
Needs merchant onboarding and a simple tech build.
Could be seen as just another gift-card scheme if the 'only together' rule is not central.

candidates.title: The Unspent Hour
candidates.core_idea: A cultural provocation: for one day a year, Mastercard encourages people to spend time instead of money. Cards pause at national retail chains for one hour (a 'Priceless Hour', with exemptions for essentials) while city-wide free community tables, games and performances fill the space, supported by Mastercard and local partners.
candidates.brand_connection: A bold, memorable reversal in which a payments brand pauses its own product to make a point about what matters, echoing Priceless.
expected_strengths: Highly provocative and headline-friendly.
Clear emotional contrast with the category.
Strong film and PR potential.
main_concerns: Commercially risky and likely to frustrate merchants and customers.
One-day stunt with little lasting behaviour change.
May seem hypocritical for a payments company to ask people not to pay.

reasons_for_selection: It targets the real barrier, which is the awkwardness of making the first move, with a behavioural mechanic rather than a message.
It is the most ownable by Mastercard: it depends on tap technology, tokenised payments and a merchant network, and it dramatises the Priceless idea through a product behaviour.
It does not label or target 'lonely people', so it invites everyone and avoids stigma and data-privacy issues.

It is a platform that can scale from a local café pilot to national gifting moments, family use (a grandchild sending a treat to a grandparent) and workplace use, and every instance generates content.
It creates real transactions and local merchant footfall, so it is commercially credible as well as emotionally resonant.

rejected.reason: The insight is clever, but it frames solo living as a problem and ties the campaign to pricing deals that depend on many merchants. It describes the cost of being alone rather than helping anyone connect.
Warm and credible, but too close to existing 'chat checkout' ideas and too passive. It gives consumers nothing to do and has weaker distinctiveness and a privacy risk around 'known by name'.
Bold and headline-grabbing, but it is a one-day stunt that risks merchant and consumer backlash and sits oddly with Mastercard's role in enabling commerce. It offers little lasting behaviour change.

revisions_after_selection.change: Unredeemed Two-Tap Treats roll over into a community pool that funds free 'Two-Tap' tables at local venues, instead of simply refunding the sender.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Removes the sense of failure or rejection for senders and ensures every gift creates connection somewhere.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a soft 'reschedule' option so the recipient can propose a new time with one tap, and the sender is told only 'they'd love to, later', never that it was declined.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Protects both parties from awkwardness and keeps the mechanic low-pressure.

revisions_after_selection.change: Positioned the launch around 'someone you've lost touch with' and family use (e.g. grandchild to grandparent), not just friends, and added physical paired cards handed out in partner cafés.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Broadens relevance beyond digitally native users, including older adults who may be most isolated, and avoids the idea feeling like another app.

revisions_after_selection.change: Made the campaign explicitly opt-in with no use of spending data to identify or target lonely people, and stated this publicly.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Maintains trust in a financial brand and avoids the stigma and privacy risks of inferring emotional states.

final_proposal.title: Two-Tap Treat
final_proposal.idea: Reaching out feels like an imposition, so we give people a reason. Two-Tap Treat lets you send a friend, relative or someone you've lost touch with a small treat at a local café, bakery or cinema. The catch: it only unlocks when both of you tap at the same place, at the same time. Money that only works together. Mastercard turns the act of paying into the act of meeting, using tap technology and its local merchant network. Unclaimed treats flow into a community pool that funds free tables for strangers, so no gift is ever wasted. It is opt-in, privacy-first and never labels anyone as lonely. It starts in neighbourhood cafés with paired physical cards, then scales to family gifting, workplaces and seasonal moments. Priceless, made practical.
follow_up_questions: What other everyday payment moments (splitting a bill, a tip, a round of drinks, a subscription) could be redesigned so they require, or reward, doing something together?

How could the 'only works together' mechanic be adapted for people who cannot easily meet in person, such as long-distance family or housebound older adults, without losing the sense of shared presence?
Which local merchants or community spaces would benefit most from a connection-driving footfall boost, and what would they need from the brand to take part beyond discounts?

task_understanding.focus: The first paycheck is a huge emotional milestone, but it is usually documented through a number on a screen or a dull payslip. Canva's opportunity is to own the moment that comes before the money: the first thing someone made that someone else valued enough to pay for. That links a universal life event to Canva's core truth, that creating is how people become professionals, and it reaches the freelancers, small business owners, students and new hires who make up Canva's growth base.
assumptions: Canva is widely seen as a friendly, democratizing design tool, and is under-recognized as the place where first professional work gets made and paid for.
The category (B2B SaaS and productivity) communicates through efficiency and features. Emotional, human storytelling is a differentiator here.
The audience spans first-time employees, freelancers, side-hustlers, solo founders and the managers or HR teams who onboard them. Many of them already made something in Canva to earn that money.
People remember the work and the feeling of their first paycheck far better than the amount. The amount can also trigger comparison, shame or privacy concerns.
The first paycheck means different things across cultures and life stages (a gift to parents, proof of independence, a first rent payment), so the idea must be flexible rather than tied to one story.
A social, user-generated campaign will work only if the participation format is extremely easy to make and share, which suits Canva's template model.

candidates.title: Welcome to Payday: the HR Moment Kit
candidates.core_idea: Treat the first payday as an onboarding moment employers can design. Canva gives HR and managers a 'First Payday' kit: a team-signed card, a short celebration visual, and a 'what your first month of work produced' recap that arrives alongside the first payslip.
candidates.brand_connection: Speaks directly to Canva's B2B and team-collaboration positioning. Shows Canva Teams, brand kits and shared workspaces as tools for culture, not just slides.
expected_strengths: Clear B2B relevance and a direct path to team and enterprise adoption.
Easy to turn into templates, a landing page and HR-community content.
Warm, human angle for a category that is usually dry.
main_concerns: Less culturally resonant with the public, so weak earned-media potential.
Reaches employees only through employers, and excludes freelancers and creators.
Risks feeling like a corporate gimmick if the payday gesture is not sincere.

candidates.title: The First Invoice
candidates.core_idea: For freelancers and side-hustlers, the first paycheck begins with an invoice they design themselves. Canva reframes the invoice as a professional coming-out moment, with a 'First Invoice' template series and a ritual of sending it with confidence.
candidates.brand_connection: Builds on Canva's functional role in small business: invoices, proposals, quotes and brand identity. A straightforward product demonstration with an emotional wrapper.
expected_strengths: Concrete product utility with measurable template usage.
Speaks to a large, growing freelancer and solopreneur audience.
Easy to support with creator partnerships and tutorials.
main_concerns: Competes with dedicated invoicing tools and can look like a feature push.
Narrow audience that excludes employees getting a first salary.
Emotional upside is limited; invoices are not an inherently shareable object.

candidates.title: The Work Behind the First Paycheck
candidates.core_idea: Nobody remembers the number, but everyone remembers what they made to earn it: the bakery menu, the wedding invitation, the first client deck, the logo for a friend's startup. Canva invites people to publish a 'First Paid' receipt, pairing the design that earned their first money with a blurred amount, the date and who paid them. final_proposal.idea: Nobody remembers the exact amount of their first paycheck. task_understanding.focus: Luxury fashion is under pressure to prove that its products last, yet repair is usually presented as a hidden after-sales service or a guilt-driven sustainability gesture. The opportunity for Dior is to make repair and reuse feel like the ultimate expression of couture: the house's savoir-faire is applied across a garment's whole life, not just at the point of sale. This turns durability from a defensive claim into a desirable, culturally interesting status signal.
assumptions: Dior's equity rests on couture craft, the ateliers, the 'petites mains', archive heritage and the New Look's reinvention of silhouette. Repair fits naturally with that equity as long as it feels like craft and not compliance.

Dior already offers repair and care services through boutiques, but they are low-visibility and not culturally famous. The campaign must make an existing capability famous rather than promise a new one. This needs validating with the client.

Target audiences are existing clients (including heirloom-minded owners of Lady Dior, Saddle and Bar jacket pieces), aspirational Gen Z and millennial buyers who engage with vintage and resale, and cultural press.
Many younger luxury consumers buy pre-owned Dior and are curious about authenticity, condition and provenance. Dior wants to stay in that conversation rather than cede it to resale platforms.
Luxury brands fear that talking about damage or secondhand goods cheapens desirability. Any idea must keep scarcity, beauty and aspiration intact.
The campaign must avoid greenwashing claims. It should be grounded in verifiable craft actions (hours, hands, techniques), not vague environmental promises.
Dior's creative leadership has recently changed. The idea should be robust enough to sit alongside any collection narrative and not depend on one designer's signature.

candidates.title: The Dior Mend
candidates.core_idea: Turn repair into a signed act of couture. The atelier creates a signature mend, a fine stitch in a Dior-specific thread, and a small numbered mark that can only be earned by a piece that has lived, been loved and been restored by the house. A repair becomes a badge of time, something that cannot be bought new. Mended pieces return with a handwritten note from the atelier hand that worked on them.
candidates.brand_connection: It puts the petites mains and the ateliers at the centre of the brand story. It extends the house's obsession with the invisible, perfect stitch into a deliberate, visible one. It also gives Dior a proprietary symbol (the mend mark) in a category where sustainability claims are generic.
expected_strengths: Reframes repair from cost and inconvenience to status and rarity, which is something only a couture house can do.
Highly visual and ownable: the mark and thread are distinctive, photographable and recognisable, so the platform can run for years.
Gives owners a reason to bring in older pieces, creating client contact and loyalty.
Naturally generates content: hands, thread, before and after, and owners' stories.
main_concerns: Risk of implying Dior products break or encouraging deliberate damage, so the framing must be about time and love, not flaws.
Operational capacity: the atelier must be able to deliver repairs at scale and with consistent quality.
Some clients will want invisible repair, so a visible mark must be optional.

candidates.title: Dior Lineage
candidates.core_idea: Treat every Dior piece as the first chapter of a longer ownership story. Each item gets a registered 'lineage' record, a digital and physical passport, so that when it is passed on, gifted, resold through the house, or restored, its history travels with it. Dior becomes the authoritative keeper of its own pieces' stories and the trusted route for second and third owners.
candidates.brand_connection: It builds on Dior's archive and heritage, where the house already treats its history as an asset. It positions Dior as the brand that remembers, with authentication and provenance as part of the luxury promise.
expected_strengths: Speaks to the real behaviour of resale and vintage shopping, and lets Dior capture value in that market.
Strong commercial logic: certified pre-owned and authenticated resale can bring new clients into the house.
Emotional storytelling potential around inheritance and gifting between generations.
main_concerns: More infrastructure and technology than creative platform, so it risks feeling like a service launch rather than a cultural idea.

Passport and traceability schemes are becoming common across luxury, so the idea may not feel ownable enough.

candidates.title: Reborn from the Archive

expected_strengths: Spectacular, press-worthy and fashion-world relevant, so it would earn attention at show moments.
Gives the creative team room for bold, collectible, craft-led output.

main_concerns: It speaks to reuse of material far more than to everyday repair, so it only partly answers the brief.

Upcycling by luxury houses can appear as a PR gesture without a measurable impact.

candidates.title: Made to Change
candidates.core_idea: Design and sell selected pieces as lifelong garments that are built to be altered: hems, seams and structures designed for let-out, re-cutting and re-proportioning as bodies, tastes and decades change. expected_strengths: A strong product truth: it changes how pieces are made, not just how they are marketed.

Creates ongoing client service touchpoints.

Visually impressive but narrow in reach and focused on reuse of materials rather than the repair of clients' own pieces. It risks reading as a one-off PR gesture and is better kept as a possible show-moment extension.

Substantively meaningful, but it depends on product design and lifetime service commitments beyond a campaign's remit, and it does not address the large number of existing Dior pieces already owned. It is better suited as a long-term product principle.

revisions_after_selection.change: Made the visible mend optional: owners choose between an invisible restoration and a signed mend.

revisions_after_selection.change: Reframed the mark as 'earned by time, never bought new', and removed any imagery of damage or deliberate distressing.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This avoids implying that Dior products are fragile or that clients should damage them, and protects the desirability and polish that luxury depends on.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a lightweight provenance element from C2: each mend is numbered and logged with the piece's story.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It strengthens the sense of collectability and gives resale and vintage buyers a reason to value mended pieces higher, not lower.

revisions_after_selection.change: Planned a phased pilot: a few iconic pieces and a handful of cities first, with capacity limits stated openly as part of the scarcity.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Atelier capacity is finite, and being open about it keeps the promise credible and avoids service failures that would undermine the whole idea.

revisions_after_selection.change: Centred the campaign on the atelier hands and the owners' stories rather than on models or environmental claims.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It keeps the idea rooted in verifiable craft and avoids greenwashing risk, while giving the campaign a human, authentic voice.

final_proposal.title: The Dior Mend
final_proposal.idea: Dior turns repair into the rarest thing the house can give: a mark that can't be bought, only earned. The atelier creates a signature mend, a fine stitch in a Dior-grey thread with a small numbered label, applied to pieces that have lived, been loved and been restored by the petites mains. Owners can choose an invisible repair or a signed one. Each returns with a handwritten note from the atelier hand that worked on it. The campaign films the hands, not the models, and the stories of people who kept their pieces: a Bar jacket worn for decades, a Lady Dior passed down. Which pieces and owner stories in Dior's history, or in clients' wardrobes, would make the most moving first chapter of this campaign?
How could the idea extend beyond Dior's own products, for instance to a client's much-loved non-Dior item, without losing exclusivity or craft integrity?

task_understanding.focus: The first paycheck is a milestone that has lost its physical ritual. Direct deposit turned a framed-worthy object into a banking notification. The opportunity is for Canva to give this moment a tangible, shareable form and tie it to Canva's B2B and team use, without becoming a finance brand. The campaign must show that Canva is where work gets made, valued and celebrated, not only where decks and posters get designed.
assumptions: Canva's brand promise is that anyone can design. The first paycheck is a 'first time I was valued for what I make' moment, so there is a natural emotional bridge.

Although the category is B2B SaaS, Canva's growth runs through individuals who bring it into work (students, freelancers, new hires, small business owners). A people-first campaign can still drive team and workplace adoption.
The audience is anyone getting a first paycheck: teens, graduates, career changers, immigrants, people re-entering work, and freelancers. It is not only Gen Z.
The amount is private and sometimes shameful or anxiety-inducing. The campaign must work without disclosing any figure.
Payslips and bank details are sensitive. Any idea that needs users to upload financial documents creates trust and compliance risk.
People already post first-paycheck stories on social media, so a native, shareable artifact will travel organically.
No budget constraints beyond a typical platform campaign are specified; the idea should be buildable mainly from Canva's own templates, product and community.

candidates.title: Frame the First One
candidates.core_idea: Direct deposit killed the ritual of holding your first paycheck, so Canva brings the keepsake back. A 'First Paycheck' template family turns the moment into a frameable artifact: the date, the job, what you did that week, who you told first, and the amount as an optional, hideable element. Employers and teams can also send one to new hires. The line of thinking is: the number is private, the milestone isn't.
candidates.brand_connection: It uses Canva's core skill, turning an ordinary moment into something designed and shareable in minutes. Team features (shared templates, brand kits, team-signed cards) give it a B2B route in through new-hire onboarding.
expected_strengths: Rooted in a real cultural loss (the physical paycheck), which gives a clear and emotional insight
Product-led: the campaign is the template, so participation equals product usage

Works across ages and life stages, not only graduates
main_concerns: Needs a strong visual signature so it does not read as just another template pack
The B2B link (employer kits) must be genuinely useful, or it feels like a bolt-on
Some people have negative or complicated feelings about first jobs and pay

candidates.title: Paid in Canva
candidates.core_idea: Target freelancers and side-hustlers whose first paycheck is an invoice they wrote themselves. Celebrate the first invoice marked 'paid' with Canva invoice, quote and proposal templates, and a 'first paid' badge users can share.
candidates.brand_connection: Directly showcases Canva's business documents, brand kits and small-business tooling, and fits the B2B category.
expected_strengths: Clear product utility and conversion path
Speaks to the creator and small-business economy, a core Canva segment
Easy to measure through template use and upgrades
main_concerns: Narrower emotional resonance than a universal first-paycheck story
Invoice templates are a crowded, commoditised space
Reads as a functional promotion rather than an idea about the topic

candidates.title: The Résumé That Got Paid
candidates.core_idea: Everything before the first paycheck was designed. Invite people to share the Canva résumé, portfolio or application that landed their first job, stamped with a 'Hired' mark, and tell the story of the first paycheck it led to.
candidates.brand_connection: Canva is already a leading résumé and portfolio tool, so the campaign connects a heavily used product to its outcome.
expected_strengths: Proof-based storytelling with real user outcomes

Connects job-seeking tools to the paycheck as the payoff
main_concerns: Design-heavy résumés can conflict with ATS and recruiter preferences, creating reputational risk

final_proposal.title: Frame the First One
final_proposal.idea: Direct deposit turned the first paycheck from an object you could hold into a notification you swipe away. Canva brings the keepsake back. The amount is hidden by default, because the number is private but the milestone isn't. No payslip uploads, ever. task_understanding.focus: Luxury buyers treat repair as an embarrassing last resort, something done quietly and late. Dior has the ateliers, skills and archive to make repair and reuse a visible mark of desirability instead of a sustainability footnote. The campaign should make an owner of a repaired or reworked Dior piece feel more proud, not less.
assumptions: Dior already offers repair and restoration through its ateliers and boutiques, but awareness is low and the service is seen as admin, not as craft.
The audience is mainly 25-45 aspirational and established luxury buyers, plus a younger group who buy resale and vintage Dior and care about longevity.
Dior's credibility rests on couture craft, named artisans, heritage pieces (Bar jacket, Lady Dior, Saddle) and the idea of timelessness. Any idea should use these, not a generic eco message.
Luxury audiences distrust sustainability claims that sound like marketing, so the campaign should show actions and craft, not make unverified environmental statements.
Resale and secondhand are growing in luxury, and brands that ignore them lose control of the story of their own products.
Dior's tone is elegant, restrained and emotional. It should not look like a thrift or DIY campaign.

candidates.title: Signed, Again
candidates.core_idea: Every repair done by a Dior atelier is signed by the artisan who did it, with a small discreet mark and a named entry in the piece's repair passport. Repair becomes a second act of authorship and a chapter in the object's story, and it adds to the piece's provenance. The campaign introduces the artisans, the marks and the owners who proudly show their repaired pieces.
candidates.brand_connection: It builds on Dior's strongest asset, the hands behind the house, and on couture's habit of crediting makers. It treats the atelier as the star and fits the brand's belief that a Dior piece is made to last.
expected_strengths: Clear and easy to understand: repair = a signature.
Gives a real product and service change that can be tracked, not just a message.
Raises the status of repair and may support resale value through documented care.
Platformable across film, in-boutique, social, press and a collectible passport.
main_concerns: Needs atelier capacity and consistent turnaround times.
Some owners may want invisible repairs, so the signature must be optional.
Risk of seeming like an add-on unless the service is accessible and clearly priced.

candidates.title: The Handover
candidates.core_idea: A campaign about passing Dior pieces between generations and owners. Dior invites people to bring in a bag or jacket they received from someone, restores it, and records its lineage in a registry. Films and stories follow real handovers, such as mother to daughter or friend to friend, ending with the piece being restored for its next owner.
candidates.brand_connection: It draws on Dior's heritage and family history, the emotional pull of icons like the Lady Dior, and the promise of timelessness.
expected_strengths: Strong emotional storytelling with real human material.
Encourages reuse in a way that feels warm, not technical.
Easy to collect user stories and extend over years.
main_concerns: Closely resembles heirloom and legacy campaigns already used by other luxury and watch brands.
Mostly serves people who already own an icon piece, which is a narrow audience.
Risk of sentimentality without a clear new behavior.

candidates.title: Wear It Out
candidates.core_idea: A cultural reframe that celebrates signs of use: creases, scuffs, softened leather and faded edges as proof a piece has been lived in. Campaign imagery shows well-worn Dior on real people, and the atelier offers a choice between restoring a piece to new or keeping its patina and only reinforcing it.
candidates.brand_connection: It plays against the pristine image of luxury and gives Dior a confident, modern voice about what ownership means, while still anchoring on quality that ages well.
expected_strengths: Provocative and surprising for a luxury house.
Speaks to younger audiences who prefer lived-in style.
Has strong visual potential.
main_concerns: Could be read as encouraging neglect or as an excuse for poor durability.
Pristine presentation is central to the luxury experience, so it might clash with store and merchandise standards.
Gives less of a concrete service or action than other options.

candidates.title: Remade at Dior
candidates.core_idea: Owners send in old or damaged Dior pieces that cannot be repaired in the usual way, and the atelier remakes them into something new, such as a jacket turned into a bag or scarves into a lining. Selected remakes are shown in a small seasonal capsule alongside atelier offcuts and leftover fabric.
candidates.brand_connection: It uses couture's skill at transformation and the house's design creativity, and gives reuse a fashion angle instead of a repair-only one.
expected_strengths: Creative and news-worthy with strong visual output.
Extends the idea of reuse beyond restoring to reimagining.
Can attract fashion press and designer talent.
main_concerns: Requires design and production resources and is hard to scale.
Risk of diluting original archive pieces or the brand's design codes.
Customers may worry about handing over valuable items to be cut up.

reasons_for_selection: It gives repair real status by crediting the people who do it, which tackles the actual barrier: repair feels like a flaw, not a mark of care.
It is built on a real Dior asset, the ateliers and artisans, so it feels credible and avoids vague green claims.
It includes a concrete product change (signature plus repair passport) that can be launched, measured and extended.
It is simple to explain and flexible enough to cover bags, shoes, tailoring and other categories, and it can include elements of the other ideas, such as handovers, later.

rejected.reason: Emotionally strong, but the heirloom angle is familiar in luxury, it speaks mostly to owners of icon pieces, and it introduces no new behavior. It works better as a story strand inside C1.

Bold and interesting, but it risks suggesting neglect and conflicts with the pristine standards of luxury. It also offers less of a practical action. Parts of its patina choice can be used in the repair options.

Creative and press-friendly, but costly, hard to scale and risky for archive pieces and brand codes. It focuses on reinvention more than the core client topic of repair, and it can be a later capsule.

revisions_after_selection.change: Made the artisan signature optional, with choices of a visible mark, a hidden mark or a digital-only record.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Some owners want repairs to be invisible, and forcing a mark would reduce acceptance.

revisions_after_selection.change: Extended the idea from bags to ready-to-wear, shoes and accessories, and added clear repair pricing and turnaround times in the plan.
revisions_after_selection.reason: A campaign that only serves the most iconic pieces would feel exclusive and narrow, and unclear cost or waiting times would undermine trust.

revisions_after_selection.change: Removed any environmental statistics or sustainability claims from the creative and focused on craft and care.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Unverified claims risk accusations of greenwashing, and the audience responds better to demonstrated craft.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added fair credit and consent for the artisans who appear and sign, including options not to be named publicly.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Putting individuals at the center of a campaign raises questions of recognition, privacy and workload that must be handled properly.

revisions_after_selection.change: Included a repair passport that can transfer to the next owner, linking to resale.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This captures the best part of the handover idea and gives repair a clear value for secondhand buyers.

final_proposal.title: Signed, Again
final_proposal.idea: Dior treats repair as a second act of making. Every piece restored in a Dior atelier can be signed by the artisan who repaired it, with a discreet mark and a named entry in a repair passport that travels with the piece to its next owner. The campaign shows the hands, the benches and the owners who wear their repaired Dior with pride. A Bar jacket, a Lady Dior or a pair of shoes is no longer less perfect after repair. It has another author and a longer story. Owners choose a visible mark, a hidden one or a digital record only. Repair becomes something to show, not hide.
follow_up_questions: What would the signature look like so it feels unmistakably Dior, such as a thread color, a stitch or a stamp, and where would it sit on different products?
How could the repair passport be used by secondhand buyers and resale platforms without Dior losing control of authenticity?
Which real owner or artisan stories would be most surprising and convincing, and how could they be found without turning the campaign into a staged testimonial?

task_understanding.focus: Luxury fashion's sustainability story is dominated by new materials and recycled fabrics, while the most radical sustainable act, keeping a garment alive for decades, is what couture has always done. The opportunity is for Dior to make repair and reuse a mark of prestige rather than a concession to thrift, so that a mended Dior piece becomes more desirable than a pristine one, and to turn its atelier heritage into a living service rather than an archive.

Luxury buyers increasingly worry about greenwashing and see 'conscious' collections as marketing, so proof through action is more credible than claims.
Younger luxury audiences (Gen Z and younger millennials) already buy pre-owned and vintage Dior, such as the Saddle bag revival, and value provenance and story over newness.

candidate.title: The Second Signature
candidate.core_idea: Every time a Dior piece is repaired, the atelier hand who restores it adds a small, discreet, numbered 'second signature' (a stitch, a thread colour, a stamped inner mark) to the garment or bag. The piece then carries two authorships: Monsieur Dior's design and the repairer's hand. Repair is no longer erasure of damage but the addition of a chapter. The campaign celebrates 'the mend as the new monogram': visible, proud, collectible. It launches with a series of film and photographic portraits of real owners and their worn, repaired Dior pieces (a grandmother's Bar jacket reworked for a granddaughter, a Lady Dior carried through three decades), shot like fashion portraits with the repairer credited as co-author. candidate.brand_connection: Dior was founded on the idea that the hand makes the difference, and Christian Dior himself built a house of lasting silhouettes, not seasonal disposability. task_understanding.focus: In luxury, repair and reuse are usually treated as a back-of-house after-sales service, or as a sustainability footnote that sits awkwardly beside the endless newness of the runway. The opportunity for Dior is to make repair and reuse feel like the most couture thing the House does, rather than an apology for making things. Dior's own heritage supports this: hand-built construction, a singular atelier culture, and the idea that a garment is made for one person and one body. The campaign should make keeping, re-fitting and passing on a Dior piece feel desirable, status-bearing and emotionally rich, without sounding like greenwashing and without encouraging people to buy more.
assumptions: Dior's pieces, particularly tailoring, ready-to-wear and leather goods such as the Lady Dior and Saddle bags, are built with couture-derived techniques that make re-cutting, restoring and refinishing feasible, though not every item or material can be repaired.

The client wants a brand-building idea with a credible service behind it, not a pure awareness stunt. Any promise must be something the House can operationally deliver, so scale, pricing and eligibility need to be confirmed with Dior.

Dior's audience spans longtime clients, aspirational younger buyers, and a large pool of secondhand and vintage owners. Many already repair, alter or resell pieces through third parties, which are channels Dior does not control.

Luxury consumers worry about greenwashing and about the sector's overproduction. Silence on the topic is a risk, but preachy or statistic-led communication would clash with Dior's tone of desire and craft.
The strongest emotional territory is the owner's relationship with a piece over time (bodies change, life stages change, pieces are inherited), more than environmental guilt.
Dior's discretion and exclusivity must be preserved. Anything that looks like a discount, a thrift programme or mass-market recycling would dilute the brand.

Current references (the New Look and Bar jacket, petites mains, 30 Avenue Montaigne, the Lady Dior's history) are used as cultural touchpoints. Specific facts and service details should be verified with the House before launch.

final_proposal.idea: Dior has always sold the first fitting: the moment a piece is made for you. Second Fitting sells the next one. task_understanding.focus: Dior sells desire for the new, but its real claim to luxury is that its objects outlive trends and owners. Repair and reuse is usually told as an eco-obligation, with grey, apologetic, 'fixing' language. The opportunity is to make repair and reuse feel more desirable than buying new, by showing that Dior craftsmanship gets richer with time and with every pair of hands that has touched it. The campaign should move repair from a hidden after-sales service to a visible, culturally charged act of couture, and should also help the House reclaim the second-life market now controlled by third-party resale platforms.
assumptions: Dior already offers repair and care services and has deep atelier and archive resources, but these are under-communicated and feel transactional or invisible.
The audience is a mix of aspirational millennials and Gen Z (drawn to vintage, visible mending and 'buy less, buy better') and established clients who own pieces they love and don't want to lose.
Luxury consumers distrust overt sustainability messaging from luxury houses and read it as greenwashing, so the idea must be rooted in craft and desire, with proof in the form of a real service.
Repair carries a stigma of damage and decline. Reframing it as authorship and legacy is more powerful than reframing it as virtue.
The House has to protect exclusivity and brand codes (elegance, femininity, savoir-faire) while making the idea feel generous and culturally current.
Operational capacity in the ateliers is limited, so the campaign must scale through storytelling and a tiered service, not unlimited free repairs.

candidates.title: Dior Lineage
candidates.core_idea: Every Dior piece that is repaired, resold or passed on is recertified by the House and gains a stitched 'lineage' label that records its owners, repairs and eras. The piece's biography becomes part of its value, so a much-loved Dior is worth more than a pristine one. Dior reclaims the resale conversation by making its own certified second-life channel.
candidates.brand_connection: Draws on Dior's archive culture, numbered couture pieces and the authority of the House to authenticate its own history. It reinforces the notion that Dior is an heirloom, not a trend.
expected_strengths: Creates a tangible system and a business model, not just a message.
Turns resale from a threat into a brand-owned asset.
Strong storytelling potential through the real histories of pieces and owners.
main_concerns: Authentication, data and logistics complexity.
Risk of cannibalising new sales or appearing to endorse a secondary market that dilutes exclusivity.
More infrastructural than emotional, so it may lack visual spark on its own.

candidates.title: The Mend Is the Signature
candidates.core_idea: Dior treats a tear, scuff or snag as an invitation for couture embroidery. The petites mains design a visible mend with the owner, such as cannage stitching, pearls along a tear or a gilded star-shaped patch. The artisan signs the mend, and the piece is recorded as 'mended by' the House. Repair becomes the most personal, most Dior act of customisation, and an imperfection becomes a mark of intimacy.
candidates.brand_connection: Puts the ateliers and the petites mains at the centre of the story. It uses Dior's embroidery vocabulary (cannage, stars, pearls) and its couture belief that the hand makes the difference. It also builds on the kind of craft the House already celebrates in its exhibitions and shows.
expected_strengths: Visually arresting and instantly shareable, and it inverts the stigma of damage.
Differentiates from competitors' care programmes by making repair creative rather than corrective.
Gives the artisans a human face and strengthens the craft narrative.
Works as a service, a film series, a window installation and a social format.
main_concerns: Risk of fetishising damage, or of being copied by people who distress new items on purpose.
Atelier capacity limits how many clients can take part.
Some clients may prefer invisible repair and need to be offered it.

candidates.title: Open Hours at Montaigne
candidates.core_idea: Dior opens a temporary repair salon where the petites mains mend any garment from anyone, whether a denim jacket, a school blazer or a cardigan, for free, in a public window. The brand gives its best skill away to everyday clothes. The mended items come with a tag that says 'Mended by Dior'.
candidates.brand_connection: Uses the prestige of the 30 Avenue Montaigne address and the artisans' skills as a gift to the city. It turns couture knowledge into a generous cultural act.
expected_strengths: Surprising and warm, and likely to generate strong press and social content.
Broadens Dior's cultural reach to people who may never buy a handbag.
Demonstrates the skill without needing to explain it.
main_concerns: Reads as a one-off PR stunt unless it is sustained.
High cost and low conversion to ongoing behaviour.
Risk of undermining exclusivity or of long queues turning into a bad experience.

candidates.title: Re-New Look
candidates.core_idea: In 1947 the New Look reshaped a world that was tired and short of fabric. Dior now invites clients to bring in older Dior pieces to be re-cut into a new silhouette: a 1990s jacket becomes a corset top, a worn scarf becomes the lining of a new bag. Reuse is framed as reinvention and as a design act, not as a retreat to the past. Each year the House's creative team sets a 'Re-New Look' brief.
candidates.brand_connection: Connects directly to the name and the founding revolution of the House: the New Look as a radical act of transformation. It links the archive to the present collection and to the creative director's vision.
expected_strengths: Frames reuse as creative and forward-looking, which is attractive to younger audiences.
Strong fit with fashion culture's love of upcycling and remixing.
Offers a natural annual platform tied to the collections.
main_concerns: Cutting up heritage pieces may offend collectors and archivists.

rejected.reason: Strategically sound but infrastructural and low on emotion. It is better as a supporting mechanism inside the chosen idea than as the campaign's creative core, and its authentication complexity and resale-cannibalisation risk are heavy for a launch.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added an 'invisible mend' option alongside the visible couture mend, so each client chooses.

revisions_after_selection.change: Ruled out any pre-distressed or intentionally damaged new products, and positioned mends as only ever created from real wear and real stories.

revisions_after_selection.change: Borrowed a light version of C1: the artisan's signature and the mend are recorded on an inner label that travels with the piece if it is passed on or resold.

revisions_after_selection.change: Planned the idea as a permanent, tiered service with transparent timing and pricing, launched through a short live window at Montaigne (a slimmed-down version of C3).

revisions_after_selection.change: Named and credited the individual artisans in all communications.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It makes the craft human and specific, which deepens the emotional pull and supports the claim that the hand is what makes the value.

final_proposal.title: The Mend Is the Signature
final_proposal.idea: Dior turns the mend into its newest signature. Clients bring in a torn Bar jacket, a scuffed Lady Dior or a snagged silk scarf, and the petites mains answer by embroidering the damage rather than hiding it: cannage stitching, pearls along a tear, a gilded star-shaped patch. Each mend is designed with the owner, signed by the artisan and recorded on the piece's inner label, so a repaired Dior becomes more valuable, not less. Purists can choose an invisible mend. The campaign films these conversations as intimate portraits of a story, a scar and a needle. It launches with a live atelier window on Avenue Montaigne, then continues as a permanent, tiered service. The message: Dior isn't kept pristine. It's kept.

Who besides the owner should be part of a mend's story, such as the artisan, the previous owner or the next one, and how would that change what is shown and shared?

task_understanding.focus: Luxury fashion sells newness, yet Dior's real asset is the opposite: the hands, techniques and archives that let a garment be rebuilt, re-cut and loved for decades. assumptions: Dior's couture heritage (the atelier, the petites mains, toiles, the Bar jacket, archive re-editions) is a more credible basis for a repair story than any claim about materials or footprint.

The primary audience is aspirational and established luxury buyers aged 25-45 who already buy pre-owned, vintage or heirloom pieces and are skeptical of green claims. A secondary audience is cultural tastemakers who treat clothes as personal archives.
Repair and reuse must feel emotional, beautiful and exclusive. Any message about guilt, scarcity or austerity would clash with Dior's brand codes of romance, craft and femininity.

candidates.title: Signed by Hand
candidates.core_idea: Turn repair from a hidden back-office service into a new couture signature. When a Dior piece is mended, the petite main who did the work embroiders a small date-and-initial mark on or near the repair. Owners choose whether the mend is invisible or celebrated. Each piece gets a ledger of its life, and the mended pieces become collectible proof of a life well lived.
candidates.brand_connection: Dior's identity is made by hands, and the houses' petites mains are usually anonymous. This idea makes them the authors of a second chapter, extending the logic of couture ('made to measure, made to last') to every piece ever sold.
expected_strengths: Reframes damage as a mark of value, so there is a real shift in meaning, not just a message.
Highly visual and platformable: film, atelier salons, a show of mended pieces, social content from owners, collectible marks.
Gives craftspeople visibility and adds to the house's craft narrative.
main_concerns: It needs real atelier capacity, so a pilot must be scoped carefully.
Visible mending could be seen as spoiling an expensive item unless the owner has real choice.
It risks becoming a logo-style 'mark' unless the signature stays personal and non-branded.

candidates.title: Provenance Passport
candidates.core_idea: Build a certified second-life circuit for Dior pieces, where each item travels with a passport recording its previous owners' notes, the occasions it was worn and any repairs. Resale becomes the continuation of a story, with a new owner's chapter added each time.
candidates.brand_connection: It draws on Dior's archive culture and the idea that the house's pieces are heirloom objects. Authenticated resale also protects the brand against counterfeits and uncontrolled secondary markets.
expected_strengths: Strong commercial logic: it captures the resale market and brings new customers in through lower entry points.
Rich storytelling material from real owners.
Digital authentication adds trust and traceability.
main_concerns: Heavily category-aligned: many luxury brands already run authenticated resale programs.
It could encourage more buying and selling rather than keeping pieces, which weakens the repair half of the brief.
Needs privacy handling for owner stories and a lot of operational infrastructure.

candidates.title: The Next Fitting
candidates.core_idea: Invite families to bring an inherited Dior piece to the atelier to be re-cut for the next wearer, such as a grandmother's dress becoming a granddaughter's. The campaign documents the fitting as a ritual: two generations, one garment and a couturier's tape measure between them.
candidates.brand_connection: Alteration and reinvention are in Dior's DNA, from the New Look onward. It also positions the house as the keeper of family memory, which fits Dior's emotional and romantic codes.
expected_strengths: Deeply emotional and easily turned into films and long-form content.
Shows reuse as transformation rather than preservation.
Strong appeal to PR and editorial coverage.
main_concerns: Narrow audience: only people who already own an inherited Dior piece can take part.
Emotional storytelling can feel sentimental or like a standard 'heritage' ad.
Hard to scale beyond a series of showcase stories.

candidates.title: The Mending Counter
candidates.core_idea: Dior opens a temporary counter where anyone can bring any garment from any brand, even a cheap T-shirt, and have it mended using couture technique. The house lends its hands to everyday clothing, turning a luxury skill into a public gesture.
candidates.brand_connection: It shows that Dior's craft is a skill and not just a status symbol, and generates surprise by having a luxury house care for ordinary clothes.
expected_strengths: Provocative and highly shareable, with strong earned-media potential.
Reaches a much wider audience and a younger demographic.
Makes the craft tangible and generous.
main_concerns: Risk of seeming like a stunt or of diluting exclusivity.

task_understanding.focus: Loneliness is rising, yet it is stigmatised, so people rarely say 'I'm lonely' or join anything labelled as a loneliness fix. Mastercard has an unexpected link to the problem: its core promise of frictionless, instant payment has quietly removed one of the last small human exchanges in daily life, the chat at the counter. For many people who live alone, work remotely or are older, that exchange is the only conversation of the day. The opportunity is for Mastercard to put human connection back into the transaction, using its Priceless platform and its small-business and community footprint.
assumptions: Mastercard's long-standing 'Priceless' positioning (moments money can't buy) gives it permission to speak about human connection without seeming opportunistic, if the action is real.
Frictionless payment is a net benefit, but it has a social cost: self-checkout, tap-and-go and delivery apps have reduced casual contact, and Mastercard can admit this honestly.
Many lonely people won't self-identify, so the campaign should create low-pressure, unlabelled reasons to linger rather than 'loneliness services'.
Small local businesses (cafés, barbers, corner shops, laundromats) are the most natural places for everyday belonging, and Mastercard already has relationships and credibility with them.
The core audience is adults living alone, remote workers, recent movers and older people, with a secondary audience of merchants and the wider public who can notice and act.
Mastercard should not use individual transaction data to identify lonely people; any insight use must be aggregate, anonymised and opt-in.
The campaign must lead with action and merchant participation, not an emotional film alone, to avoid accusations of 'caring-washing'.

candidate.title: The Slow Lane
candidate.core_idea: The world's most efficient payments network deliberately builds back the thing it removed: a reason to linger. Mastercard launches 'The Slow Lane', a programme for neighbourhood businesses to create unhurried, welcoming moments at the point of payment. Participating merchants get a simple kit: a 'No rush' counter or lane, terminal messaging that appears after the tap ('Stay a while?'), a prompt card with easy conversation starters for staff, and a slowed-down, more open variant of the Mastercard tap sound that works as an audible 'pause'. Participating spots appear on a Priceless-powered map. Nobody is ever labelled lonely. The invitation is simply 'no rush', which anyone can accept without admitting anything. Campaign content shows five-minute, unhurried exchanges as the hero moment, and Mastercard shares it as a challenge: 'Be a regular somewhere.' Being a regular is the lowest-barrier form of belonging.
candidate.brand_connection: It turns Priceless from a tagline into a service: the most valuable part of a purchase is often the human moment around it. It is also a surprising, credible admission by the brand known for speed that sometimes slower is better. It uses assets Mastercard already owns (the sonic identity, the terminal and checkout moment, small-business programmes, Priceless experiences and mapping) rather than inventing a new platform.
expected_strengths: Counterintuitive brand stance ('we chose to be less fast, on purpose') that is memorable, shareable and press-worthy.
Fits the payment moment exactly, so the idea lives where Mastercard actually operates, not in a generic wellbeing space.
Removes stigma by offering unlabelled, low-pressure participation; the 'regular' is aspirational rather than pitiable.
Highly platformable: sonic pause, terminal messages, a 'regulars' map, merchant stories, city-by-city rollouts, partnerships with charities and local councils.

Produces real-world proof and user-generated stories that can fuel content over time.
main_concerns: Risk of trivialising loneliness: a friendlier checkout won't fix a serious social problem, so the campaign must be modest in its claims and partner with credible loneliness organisations.

Staff burden and variable execution at merchants; kit must be extremely simple and staff must feel it is optional and not scripted.

Scaling beyond a pilot of cooperative merchants, and avoiding 'wellness-washing' if participation is thin.
Terminal messaging may need approval from acquirers and device makers in different markets.

final_proposal.idea: Tap-to-pay made paying silent. For many people who live alone, the checkout was the last daily conversation. Cafés, barbers and corner shops opt in with a simple kit: a 'No rush' counter, a terminal that says 'Stay a while?' after the tap, and a slowed-down Mastercard tap sound that works like an audible pause. task_understanding.focus: Dior's opportunity is to make repair and reuse feel like the highest form of luxury rather than a sustainability concession. Luxury already claims 'forever' pieces, yet most consumers (especially under-40s) see repair as an afterthought, a hassle, or a sign of brand guilt. The campaign should turn repair and reuse into a desirable, culturally visible act that deepens emotional ownership and extends Dior's couture heritage of the atelier into everyday wardrobes.
assumptions: Dior's strongest equity is craftsmanship, the atelier, and the 'Christian Dior' founder mythology, which makes repair a credible rather than opportunistic territory.
Brand risk is greenwashing perception: luxury houses sell newness, so any repair message must be backed by real services (repair, resale, restoration, alteration) and not only communications.
The core audience is two-sided: aspirational Gen Z/Millennials who buy vintage and resale, and established clients with decades-old Dior pieces in their wardrobes.
Many owners already hold emotionally loaded Dior items (a mother's Saddle bag, a Bar jacket, a Lady Dior gift) and hesitate to use or alter them for fear of damaging value.
Resale and vintage culture has made 'pre-loved' prestigious, so a Dior-authored version of reuse can compete with third-party platforms for control of the narrative.
The client has real or plannable repair infrastructure (ateliers, boutique services, possibly a certified pre-owned or restoration program), which the campaign can showcase and scale.
The tone must remain elevated, poetic and couture-led, not preachy or utilitarian.

candidates.title: The Scar Is the Signature
candidates.core_idea: Reframe visible repair as a new Dior codification of beauty. Dior atelier artisans repair worn pieces using deliberate, signature 'Dior mends': toile-de-Jouy stitching, cannage patterning, or gold thread in the style of kintsugi. Each repair becomes a design feature that marks the item as lived-in and loved. The campaign celebrates the imperfection as proof of a life well lived with Dior.
candidates.brand_connection: Draws on cannage, toile de Jouy, and the atelier's savoir-faire. Makes the repair itself a piece of Dior craft and a new collectible aesthetic.
expected_strengths: Highly visual and shareable; repair becomes a status marker.
Creates a distinct ownable design language for repair.
Could extend into limited 'mended' editions and collaborations with artists.
main_concerns: Kintsugi-style imagery is a familiar trope and risks cliché if executed literally.
Some clients may prefer invisible restoration and see visible mending as damage.
Needs careful guardrails to avoid seeming to glamorize wear in a way that undermines product perfection.

candidates.title: Dior Heirloom Passport
candidates.core_idea: Every Dior piece gets a living provenance record, a 'passport' that logs owners, repairs, journeys, and stories across generations. Repair visits add stamps and handwritten atelier notes. A piece with many stamps becomes more valuable and more storied, not less. The campaign invites people to submit the stories behind their pieces and reveals the most remarkable passports.
candidates.brand_connection: Builds on Dior's heritage, authentication, and clienteling. Positions the house as keeper of memory, not just seller of objects.
expected_strengths: Rooted in a real product truth: Dior pieces do circulate across generations.
Ties repair, resale and reuse into one system and raises resale value, which benefits the brand.
Generates rich human-interest content from real clients.
main_concerns: Digital passports are an established idea (blockchain IDs, resale authentication) and may feel not novel.
Operationally heavy: requires data, systems and consistent atelier participation.
Could read as a resale-value pitch rather than an emotional proposition.

candidates.title: Dior Second Collection
candidates.core_idea: Each season, Dior's creative teams design a collection built entirely from reclaimed or returned Dior material: deadstock, retired samples, and unrepairable pieces donated by clients. Creatives rework them into one-of-a-kind items, presented on the runway as a 'second life' show-within-the-show.
candidates.brand_connection: Plays to Dior's runway theatricality and creative-director authorship. Links the reuse theme to fashion's highest-attention moment.
expected_strengths: Spectacle and press value; strong fit with show culture.
Elevates reuse to creative ambition, not compromise.
Easy for the media to understand.
main_concerns: Upcycled capsules are common among luxury and streetwear brands, so the idea is less distinctive.
Focuses on the brand's production, not on customers' own pieces, so it is weaker on repair.
One-off scarcity may be seen as just another limited drop.

candidates.title: The Wear-It-Out Dare
candidates.core_idea: Challenge the fear of ruining precious things. Dior says: stop keeping your best pieces in the dust bag. The campaign encourages clients to actually live in their Dior (rain, dancing, travel, late nights) with a promise that the atelier will take care of whatever happens. A 'Come Back to Us' repair promise turns damage into a story, and the campaign shows wear and tear as evidence of joy. Real clients return pieces to the atelier with stories of the night that did it.
candidates.brand_connection: Dior is about femininity, celebration, and joy in dressing. This idea permits use rather than preservation, and positions repair as an act of care the house provides, not a burden the owner bears.
expected_strengths: Rests on a genuine human tension: luxury owners are afraid to use what they love.
Counters the 'investment piece in a closet' behavior and makes reuse frequent, not occasional.
Flexible platform: stories, atelier films, in-store repair bars, social challenges.
Emotional and warm, consistent with Dior's romantic tone.
main_concerns: Encouraging hard use might conflict with brand's pristine image if not art-directed with taste.
Needs a credible, scalable repair promise or it will backfire.
Could be misread as encouraging carelessness or consumption of repair services.

reasons_for_selection: It is built on the sharpest human insight of the four: people treat luxury as something to protect, which quietly defeats the purpose of owning it and shortens its useful life.
It makes repair the enabler of a more joyful behavior, not a guilt-driven afterthought, which suits Dior's celebratory, romantic tone.
It puts the customer's own pieces and stories at the center, so repair and reuse are lived rather than only claimed.
It is platformable: atelier repair bars, client story films, seasonal 'wear-it' moments, and a service promise can all sit under one idea.
It can absorb the best parts of the other ideas, such as a signature mending touch from C1 or provenance notes from C2, as later extensions.

rejected.reason: Visually strong but relies on a kintsugi-style trope that feels familiar, and visible mending may alienate clients who want invisible restoration. Better used as an optional service layer under the chosen idea.

Credible and valuable, but passports and provenance tracking are already common in luxury resale and lean toward system and value rhetoric over emotion. It is operationally heavy and less surprising as a campaign idea.

Great spectacle, but upcycled capsules are widely used and it centers on the brand's production, not on repair of clients' own pieces. It risks reading as a one-off show moment rather than a lasting behavior shift.

revisions_after_selection.change: Reframed the promise from 'wear it out' (which could imply carelessness) to 'live in it', with the atelier's care as the counterpart, and renamed the platform accordingly.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Avoids the reading that Dior encourages reckless use or disposability, and keeps the tone elegant and aligned to a luxury house.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a clear service backbone: a named atelier repair service with defined timelines and a guarantee, launched before or alongside communications.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Prevents greenwashing criticism and ensures the promise is real and scalable.

revisions_after_selection.change: Folded in an optional signature mending touch (from C1) and a handwritten atelier note on returned pieces (from C2) as service details, not as separate campaign ideas.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Strengthens craft storytelling and emotional ownership without diluting the single core idea.

revisions_after_selection.change: Chose stories of ordinary occasions (a rainy wedding, a missed train, a first night out) over dramatic damage, and art-directed them with couture polish.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Keeps imagery aspirational and relatable and protects the pristine brand image.

final_proposal.title: Live In It
final_proposal.idea: Dior owners guard their best pieces like museum objects, and a bag that never leaves its dust bag never gets loved. Live In It gives permission to wear Dior through rain, dancing and delays, backed by an atelier promise: whatever happens, bring it back. Repair becomes the house's act of care, not the owner's burden. Real clients return pieces with the story of the night that marked them, and the atelier mends each one, adding a small handwritten note and, if wanted, a subtle signature stitch. Films, in-boutique repair salons and client stories show the wear as proof of a life fully lived, making the most repaired Dior piece the most desirable one.
follow_up_questions: What would a repair promise need to include (speed, cost, guarantee) to feel truly generous and make people dare to use their best pieces?
How could the campaign make a repaired or well-worn piece a visible status symbol among younger vintage and resale-minded audiences?
Which real moments of joy and mishap would feel most true to Dior's world, and how can they be shown without losing couture elegance?

task_understanding.focus: The first paycheck is a rite of passage, and for many young workers it is also the first time they find out what work really is. In most first jobs, that includes making things look good: slides, flyers, social posts, one-pagers. Canva is known as a design tool, but in B2B it needs to be seen as the everyday work tool for people who were never hired as designers. The opportunity is to tie Canva to the moment a new worker realises they are being paid for more than their job title says, and to the moment they start building a case for their next paycheck.
assumptions: The primary audience is early-career employees (roughly 18-28) in non-design roles, such as marketing, operations, sales, admin and education. Secondary audiences are the managers and small-business owners who buy team plans.
The first paycheck is emotionally loaded: pride, relief, disbelief, and often a quiet anxiety about whether you deserve it. Brands usually handle it with sentimental or money-tips clichés.
Canva has strong awareness and goodwill among students and Gen Z. It has less credibility as a serious workplace tool, which is where Teams and Enterprise growth comes from.
A large share of Canva's workplace users are 'accidental designers' who picked up design as an unlisted duty rather than a chosen craft.
Canva is not a payroll or fintech company, so the campaign should borrow the paycheck as a cultural moment and not claim any financial expertise.
Any campaign that appears to criticise employers needs care, because employers are also Canva's B2B buyers.

candidates.title: The Pay Stub, Redesigned
candidates.core_idea: The first pay stub is one of the ugliest documents in modern life, yet people screenshot and keep it. Canva redesigns it into something worth framing, with templates, keepsake layouts and a 'my first paycheck' poster format.
candidates.brand_connection: It demonstrates Canva's core promise, that anything can look better and be personal, using a document everyone has seen.
expected_strengths: Simple, visual and instantly understood
Highly shareable, since people already post first-paycheck moments
Low production complexity
main_concerns: It is a one-off gimmick with little platform depth
It leans on sentimentality, which is a category cliché
It has little connection to the B2B and productivity positioning
Real pay data is sensitive, and the idea could raise privacy concerns

candidates.title: Proof of Work: The Résumé That Got Paid
candidates.core_idea: Pair the Canva résumé, portfolio or pitch that landed a job with the first paycheck it led to. Real people tell the story of one document that turned into one payday, shown as 'before and after' diptychs.
candidates.brand_connection: Canva is already part of the job-hunting journey, and this places it at the start of a career narrative.
expected_strengths: Strong user-generated content potential
Clear link between product use and a life outcome
Authentic and emotionally resonant
main_concerns: It implies Canva causes people to get hired, which creates a claims risk
It is familiar, because many brands run success-story campaigns
It speaks to job seekers and not to teams and workplaces, so it adds little for B2B

candidates.title: The Signer
candidates.core_idea: Flip the perspective to the person who signs the first paycheck: the founder or small-business owner running their first payroll. The campaign explores the weight of making someone's first income and gives them a 'welcome kit' toolset in Canva, covering offer letters, onboarding decks, team culture and brand basics.
candidates.brand_connection: It speaks directly to the B2B buyer (small business, startups) and positions Canva as the tool that helps a new company feel real and credible to its first hire.
expected_strengths: Fresh angle on the topic
Directly relevant to SMB team-plan acquisition
Emotionally honest about the responsibility of employing someone
main_concerns: It is narrower in audience and less culturally sticky
It risks drifting into HR and payroll territory, where Canva has no authority
It has less natural social virality

candidates.title: Line Item: Not in the Job Description
candidates.core_idea: Every first paycheck quietly pays for something nobody hired you for, and it is often making things look good. The campaign reveals the invisible line item on the first pay stub, 'Designing the thing nobody else wanted to design', and celebrates the accidental designer. It then gives those people a tool to make that hidden skill visible, a 'skills receipt' and a 'make the case for your next paycheck' template.
candidates.brand_connection: It reframes Canva as the workplace tool for people who are not designers. It is built around the insight that design is an everyday work skill, which supports the Teams and Enterprise story.
expected_strengths: A genuine, humorous and relatable insight that is easy to recognise and share ('me, in my first job')
Platformable: new line items, new roles, new industries
Moves Canva's perception from a student tool to a career tool

main_concerns: It could read as complaining about unpaid extra work, which might alienate employer buyers

reasons_for_selection: It has the strongest insight: the first paycheck pays for skills no one lists, and design is one of the most common of them. People recognise this immediately.
It connects Canva's strengths (accessibility, speed, design for non-designers) to the audience's real experience and to a B2B workplace context.
It is the most platformable: the 'line item' device can extend across social, out-of-home, creator partnerships, templates and workplace content.
It ends with a useful action, using Canva to document and present your contribution, which makes it both emotional and productivity-oriented.

rejected.reason: Charming, but it is a one-time artefact with a sentimental tone, little B2B relevance and a privacy risk around pay data. It is better used as a supporting activation than as the core idea.
Authentic, but it is familiar, carries claims risk about causing hires, and is aimed at job seekers more than at the workplace users and teams that matter for B2B growth.

A fresh perspective and relevant to SMB buyers, but its audience is narrow, it moves toward HR and payroll where Canva lacks credibility, and it has less cultural reach. It could be a future extension for small-business content.

revisions_after_selection.change: Reframed the tone from 'unpaid extra work' to 'hidden talent you should be recognised for'.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Avoids a grievance narrative that would put off employers and managers who buy Canva for their teams, while keeping the relatable insight.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a 'make the case for your second paycheck' output: a Canva template for a skills receipt or raise and review pitch.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Gives the idea a practical product role and a clear call to action, and ties the campaign to the paycheck and to career progression instead of general workplace humour.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a manager-side extension: 'Notice the line item', a short template managers can use to acknowledge hidden contributions.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Makes the campaign relevant to the B2B buyer and keeps it positive for both employee and employer.

revisions_after_selection.change: Anchored the visual device in the real first-paycheck moment, with an extra line added to a stylised pay stub, instead of a generic workplace theme.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Keeps the campaign clearly linked to the client's topic and gives it a recognisable, ownable look.

final_proposal.title: Line Item
final_proposal.idea: Look closely at your first pay stub and you'll find a line that isn't there: the design work nobody put in the job description. The slide deck you rescued. The flyer you made at 9pm. The onboarding doc that finally made sense. Canva reveals this missing line item and celebrates the accidental designer in every first job. People add their own line items to a stylised pay stub, with real stories shared across social, out-of-home and creator partnerships. Then Canva gives them a way to use it: a skills receipt and a 'case for your second paycheck' template to show what they really bring. A companion manager version helps teams notice the hidden contributions. The tone is proud and funny, never bitter.
follow_up_questions: What other 'invisible line items' do first jobs pay for (organising, translating, calming people down), and which of them could Canva own alongside design?
How could the campaign work for employers and managers as well as employees without turning into a pay or HR debate?
Which real people or communities (interns, teaching assistants, junior marketers, small-shop staff) would tell this story most credibly and surprisingly?
