Brand: Mastercard (category: Finance, Fintech & Insurance)
Topic from the client: loneliness

Please prepare an idea development worksheet for one campaign for this brand on this topic. The worksheet has these sections:

1. task_understanding: the problem or opportunity the campaign focuses on, and the assumptions about the brand, topic and audience.
2. candidates: exactly 4 candidate campaign directions whose core ideas differ from each other (not just different executions of one idea). For each: the core idea, how it connects to the brand, expected strengths and main concerns.
3. selection: which candidate is recommended and why, and for every other candidate why it was not recommended.
4. revisions_after_selection: changes made to the recommended idea after reviewing it, with the reason for each. Use an empty list if there are none.
5. final_proposal: the recommended idea written for a human reader (at most 150 words), plus exactly 3 open questions that would help the reader develop further ideas of their own.

Write in English. Return the worksheet as a single JSON object with this structure and nothing else:
{
  "task_understanding": {"focus": "...", "assumptions": ["..."]},
  "candidates": [
    {"id": "C1", "title": "...", "core_idea": "...", "brand_connection": "...", "expected_strengths": ["..."], "main_concerns": ["..."]},
    {"id": "C2", "...": "..."},
    {"id": "C3", "...": "..."},
    {"id": "C4", "...": "..."}
  ],
  "selection": {"selected_id": "C?", "reasons_for_selection": ["..."], "rejected": [{"id": "C?", "reason": "..."}]},
  "revisions_after_selection": [{"change": "...", "reason": "..."}],
  "final_proposal": {"title": "...", "idea": "...", "follow_up_questions": ["...", "...", "..."]}
}

reasoning.note: thinking tokens are not reported separately; output_tokens_total includes them

task_understanding.focus: Loneliness is partly a problem of initiating. Many people want company but feel that reaching out is an imposition, a risk, or too much effort. Meanwhile, the daily moments of incidental human contact (the cashier, the barista, the regular table) are being removed by the frictionless payments the industry has built. The opportunity is for Mastercard to use its most ownable asset, the moment of paying, to make connection easier to start rather than to make spending easier.
assumptions: Mastercard's 'Priceless' platform is about what money can't buy, which makes human connection a credible territory rather than an opportunistic one.
The brand has permission to act on loneliness only if it does something real and tied to payments. A sympathetic film alone would feel like cause-washing.
Loneliness carries stigma, so the campaign should avoid labelling people 'lonely' and instead make reaching out feel normal and light.
The core audience is adults 25-45 with drifting friendships (post-move, post-remote work, post-kids), plus older adults as a secondary audience. They are time-poor but cash-comfortable.
The cost of an invitation, including awkwardness and the implied 'you owe me', is a real barrier that a payment brand can lower.
Any use of transaction data must be opt-in, aggregated or minimal, and privacy-safe to protect trust.

candidates.title: The Slow Lane
candidates.core_idea: Partner with retailers, cafes and pharmacies to create 'Slow Lane' checkouts with a human who has time to chat, signalled by a Mastercard sticker. Frame it as deliberately re-adding the friction that frictionless payments removed.
candidates.brand_connection: Mastercard helped remove checkout friction. Owning that and giving some of it back is a self-aware, honest brand gesture rooted in the payment moment.
expected_strengths: Highly visual, press-friendly and culturally provocative, since a payments brand is choosing to slow down.
Directly addresses the loss of incidental contact.
Easy for retailers to join and for people to understand.
main_concerns: Reach is limited to participating stores and is hard to scale.
It can feel like a gimmick or an operational burden for staff.
It is passive, so it does not help people who stay home.

candidates.title: Table for One, Seats for More
candidates.core_idea: Priceless dining experiences where solo cardholders can opt into shared 'open tables' at local restaurants on quiet nights, unlocked by tapping a card at the door.
candidates.brand_connection: It extends Priceless Cities and its experience curation. The card becomes the ticket to meeting strangers.
expected_strengths: Delivers concrete, tangible experiences.
Supports local restaurants on slow nights, which gives a commercial win-win.
Fits Mastercard's existing experiential playbook.
main_concerns: Strangers at a table is a high-anxiety format that many lonely people will avoid.
It is a familiar pattern (supper clubs, meetup apps), so it is less surprising.
It requires heavy logistics and curation city by city.

candidates.title: Regulars
candidates.core_idea: Celebrate neighbourhood places where people are known by name, and use anonymised, aggregated Mastercard insights to reveal which local third places are vanishing and which are holding communities together. Give these places a 'Regulars' mark and fund their survival.
candidates.brand_connection: Mastercard's data and small-business commitments let it show where community lives and dies in spending patterns.
expected_strengths: A strong, ownable data-driven insight that is newsworthy.
Aligns with Mastercard's small business support.
Gives local media and cities a reason to engage.
main_concerns: The loneliness link is indirect, since it acts on places rather than people.
Data use is sensitive and could provoke surveillance concerns.
It risks becoming a CSR report rather than a behavioural idea.

candidates.title: My Treat
candidates.core_idea: The reason people don't reach out is that an invitation feels like asking for something. 'My Treat' lets anyone send a friend they've drifted from a simple invite: 'Overdue catch-up. First round's on Mastercard.' When both people tap their cards at the same participating local spot, a small amount (a coffee, a pastry) is credited. Money becomes the excuse that makes saying 'I miss you' easy.
candidates.brand_connection: The mechanic only works because of payments: two taps, one meeting. It turns Priceless into a behaviour, in which a small price unlocks something the money can't buy, which is time together.
expected_strengths: It tackles the real barrier of initiating, with a clear, shareable behaviour.
It is platformable, with versions for friends, siblings, ex-colleagues and neighbours, and it scales through small businesses.
Its proof of success is people actually meeting, not impressions.
It avoids stigma because the language is 'overdue catch-up', not 'loneliness'.
main_concerns: Cost control and fraud risk in verifying that a meeting took place.
Privacy concerns around matching two taps.
Risk of feeling like a coupon promotion rather than something meaningful.

reasons_for_selection: It addresses a specific, human barrier (inviting feels like imposing) with a mechanic that only a payment brand can deliver.
It converts the topic into action. The measure of success is real-world meetings rather than awareness.
It is destigmatised and joyful, which fits Priceless better than a sombre loneliness message.
It is highly platformable across invitations, partners, markets and seasonal moments, and supports local small businesses.

rejected.reason: Charming and provocative, but limited in scale and passive. It helps only people already out in stores, and it risks being seen as a stunt.
Asks lonely people to sit with strangers, which is the highest-anxiety route, and it is a familiar format with heavy logistics.
Insightful and good for PR, but indirect. It improves places rather than prompting human contact, and it carries data-privacy risk. It could work as a supporting layer instead.

revisions_after_selection.change: Verify the meeting through an opt-in matching of two taps at the same merchant within a set time window, with no location sharing or tracking.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Protects privacy and trust while still proving the meeting happened.

revisions_after_selection.change: Fund the treat jointly with participating local cafes and small businesses, with Mastercard covering a capped amount.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Controls cost, drives footfall to small businesses, and strengthens the local-community role.

revisions_after_selection.change: Position the invitation as an 'overdue catch-up' and avoid the word 'lonely' in the user experience, saving the loneliness story for campaign storytelling.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Reduces stigma and makes sending an invite feel normal and light.

revisions_after_selection.change: Make the invitation non-exclusive to Mastercard holders for the recipient, who can join with any payment method, with the sender's card as the anchor.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Removes a barrier for the invited person and prevents the idea from feeling like a loyalty gate.

revisions_after_selection.change: Add a limited number of invites per person per month.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Discourages abuse and makes each invitation feel meaningful.

final_proposal.title: My Treat
final_proposal.idea: We don't reach out because inviting someone feels like asking for something. So Mastercard takes care of the awkward part: the price. With My Treat, you send a friend you've drifted from a simple invite: 'Overdue catch-up. First round's on us.' When you both tap at a participating local café, bar or bakery, the first round is credited. No tracking, no sign-up for your friend, just a small push that turns 'we should catch up' into a real afternoon. Local businesses co-fund and fill quiet hours. The campaign tells stories of long-overdue reunions, invites people to nominate who they owe a catch-up, and measures success in meetings, not impressions. Priceless has always been about what money can't buy. My Treat uses a small amount of money to start it.
follow_up_questions: Who is the person you've been meaning to see for years, and what small barrier has stopped you from reaching out?
Beyond coffee and friends, which other moments (a neighbour, a former colleague, a parent) could a small, well-placed treat help restart?
How could the mechanic be applied to other payment moments, such as splitting a bill, tipping or a gift, to create more connection rather than less?

task_understanding.focus: Luxury fashion's sustainability story is dominated by 'new and better' (recycled fabrics, low-impact materials), while the most credible luxury behaviour, keeping things for decades and passing them down, goes unclaimed. The opportunity for Dior is to make repair and reuse feel like the highest form of couture rather than a green concession, by turning the mark of a garment's past life into a mark of status and emotion.
assumptions: Dior's core equity is craftsmanship: the ateliers, the savoir-faire, the Bar jacket, and the idea that a piece is made by hands and can be remade by hands.

Dior already has repair and heritage infrastructure (atelier skills, archives, Dior Heritage, Dior Lady Art, restoration services), though most customers do not know how deep it goes or think of it as a benefit.
The audience spans aspirational buyers and established clients, from Gen Z and millennials who buy and resell vintage or pre-loved pieces to older clients with wardrobes full of unworn heirlooms.
Luxury shoppers are increasingly sceptical of green claims and respond better to proof and craft than to eco-messaging.
Repair and reuse must not signal 'lower value' or 'second-hand' in a way that dilutes desirability or brand control.
Pre-loved luxury is growing and Dior wants to participate in it on its own terms rather than cede it to third-party resale platforms.

candidate.title: The Second Atelier
candidate.core_idea: Dior opens a 'second atelier' dedicated to giving existing Dior pieces a new life, and treats each repaired or reworked piece as a signed, numbered creation. Any Dior piece, of any age, can be brought in and either restored invisibly or reimagined by an atelier artisan, with the visible choice of leaving the repair on show as a deliberate Dior signature (for example a golden thread, a hand-embroidered patch, a re-cut Bar jacket). Each piece receives a 'second life' label that records its owners, its repairs and the hands that worked on it, creating a documented lineage that raises rather than lowers its value. The campaign tells these stories through short portraits pairing the owner, the artisan and the garment: a mother's 1990s jacket re-cut for her daughter, a scuffed Saddle bag becoming a conversation piece, a vintage Dior dress brought back for a wedding. The campaign line of thought is 'A Dior is never finished', so the brand positions itself as the author of the whole life of the garment and not just the moment of sale.
candidate.brand_connection: Christian Dior built the house on the idea that clothes are architecture made by hand, and the ateliers are the brand's most distinctive asset. Repair and reuse puts the atelier at the centre of the story and extends the New Look's spirit of reinvention to the garment itself. It also gives Dior a way to enter the pre-loved conversation with authority: only the maker can certify, restore and continue a piece's story.
expected_strengths: Turns a sustainability obligation into a craft and status story that fits Dior's luxury codes.
Makes the atelier visible and gives the brand fresh, human, non-product content grounded in real artisans and real clients.
Creates a new kind of desirability: documented provenance and lineage that make pieces more valuable over time, supporting resale value and loyalty.
Strengthens relationships with existing clients and creates a reason to return beyond new collections.

Highly platformable: portraits, an in-store atelier, limited 'second life' capsules by the creative directors, collaborations with artists on visible repair, and archive pieces reworked for the runway.
Credible and hard to copy because it relies on real capability rather than claims.
main_concerns: Operational capacity: atelier time is scarce and demand could exceed supply, so access must be scaled carefully (by appointment, tiers, or regional hubs).
Risk of seeming to encourage buying less from a brand that sells new products; the message needs to reframe value rather than preach restraint.
Brand control and authenticity: altering iconic designs may upset purists, and the process needs clear guidelines on what can be reworked.
Accessibility: if only top clients can use it, the campaign may read as exclusive or tone deaf; pricing and entry points need thought, such as repair for entry-level pieces.
Greenwashing scrutiny: the campaign should be backed by transparent data on volumes repaired, and not stand in for improvements in the core supply chain.
Counterfeit and fraud risk around 'second life' labels, which would require traceable authentication.

final_proposal.title: A Dior Is Never Finished
final_proposal.idea: Dior opens the Second Atelier, where its artisans restore or reimagine any Dior piece ever made. Instead of hiding the repair, clients can choose to wear it as a signature: a golden thread along a mended seam, a hand-embroidered patch over a scuff, a Bar jacket re-cut for a daughter. Every piece receives a numbered 'second life' label recording its owners, its repairs and the hands that worked on it, so a piece's history adds to its value instead of subtracting from it. The campaign shows these stories as intimate portraits of owner, artisan and garment, and the creative directors release occasional capsules reworked from archive pieces. Dior stops being the brand that sells you something new and becomes the author of the whole life of what you own.
follow_up_questions: What would make a visible repair feel like a badge of status rather than a sign of wear, and which cultural precedents (kintsugi, patched denim, military insignia) could inform that?
How could the Second Atelier stay exclusive in craft yet open in access, so that a first-time buyer feels as welcome as a lifelong client?
If a piece's provenance and lineage become part of its value, how might that change the way people buy, resell, gift and inherit luxury, and what role should Dior play in that ecosystem?

task_understanding.focus: The first paycheck is one of life's biggest 'I'm an adult now' moments, yet direct deposit has turned it into a silent number in a banking app. There is nothing to hold, frame or show anyone. The opportunity is to make Canva the brand that gives this milestone a form. assumptions: Most first paychecks today arrive as a bank notification, not paper, so the old ritual of framing the first check or dollar has lost its object.

In a B2B and productivity category, the strongest route is one that gives both employees and employers (small businesses, retail, hospitality, HR teams) a reason to use Canva.

The audience is first-time earners, typically 16-24, plus the managers and owners who hire them. They are digital-native, share milestones socially, and respond to warmth and humour more than to feature talk.

candidates.title: Pay Stub, Redesigned

candidates.title: The Paper One

candidates.title: Paid in Design

candidates.title: Résumé to Receipt

assumptions: The core audience is people entering work for the first time, mainly Gen Z and young millennials. This includes interns, part-timers, gig and freelance workers, and new small-business owners, not only salaried graduates.

Money amounts are sensitive. A campaign that centres on salary risks comparison anxiety and pay-gap discomfort, so it should celebrate the work rather than the number.
Canva's brand strengths are accessibility, democratised creativity and visual communication. Its credibility in the category comes from helping non-designers produce work that looks professional.

candidates.title: Frame It
candidates.core_idea: Treat the first payslip or cheque as a keepsake. Canva offers templates that let people redact and remix it into a framed piece of art, a scrapbook page or a story post, honouring a moment that normally ends up in a drawer.
candidates.brand_connection: A direct use of Canva's core strength: turning ordinary documents into beautiful, shareable design with almost no skill.
expected_strengths: Easy to understand and highly shareable, since it fits existing social behaviour.

main_concerns: It is nostalgic and personal but weak on B2B and productivity relevance.

candidates.title: First Invoice

candidates.brand_connection: Links to Canva's small-business and Teams offer and its brand kit and document tools, with real productivity value.
expected_strengths: Clear commercial benefit and a direct link to paid plans.

Practical and credible.
main_concerns: It narrows the topic to the self-employed and loses the broader emotional universality of a first paycheck.

candidates.title: Decode the Deductions

candidates.brand_connection: Canva as the champion of clear visual communication, applying the belief that good design makes complex things understandable.
expected_strengths: Real insight: the confusion and 'where did it go?' shock are universal.

main_concerns: It moves into financial education, a category where Canva has little authority and some legal and accuracy risk.

final_proposal.title: The Hello Tap

Mastercard funds a small fee rebate for merchants who switch it on, so warmth costs them nothing, and a 'Hello' sticker on the door tells customers talking is welcome. task_understanding.focus: Dior wants to own the repair and reuse conversation without cheapening couture or sounding like a sustainability apology. The opportunity is a paradox: luxury owners love their pieces so much that they keep them untouched, afraid to alter, repair or re-wear them differently. The campaign should turn Dior's craft authority into permission to keep living in what you own, so repair and reuse become the most Dior thing a client can do.
assumptions: Dior's strongest equity here is the atelier: couture heritage, skilled hands and the idea that a garment is made, not manufactured. This is more credible than any green claim.

Dior already offers some repair and aftercare services, but they are low-visibility and transactional. This campaign makes them emotional and culturally visible. Any specific service details need client confirmation.
Luxury audiences distrust loud sustainability messaging. They respond to craft, provenance, emotion and status, so the tone must be aspirational, not virtuous.
Younger affluent consumers (late 20s to 40s) already buy pre-owned, value story and provenance, and are curious about mending as a craft.
Repair and reuse should not read as 'buy less Dior'. The commercial logic is deeper loyalty, longer customer lifetime value and protection of brand desirability.
The campaign must work in social and film as well as in boutiques and ateliers, and must not depend on celebrity endorsement to be believable.

candidates.title: The Atelier Signature
candidates.core_idea: Every repair done by a Dior atelier is marked with a small hand-embroidered detail inside the lining: the date, the atelier and the initials of the petite main who did the work. Repair stops being hidden and becomes a collectible layer of the garment's biography. A bag with three signatures is worth more to its owner than a pristine one.
candidates.brand_connection: It draws on the atelier culture and the idea of the couturier's hand. It extends the signed, numbered tradition of couture into the life of the garment after purchase.
expected_strengths: Simple, visual and ownable: a small mark that can become a recognisable symbol.
Turns repair into status and a reason to return to Dior.
Credits the artisans, which strengthens brand authenticity.
main_concerns: Visible mending and 'celebrating the scar' is a familiar idea (kintsugi, visible mending trend), so it risks feeling derivative.
Depends on the repair service having real capacity.
Narrow in scope: a feature more than a full campaign platform.

candidates.title: Seconde Vie Dior
candidates.core_idea: A certified Dior pre-owned programme in which returned pieces are restored by Dior's own ateliers, authenticated and re-released with a documented history and a new care warranty. Reuse is positioned as a second chapter authored by the house, not a discount channel.
candidates.brand_connection: It uses Dior's authentication authority and craft capability to control quality and brand image in a resale market that already exists outside its control.
expected_strengths: Addresses real market behaviour: consumers already resell and buy pre-owned Dior.
Brings resale value and brand control back to the house.
Offers a clear commercial model and measurable results.
main_concerns: Risk of diluting exclusivity or cannibalising new sales.
Operationally heavy: authentication, logistics, pricing and legal.
More business model than creative idea, so it may be hard to make culturally emotive.

candidates.title: The Second Fitting
candidates.core_idea: Invite clients to bring in a Dior piece they love but no longer wear, such as an inherited jacket, a worn-out Saddle bag or a dress from an event long past. A Dior atelier gives it a second fitting: repairing, reshaping or reimagining it so it can be worn again. candidates.brand_connection: It builds on the original fitting ritual of couture, in which a garment is shaped to a person over several appointments. Dior has the authority to say a garment is never finished, giving owners permission to alter what they fear to ruin.
expected_strengths: Rooted in a genuine human tension: love that keeps things in the closet.
Highly filmable and emotional, with built-in before-and-after storytelling.
Platformable across films, boutique events, a social series, atelier residencies and client-submitted stories.
Drives boutique traffic and repeat engagement without discounting the brand.
main_concerns: Atelier capacity is limited, so it needs a curated, scarce format.

Needs careful handling so it does not read as encouraging customers to buy less.

candidates.title: Petites Mains Open School
candidates.core_idea: Dior opens its craft knowledge through hands-on mending and alteration workshops taught by atelier artisans, in boutiques and online. Participants learn to restore a hem, re-stitch a strap or care for leather, so the skill of keeping becomes an aspirational craft.
candidates.brand_connection: It positions Dior as the keeper of savoir-faire and shares a taste of couture technique, deepening the sense of craft behind each piece.
expected_strengths: Taps into the growing interest in sewing and mending as a mindful, social activity.
Gives the artisans a visible, human role.
Creates community and content with a low risk of controversy.
main_concerns: Teaching DIY repair risks undermining the exclusivity and perceived complexity of Dior craft, and the risk of damaged pieces.

It is the most platformable of the four: real stories, real pieces and the fitting ritual give it a repeatable format across film, social, boutique and PR.
It showcases the atelier as the hero without requiring a new business model, so it can launch quickly and scale in phases.
It supports commercial goals through client loyalty, boutique visits and emotional attachment rather than through discounting.

rejected.reason: A strong detail but a narrow idea, and visible mending is already a familiar cultural trope. It works better as a signature element inside C3 than as the whole campaign.

revisions_after_selection.change: Borrowed the atelier signature from C1: each piece finishes its second fitting with a small embroidered date and artisan initials inside the lining.

revisions_after_selection.change: Chose real clients and their stories as the lead voices rather than celebrities.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Celebrity glamour would weaken the honesty of the idea, and real stories of attachment make the insight believable.

revisions_after_selection.change: Framed the message around 'more of you in it' rather than 'buy less' or 'save the planet', and limited the format to a curated number of atelier appointments each season.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Avoids sounding like a sustainability apology or contradicting Dior's commercial model, and keeps scarcity so the atelier capacity concern is managed rather than hidden.

final_proposal.title: The Second Fitting
final_proposal.idea: Owners of Dior pieces often keep them untouched because they love them too much to risk changing them. The Second Fitting gives permission. Clients bring a treasured piece they no longer wear: a mother's jacket, a scuffed Saddle bag, a dress from a decade ago. A Dior atelier fits it again, repairing, reshaping or reinventing it so it can be worn. A film series follows real clients and the artisans through each appointment, from fear to the first wear. Every finished piece gets a small embroidered date and the artisan's initials inside the lining. The message: a Dior is never finished, it is only fitted to the next chapter of your life. It lives in ateliers, boutiques, social and client-submitted stories, with a limited number of appointments each season.

How could the embroidered second-fitting mark become a recognisable status symbol without turning into a gimmick, and who should be credited by name?
How can the campaign stay scarce and desirable while still inviting people with a modest, everyday Dior piece, not just the most privileged clients?

task_understanding.focus: The first paycheck is a rite of passage that has lost its physical form. Direct deposit turned a moment that used to be a handed-over check, a framed dollar or a pay envelope into a push notification. assumptions: Canva's brand truth is that anyone can make something that looks and feels professional, so it fits a moment when someone first feels like a professional.

The core audience is 16-26-year-olds entering work, plus first-time freelancers and side-hustlers. Parents, grandparents and employers are secondary audiences who hold the nostalgia and the buying power.
Most first paychecks are small. The emotional value lies in what the pay means (independence, proof of worth), not in the amount, and the campaign must never make small sums feel embarrassing.
Canva already has the assets to deliver this: templates, Canva Print, Canva for Teams and a huge sharing culture. The campaign should drive template use and team adoption rather than just awareness.

candidates.title: Frame the First One
candidates.core_idea: Direct deposit killed the first paycheck as an object, so Canva brings the ritual back. candidates.brand_connection: Canva makes ideas tangible and shareable. The campaign uses templates, Canva Print and the community gallery, and it positions Canva as the tool for marking life milestones, including work ones.

The campaign should move repair from a back-of-house service to a visible, desirable expression of the house's savoir-faire.
assumptions: Dior's equity rests on couture ateliers, hand craft and heritage (the Bar jacket, Lady Dior, the New Look), which makes repair a natural extension of the brand and not a bolt-on.
The client's topic signals a need to answer sustainability scrutiny of luxury groups without greenwashing or discounting, so the idea must be credible and operational, not just rhetorical.
The core audience is affluent, culturally literate 25-45 year olds who also shop resale and vintage, and who see worn-in, storied pieces as more authentic than pristine ones.
A secondary audience is aspirational fans who may never buy new but are drawn to the house, and who can enter through repair, reuse and archive culture.
Dior can draw on real assets: atelier talent, an archive, an existing repair and after-sales service, and a global boutique network.
Luxury must protect desirability, so the tone should be romantic and confident, not guilt-driven or utilitarian.

candidate.title: The Atelier Remembers
candidate.core_idea: Every Dior piece that is repaired gets a signed, visible mark of its history: a small embroidered 'repair stitch' in the house's signature gray or a discreet numbered label recording who mended it, where and when. The campaign reframes damage as the beginning of a piece's second chapter. Dior publicly celebrates the most storied repaired pieces (a 1998 saddle bag re-lined by an atelier hand, a jacket passed through three generations) in a living 'Archive of Second Lives'. Owners can bring in any Dior piece, including pieces bought secondhand, and the atelier's mark becomes a new form of provenance that raises a piece's value on the resale market. Repair becomes a collectible signature, not a fix.
candidate.brand_connection: Dior's mythology is built on the hand: the petites mains, the toile, the fitting. This idea puts those hands at the center of the story after the sale, not just before it. It echoes Christian Dior's own belief in clothes as architecture built to last, and it gives the house a way to own the heritage and resale conversation instead of ceding it to third-party platforms. A visible atelier signature also fits luxury's logic of authorship, turning repair into a proof of authenticity.
expected_strengths: Makes repair desirable and status-bearing by giving it a signature, which flips the stigma of 'broken'.
Creates a new kind of provenance that can lift resale value and keep Dior pieces in circulation under the house's authority.
Highly shareable and visual: close-ups of embroidery, atelier hands and before/after stories suit film, social and exhibitions.
Authentic to the brand because it uses real craft assets, not borrowed sustainability language.
Opens a platform that can extend to events, pop-up repair ateliers, collaborations with artists, and an archive exhibition.
main_concerns: Capacity: atelier time is scarce, so the service may need tiering or limited drops to avoid bottlenecks and unmet promises.
Risk of seeming to discourage new purchases, which may conflict with commercial goals unless framed as deepening loyalty and lifetime value.
Visible repair marks could clash with some customers' wish for pristine pieces, so the mark must be optional and beautifully designed.
Scrutiny of the wider luxury group's practices means claims must be precise and backed by real operational commitments.
Extending to secondhand pieces needs authentication processes and legal care around counterfeits.

final_proposal.title: The Atelier Remembers
final_proposal.idea: What if a Dior repair was the most coveted thing a piece could receive? Bring in a worn bag, a torn jacket or a secondhand find, and the atelier mends it by hand, then signs the work with a small embroidered mark in Dior gray, recording who mended it, where and when. The mark becomes a new kind of provenance: proof that the piece has lived, been loved and been restored by the house. Dior shares the most extraordinary second lives in an Archive of Second Lives, told through film, exhibitions and owners' own stories. Damage stops being the end of luxury and becomes the beginning of a chapter. The idea turns craft into a lasting relationship and makes keeping a Dior piece the ultimate sign of taste.
follow_up_questions: How could the repair mark be designed so it feels like a collectible signature that owners want to show off, and not a scar they want to hide?
Which real atelier stories, archive pieces or owner memories would make the strongest first chapter of the Archive of Second Lives?
How might Dior balance limited atelier capacity with broad cultural reach, for example through tiered services, seasonal repair residencies or collaborations with emerging artisans?

The campaign has to turn mending, remaking and passing on into something desirable, emotional and distinctly Dior, built on the atelier's craft rather than on eco-messaging. It should avoid greenwashing and avoid cannibalising Dior's aspirational image.
assumptions: Dior's strongest and least copyable asset is its atelier craft: the petites mains, the premières and the couture know-how. Repair and reuse should be shown as craft, not logistics.
The New Look turns 80 in February 2027, which gives a natural cultural moment. The New Look was a post-war statement about abundance, so reversing its logic is meaningful.

Dior already offers some repair and aftercare, and its pieces, especially bags like the Lady Dior, are often kept for years or inherited, so the repair story is real. Any claims must be checked with the client.

The core audience is affluent, culturally literate 25-45 year olds, plus heritage clients. They distrust preachy sustainability messaging but respond to emotional storytelling, scarcity, craft and status.
Luxury owners tend to hide wear and damage. A key tension to exploit is that the pieces people love most are the ones that show a life lived.
Reuse must not read as discounting or as lowering the brand. It must feel more exclusive, not less.
The client wants one platformable campaign idea, not a CSR programme, so it needs a clear hero moment and room for ongoing content.

candidates.title: The Visible Mend
candidates.core_idea: Dior creates a signature repair mark: a recognisable thread, stitch pattern or embroidered detail that atelier hands add whenever a piece is mended. Wear becomes a badge of devotion, and a mended Dior becomes more prestigious than a pristine one. Campaign imagery celebrates tears, scuffs and darns as beautiful, in the spirit of kintsugi but with couture precision.
candidates.brand_connection: It uses Dior's obsession with detail and codes (cannage, the grey, the pearl-like details) and turns craftsmanship into a visible, collectable signature.
expected_strengths: Visually striking and instantly shareable.
Reframes damage as status, reversing luxury's usual fear of imperfection.
Easy to extend into editorial, social and in-store content.
Gives owners a reason to repair rather than replace.
main_concerns: Kintsugi-style visible mending is a known idea in fashion, so it risks feeling borrowed.
Could be read as a styling trend rather than a behaviour change.
Some luxury clients may want invisible repairs, so the mark must be optional.

candidates.title: Lineage
candidates.core_idea: Every Dior piece gets a lifetime provenance record. When a bag or garment is repaired, resold or passed on, the atelier records the new chapter and a small discreet mark or name tag is stitched inside next to the previous owner's. A Lady Dior becomes a piece with a biography, not a product with an expiry date.
candidates.brand_connection: It builds on Dior's heritage, authenticity and the heirloom status of its icons, and positions Dior as the brand pieces are inherited from.
expected_strengths: Turns resale and reuse into an extension of luxury value rather than a threat to it.
Supports authentication and fights counterfeits.
Rich storytelling about owners and generations.
Strong long-term CRM and loyalty potential.
main_concerns: Heavy operational and data infrastructure.
Could encourage resale over repair and cannibalise new sales if not handled carefully.
Privacy questions around naming owners.
Less visually dramatic as a hero campaign moment.

candidates.title: The New Look, Again
candidates.core_idea: For the New Look's 80th anniversary, Dior inverts its 1947 gesture. Then, abundance answered scarcity. Now, the radical luxury is what already exists. Dior invites people to submit a garment they cannot let go of, with its story, and the atelier remakes a selection into couture pieces, documented from first cut to final fitting. The anniversary show closes with the remade pieces worn by their original owners.
candidates.brand_connection: It anchors the idea in the founding myth of Dior, its couture ateliers and the heritage calendar, and reframes the New Look as an ongoing act of reinvention.
expected_strengths: Strong cultural hook and a natural hero moment.
Emotional human stories, with the garment as memory.
Showcases the highest craft in the house.
Platformable: submissions, films, show, exhibition, boutique services.
Gives a provocative, strategically grounded reason to talk about reuse in couture.
main_concerns: Couture remakes reach only a few people and could feel elitist or like greenwashing.
Needs a broader service tier to be credible.
Questions about whether non-Dior garments should be accepted.
Anniversary timing leaves limited lead time.

candidates.title: Petites Mains, Open Hands
candidates.core_idea: Dior opens its ateliers' knowledge to the public. Dior artisans teach repair skills through pop-up workshops and short films, covering how to darn, reline, re-stitch and re-hem, for any garment from any brand. The new luxury is knowing how to look after what you own.
candidates.brand_connection: It puts the often-invisible petites mains at the centre of the brand and positions Dior as the keeper of craft knowledge and a cultural patron.
expected_strengths: Generous, brand-positive and highly shareable.
Humanises artisans and elevates craft.
Builds a skill-based community and earned media.
Credible with a younger audience that values DIY and craft.
main_concerns: Risks diluting exclusivity or feeling like a charity project.
Does not directly drive Dior's own repair and reuse behaviours.
Hard to scale beyond a few cities.
Teaching can feel off-brand for a house built on mystique.

reasons_for_selection: It has a real cultural trigger, the 80th anniversary of the New Look, and turns Dior's own origin story into a statement about reuse, so the idea feels earned rather than opportunistic.
It makes reuse look like couture rather than compromise, which directly solves the status problem.
It is the most platformable: submissions, atelier films, a show finale, an exhibition, and boutique services can all flow from one idea.
It carries emotion at human scale, since the owners and their garments are the story, which avoids preachy sustainability tone.
Its main weakness, limited reach, can be fixed by adding an accessible service tier, whereas the weaknesses of the other options are harder to fix.

rejected.reason: Visually strong but the visible-mending aesthetic is already familiar in fashion and it is more a styling device than a campaign platform. It works better as a design element inside C3 than as the core idea.

Strategically smart and commercially valuable, but it is infrastructure-heavy, raises privacy and resale-cannibalisation questions, and lacks a dramatic hero moment. It is better as a long-term programme following the campaign.

Generous and craft-led, but it positions Dior as a teacher for all brands rather than showing the value of Dior pieces being kept alive. It risks diluting mystique and has a weaker link to the brand's own repair and reuse offer.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a three-tier boutique service ladder (Mend, Remodel, Remake) beneath the couture remakes.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Couture-only remakes would reach very few people and invite accusations of elitism or greenwashing. A ladder lets many clients participate while keeping couture as the aspirational peak.

revisions_after_selection.change: Borrowed C1's idea: the original stitches and wear are deliberately left visible in remade pieces, and each owner's story is embroidered inside.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It makes the history of the garment the beauty of the piece and gives a distinctive visual signature that photographs well.

revisions_after_selection.change: Selection of couture remakes is based on story and emotional meaning, not on celebrity or spend, and owners wear their pieces in the anniversary show.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This keeps the campaign human and credible, and prevents it from becoming a VIP showcase.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a commitment to publish, honestly and in simple terms, how much existing material goes into the anniversary collection and the services.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Transparency guards against greenwashing criticism and gives the idea substance beyond the show.

final_proposal.title: The New Look, Again
final_proposal.idea: In February 2027 the New Look turns 80. Dior's 1947 revolution answered wartime scarcity with abundance. Today's revolution is the reverse: the most radical luxury is what you already own. Dior invites people worldwide to submit a garment they can't let go of, such as a torn wedding jacket or a mother's Dior suit, with its story. The ateliers choose a number and remake them into couture pieces, filmed from first cut to final fitting, with the original stitches left visible and the story embroidered inside. The anniversary show closes with these pieces worn by their owners. Beneath it, a boutique ladder of Mend, Remodel and Remake brings the idea to many more people. Dior's new silhouette is not a shape but a second life.
follow_up_questions: What would make a remade garment feel more desirable than a new one: its story, its visible stitches, or the hands that remade it?
How could the campaign reach people who will never own couture without losing the exclusivity that gives the idea its power?
Beyond the anniversary, what recurring ritual could keep reuse part of Dior's calendar, as a season, a service or a collection?

task_understanding.focus: Luxury fashion treats repair and reuse as a back-of-house service, or as a sustainability footnote that sits awkwardly beside newness. The opportunity is to make repair and reuse feel like the most desirable, most Dior thing a client can do. It should read as an act of creativity and devotion, not guilt or damage control.
assumptions: Dior already offers some repair, restoration and alteration services through boutiques and ateliers, but these are under-communicated and not culturally famous.

The audience is mixed. Core clients own pieces they love and may keep for decades. Aspirational fans engage through culture, film and social media. Younger buyers are increasingly comfortable with vintage and resale.

Dior's strongest ownable assets for this topic are the 1947 New Look and the Bar jacket (a history of reinventing silhouette), the couture ateliers and their artisans, the archive and Galerie Dior, and Christian Dior's lucky charms and superstitions (the star, lily of the valley).
Dior cannot lecture. Sustainability claims must be specific and credible to avoid greenwashing accusations, and the tone must stay aspirational, not austere or moralising.
Brand equity depends on exclusivity and desirability, so any scheme must protect that and not read as discounting or mass-market recycling.
Atelier capacity is limited, so the idea must work with scarcity and use it as part of the appeal.

Insight: people repair what they love. In couture, fittings and alterations were always the intimate ritual of ownership, and ready-to-wear lost that. Repair is luxury's original service, not a new virtue.

candidates.title: The New Look, Again
candidates.core_idea: Each season, Dior's ateliers invite clients to bring in a treasured piece from any year. It could be a tired Bar jacket, a worn Lady Dior or an inherited coat. The ateliers re-cut, repair and reinterpret it into the season's silhouette. A selection of these transformed pieces appears in a runway moment and a film series alongside the new collection. Reuse becomes a creative act, echoing how the 1947 New Look reinvented fashion by reshaping what already existed.
candidates.brand_connection: The New Look was a radical act of reinvention. Dior's craft authority lives in the ateliers, and its archive and long-lived icons (Bar, Lady Dior) are built to outlast trends. The idea makes 'Dior is always becoming' a lived service.
expected_strengths: Turns repair from a defensive service into a creative, desirable event that earns fashion-press and social attention
Repeatable seasonal platform with a built-in runway, film, editorial and client-event structure
Strong emotional storytelling, because every piece comes with a real owner and a memory
Reinforces long-term ownership and the lifetime value of icons without discounting
main_concerns: Atelier capacity limits scale, so access could feel elitist
Could be read as a one-off stunt unless it becomes a standing service
Needs credible, specific impact proof to avoid greenwashing accusations

candidates.title: The Mended Star
candidates.core_idea: Dior introduces a signature visible-mending mark: a tiny hand-embroidered star, drawn from Christian Dior's lucky charm, stitched over repairs. Repaired pieces become badges of love and longevity, and the mark becomes a status code, a sign that a piece has been cherished enough to be fixed.
candidates.brand_connection: Draws on Dior's star superstition, craft embroidery and the idea of the talisman. It gives the brand an ownable visual code for repair.
expected_strengths: A simple, highly shareable visual symbol that can spread through street style and social media
Reframes flaws as luck and love, which is emotionally warm and brand-specific
Easy to apply across product categories
main_concerns: Risks sparking fake distress and 'damage as fashion', encouraging people to break pieces for the mark
Some luxury clients may not want visible evidence of repair on a pristine piece
More of a graphic device than a full campaign platform

candidates.title: Dior Lineage
candidates.core_idea: Every significant Dior piece is given a lineage record covering its atelier, first owner and repairs. When a piece is passed on or resold through a Dior-verified channel, the atelier refreshes it and the new owner is formally welcomed, with the previous owner's note attached. Reuse becomes inheritance and provenance, not second-hand.
candidates.brand_connection: Builds on Dior's heritage, archive culture and the authority of its ateliers to authenticate and restore.
expected_strengths: Makes resale feel prestigious and keeps value and control in the Dior ecosystem
Fights counterfeits through provenance
Emotional handover stories with strong content potential
main_concerns: Resale could cannibalise new sales or be seen as devaluing the brand
Heavy operational and data infrastructure
More of a business model than a culturally sparking idea

candidates.title: Petites Mains Open Hours
candidates.core_idea: Dior's artisans set up pop-up repair clinics in cities around the world and fix any garment from any brand, including fast fashion, for free. Passers-by watch couture hands mend a high-street hoodie. Dior positions skill, not logo, as the ultimate luxury and publicly shares repair craft.
candidates.brand_connection: Puts the petites mains, the heart of Dior's authority, in front of the public and shows the brand's generosity of skill.
expected_strengths: Provocative and highly newsworthy, with a strong human-interest angle
Reaches non-clients and builds goodwill and cultural relevance
Elevates artisans as the true stars of the brand
main_concerns: Could dilute exclusivity if skill is perceived as commoditised
Costly and capacity-hungry, and risks looking like a charity stunt
Weak link to Dior's own products and ownership, so unclear commercial return

reasons_for_selection: It is the most ownable to Dior, because it rewrites the New Look story: reinvention of existing material as the brand's founding gesture.
It reframes repair and reuse as aspirational and creative, which solves the core problem of repair feeling like a guilt-driven or defensive service.
It is a true platform. It generates seasonal runway content, client stories, films, editorial and events, and can grow year after year.
It strengthens the desirability of Dior icons and long-term ownership without discounting or compromising exclusivity.
Scarcity of atelier capacity becomes part of the appeal instead of a weakness, provided access is widened carefully.

rejected.reason: A strong symbol but a narrow idea. It risks encouraging fake distress and conflicts with clients who prefer pristine pieces. It works better as a supporting detail within C1 than as the campaign.
Commercially smart but operationally heavy and more business model than cultural idea. Resale cannibalisation and brand-control risks make it better as a later phase.

revisions_after_selection.reason: Reduces the risk of elitism and broadens cultural reach while keeping scarcity as part of the appeal.

revisions_after_selection.change: Made the transformation service a standing, bookable year-round offer, with the seasonal runway and film moment as the showcase.

revisions_after_selection.change: Centred the communications on real owners and their pieces, with the artisans credited by name, and used the C2 star as a discreet optional signature stitched inside the piece, not visible on the outside.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Keeps the tone emotional and authentic, spotlights craft, and borrows the best part of C2 without encouraging visible distress.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a commitment to publish specific, verifiable facts about what was repaired and reused, with no broad sustainability claims in the creative.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Protects credibility and avoids greenwashing criticism, and lets the tone stay aspirational.

final_proposal.title: The New Look, Again
final_proposal.idea: In 1947, Dior changed fashion by reshaping what already existed. Today, the ateliers do it again. Each season, clients bring in a piece they love, such as a worn Bar jacket, a scuffed Lady Dior or an inherited coat, and the petites mains repair, re-cut and reimagine it into the season's silhouette. The best transformations walk in a runway moment and star in a film series, each told through its owner's memory and the artisan who remade it. The service stays open year-round, with some places offered by public draw. Repair stops being what you do when something breaks and becomes what you do when you love something too much to let it end. A discreet star stitched inside marks every piece reborn.

How could scarcity, such as limited atelier slots, be used as a feature of the campaign without making the idea feel closed or elitist?
Which other brand icons or founder moments contain an act of reinvention that could turn repair and reuse into a heritage-led story?

Builds goodwill with emerging creatives and schools.
Collectible capsule potential.

revisions_after_selection.change: Positioned mends as proof of a piece being loved, not as damage to be celebrated, and used real owners' stories rather than only celebrities.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Avoids implying that wear is glamorous for its own sake and keeps the emotion believable.

final_proposal.title: Signed Twice
final_proposal.idea: Couture was always repair culture: Dior's petites mains have altered, restored and remade garments since the house began. Signed Twice makes that hidden truth the campaign. When a Dior piece returns to the atelier, it is mended with a deliberate, visible couture gesture, such as a gold-thread darn on a Bar jacket elbow or a hand-embroidered star over a burn. The artisan adds a second signature inside the garment. The campaign films each mend as a portrait of the owner, the damage and the hands that fixed it. A repaired Lady Dior outranks a pristine one because it proves it was loved. The service is open to Dior pieces of any era, including secondhand, so reuse and resale join the story. Luxury's oldest promise, made to last, becomes visible, human and collectable.
follow_up_questions: What would a mend look like if it carried unmistakable Dior codes, and how could it differ from existing visible mending traditions?
How could the house make the second signature meaningful to owners and future buyers without turning it into a resale gimmick?
Which real owners and artisans, beyond celebrities, would make the strongest and most believable stories, and how could the service scale without losing its craft?

task_understanding.focus: Luxury fashion's sustainability story is dominated by 'buy new, but responsibly made.' Dior has an opening to own the opposite: the idea that true luxury is something you never throw away. Repair and reuse is a chance to move Dior from selling garments to stewarding them, turning care, alteration and second lives into a mark of status rather than a sustainability footnote. The campaign needs to make repair desirable, visible and culturally cool, not worthy or apologetic.
assumptions: Dior's heritage in haute couture, with its atelier craft, hand finishing and made-to-measure tradition, is the most credible asset for a repair and reuse story. Repair is simply couture logic applied after the sale.
Luxury buyers increasingly distrust green claims, so proof (visible craft, real people, real garments) will persuade more than pledges.
Younger affluent audiences already buy vintage Dior (Galliano-era, Saddle bag, Book Tote) and value provenance. Resale is thriving but the brand currently gains little from it culturally.
Many owners treat their Dior pieces as inheritable but are unsure how to maintain, alter or restore them, or fear 'ruining' them by touching them.
The brand must protect exclusivity and aspiration. Repair cannot read as discounting, downmarket, or an admission that products wear out.
Operational capacity (atelier time, boutique services, pricing for repairs) can be scaled or staged, and the campaign can launch with a limited pilot in key cities.

candidate.title: The Second Fitting
candidate.core_idea: Reframe every Dior repair, alteration or reuse as a 'Second Fitting': a ritual in which a garment or bag returns to the atelier and is reimagined for its next chapter. Customers bring in a piece with a story (a mother's Bar jacket, a worn Lady Dior, a wedding-guest dress worn once). Atelier artisans restore it, adapt it or transform it, and leave a discreet, signed 'Fitting Number' stitched inside the lining, so each piece accumulates a visible lineage of lives. The campaign shows these transformations as short, intimate films and an exhibition of garments with multiple Fitting Numbers, treating the most-repaired piece as the most prized. Dior also invites owners to pass pieces on through a Dior-certified 'Next Owner' programme, where the lineage travels with the garment. The platform line of thinking: a first fitting makes it yours; a second fitting makes it last.
candidate.brand_connection: Couture is built on fittings: iterative, personal, hands-on refinement. Extending the fitting beyond the point of sale draws directly on Monsieur Dior's atelier legacy and the maison's obsession with savoir-faire. It makes the unseen craft of the ateliers the hero and reframes sustainability as the natural outcome of making things worth keeping, rather than as a separate corporate initiative. It also gives Dior a way to participate in the vintage and resale conversation on its own terms, with authenticity and lineage controlled by the house.
expected_strengths: Ownable and platformable: the Fitting Number is a physical, collectible brand device that can run across film, exhibition, boutique services, social storytelling and resale.
Turns repair from a cost centre into a status signal; a piece with many Fitting Numbers becomes a badge of honour, inverting fast-fashion logic.
Rooted in real Dior craft, so it is credible and difficult for competitors to copy without similar atelier depth.
Emotionally rich content: each garment carries a human story, giving endless, non-repetitive storytelling.
Creates ongoing customer relationships and lifetime value after the first purchase, and strengthens the authenticity of the resale market for Dior pieces.
Appeals to both heritage clients and younger vintage-minded audiences.
main_concerns: Atelier capacity and cost: scaling bespoke repair without diluting craft or creating long waiting times; likely needs a staged rollout and tiered services.
Risk of seeming to suggest that Dior products need repair, or of being read as greenwashing if not backed by accessible pricing and genuine service quality.
Exclusivity tension: a Next Owner programme may blur positioning if it appears to encourage secondhand buying over new.
Cannibalisation worries internally if repair and reuse reduce new sales, so the business case should highlight loyalty, higher-value engagement and brand desirability.
Needs clear guidelines for authenticity, ownership transfer and data privacy for the lineage records.

final_proposal.title: The Second Fitting

Each time, the artisans stitch a discreet Fitting Number inside the lining, a signed record of another life lived. Short films follow the garments and the hands that renew them, and an exhibition celebrates the most-fitted pieces as the most precious. When a piece moves on, its lineage travels with it through a Dior-certified Next Owner programme. Repair stops being an afterthought and becomes the highest form of luxury: proof that something was made to be kept.

task_understanding.focus: The first paycheck is a rare moment when a young person's work becomes a number. It is intensely emotional and widely shared, yet it has no ritual, no object and no design. Canva's opportunity is to give this moment a visible, shareable form and show that it is the tool for marking what matters at work. The campaign should also lead credibly into Canva's B2B side, because employers and teams are the ones who onboard new hires and run payday.
assumptions: Canva's B2B and team growth depends on the product being loved by individuals first. Emotional, personal moments therefore build the bottom-up adoption that team and enterprise plans rely on.

The core audience is first-time earners (Gen Z interns, graduates, apprentices, part-timers and young freelancers). Secondary audiences are the HR, People and team leads who onboard them, and the parents and mentors who shaped them.

First paychecks carry very different meanings across cultures. In many places the first salary traditionally goes to parents or elders as thanks, while in others it is a personal milestone or a shock about taxes and deductions.
Canva's role is not to give financial advice. Its credible territory is turning moments, ideas and feelings into something people can make, share and keep.
A pay stub is a famously unloved document made of line items, which makes it a strong visual and conceptual hook.
People already post screenshots, photos of checks and 'first pay' stories on social platforms, so there is existing behavior to build on rather than behavior to invent.

candidates.title: Line Item Zero
candidates.core_idea: Before taxes, rent or treats, the first line on your first paycheck is a thank-you. Canva turns the pay stub into a canvas. Users add a 'Line Item Zero' naming the person who got them here (a parent, teacher, aunt, coach or friend) and design a thank-you to send. It gives a ritual to the many cultures where first pay is shared with elders, and invites everyone else to invent one.
candidates.brand_connection: Canva exists to help people express something and share it. This idea uses the most familiar template in adult life, the pay stub, as a creative starting point. It also has a B2B route: employers can hand new hires a branded 'First Payday Kit' built in Canva Teams.
expected_strengths: Emotionally universal but locally adaptable, because each culture can fill the ritual with its own meaning.
Highly shareable, since the thank-you is sent to a real person and creates a second wave of recipients who see Canva.
The 'Line Item Zero' language is a platformable device that works across film, social, OOH, templates and employer kits.
Bridges consumer emotion and B2B utility through onboarding and employer-brand use.
main_concerns: It could feel sentimental or consumer-greeting-card-like for a B2B-categorized brand.
It assumes a family-gratitude frame that may not fit every user's situation, such as those supporting their families financially or with complicated family ties.
It needs employer and payroll partners to reach its full B2B potential.

candidates.title: Paid By Design
candidates.core_idea: Spotlight everything made before the first paycheck: the resume, the portfolio, the pitch deck, the first invoice. The message is that the first paycheck is the end of a design process, and Canva was in the room for it. Real first earners show the artifacts behind their first pay.
candidates.brand_connection: It positions Canva as practical career infrastructure for freelancers and early-career workers, which fits the productivity and SaaS category directly.
expected_strengths: Strong product proof, because it showcases real use cases such as resumes, invoices and decks.
A clear and credible link to conversion and to freelancer and small-business acquisition.
User-generated stories are easy to collect.
main_concerns: It is the most category-conventional approach, with 'tools that help you succeed' messaging that many SaaS brands already make.
It treats the paycheck only as an outcome and misses the emotion of the moment itself.
It could read as self-congratulatory brand credit-taking.

candidates.title: The Payslip Translator
candidates.core_idea: First-paycheck shock comes from the gap between the salary on the offer letter and the number in the bank. Canva redesigns the confusing payslip into a clear visual explainer showing where each part of the money goes, using a free template and an employer toolkit. The proposition is that confusing documents can be redesigned to be understandable.
candidates.brand_connection: Clarity through visual communication is core to Canva. This idea also gives HR and finance teams a practical B2B reason to use Canva for employee communications.
expected_strengths: Genuinely useful and likely to earn press and conversation.
A strong B2B angle, since HR teams can adopt it directly.
Taps into a real, widely felt pain point.
main_concerns: Tax and payroll rules vary by country, so accuracy and liability risks are high.
It moves Canva toward financial education, which is not its credible territory.
The tone is more informational than emotional and may not spark cultural conversation.

candidates.title: The Framed Dollar, Reborn
candidates.core_idea: Revive the shopkeeper tradition of framing the first dollar earned, for a world where pay is digital and there is nothing to frame. Canva makes 'first pay' keepsakes (digital frames, prints, wall art and widgets) that turn the abstract first deposit into a physical symbol of a first achievement. Employers can gift them at the first payday.
candidates.brand_connection: Canva is the design tool people use to turn digital moments into tangible, meaningful objects through its print and brand-kit capabilities.
expected_strengths: A visually appealing and nostalgic hook with a clear lost-ritual insight.
It connects naturally to Canva's print and merchandise offering.
Easy to execute as a template pack.
main_concerns: The framed-dollar tradition is largely a Western small-business custom and may not resonate globally.
The keepsake focuses on the self and money, which is less emotionally rich than thanking another person.
It could look like a commercial print upsell.

reasons_for_selection: It has the strongest human insight. The first paycheck is an emotionally loaded 'thank you' moment in many cultures, and no brand owns the ritual.
The pay stub is a distinctive creative device. 'Line Item Zero' gives the campaign a memorable name and a visual and verbal system that can scale across channels.
It is the most socially propagating option, because every thank-you sent exposes a new person to Canva in a warm context.
It fits Canva's brand purpose of helping people express themselves and share it, rather than selling a function.
It can lead into B2B through a First Payday Kit for employers, so the emotional idea supports Canva's category commercially.

rejected.reason: Practical and conversion-friendly, but it is the most category-typical idea and misses the emotional core of the first paycheck. Its product proof can be folded into the main campaign as supporting content.
Useful, but it carries legal and accuracy risk across countries and pushes Canva into financial education. It is also more informational than culturally sparking.

Charming, but the framed-dollar tradition is culturally narrow and self-focused, and it risks feeling like a print upsell. C1 keeps the idea of marking the moment but makes it relational and more widely applicable.

revisions_after_selection.change: Broadened 'Line Item Zero' from thanking parents to thanking anyone who helped, and gave the pay stub a flexible 'who got you here' line.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Family situations vary widely, and a parent-only frame would exclude users and risk feeling prescriptive. A broader frame stays inclusive and still honors cultures where first pay goes to elders.

revisions_after_selection.change: Removed any display of salary amounts from templates and shared assets. The thank-you card shows the line item but keeps the figure private or hidden.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Pay is sensitive, and making amounts public could create comparison pressure, privacy concerns or workplace issues.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added an employer route (the First Payday Kit: onboarding templates for HR and managers to send a personal Line Item Zero note to new hires, and a version for new hires to send out).
revisions_after_selection.reason: Without a B2B route, the idea risks reading as a consumer greeting-card campaign. This ties it to Canva Teams and employer-brand needs.

revisions_after_selection.change: Set the campaign tone as warm and wry, treating the pay stub as the most boring document in the world that for one day gets to be the most moving, rather than purely sentimental.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It keeps the campaign in Canva's playful, accessible voice and avoids greeting-card schmaltz.

revisions_after_selection.change: Folded C2's product proof into the campaign as a supporting layer, showing the resume, invoice or deck that led to the first pay as optional 'Line Item Zero' stories.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It adds practical credibility and a conversion path without changing the core emotional idea.

final_proposal.title: Line Item Zero
final_proposal.idea: A pay stub is the most boring document in adult life, full of deductions. But before anything is deducted, your first paycheck deserves a line item zero: the person who got you here. Canva turns the first pay stub into a canvas where first-time earners add a name (a parent, teacher, aunt, coach, friend) and design a thank-you to send before they spend a cent. It gives a shared ritual to cultures where first pay is offered to elders, and invites everyone else to invent theirs. Each thank-you travels to a real person and spreads Canva in its warmest context. For B2B, a First Payday Kit lets employers welcome new hires with a personal note and a template to pass the gratitude on. Pay amounts stay private. The line is the only thing shared.

task_understanding.focus: The first paycheck is the moment a person becomes an economic actor, and it is also the moment they first have to present themselves as a professional: the offer letter, the LinkedIn update, the 'I got the job' post, the first pitch deck, the first invoice. The opportunity for Canva is to move from being the tool people use for school projects and side hustles to being the tool of their professional identity, by owning the first-time-professional moment. That moment is when workplace tool habits form and when people become future team seat-holders and buyers in B2B.
assumptions: Canva is already widely known and liked among students and creators, but is still perceived as a 'design tool', not a core workplace or career tool. Moving that perception is the commercial prize, especially for Canva Teams and Enterprise.
The 'first paycheck' is not only about money. It is emotionally about proof, independence and 'I made it', and it is often mixed with imposter feelings and the question 'what do I do with this?'.

The core audience is 18-27 year olds: new graduates, first-job starters, first-time freelancers and gig workers. They are digital natives who share milestones publicly and privately, with family as a key secondary audience, because parents often frame or celebrate the first paycheck.
Canva's role is not to give financial advice. It should stay in its lane of visual communication, making things, and making people look and feel capable.

Many first paychecks are now irregular (freelance, gig, creator income) and arrive as an invoice or a payment notification rather than a physical check, so the ritual has weakened and is open for reinvention.
Campaign should work globally, with local cultural variations in how the first paycheck is marked (e.g. giving gifts to parents, first treat, first savings).

candidates.title: The Framed First Check
candidates.core_idea: Revive the lost ritual of marking the first paycheck. People used to frame the first dollar or photocopy the first check; now it is a silent bank notification. Canva launches a 'Frame It' toolkit: templates that turn a first payslip, invoice or payment notification into a keepsake (redacted automatically for privacy), with a wall of real first-pay frames from people and public figures. The paycheck becomes a design object.
candidates.brand_connection: Canva turns ordinary moments into things worth sharing and keeping. It owns the 'make something of it' territory, and this applies it to a milestone nobody has designed for yet. It places Canva at the start of the working life.
expected_strengths: Emotionally simple and instantly understandable
Highly shareable user-generated content with a built-in template mechanic
Product-led: every post is a demonstration of Canva
Works across cultures with local framing styles
main_concerns: Skews sentimental and consumer, with a weaker link to B2B and workplace use
Privacy sensitivity around showing pay data
Risk of feeling like a one-off seasonal gimmick

candidates.title: Paid to Be Professional
candidates.core_idea: The insight: the first paycheck arrives before the first-timer feels like a professional. People feel like imposters with a salary. The campaign reframes the first paycheck as a deadline for the identity to catch up. Canva offers 'Day One Professional' kits (the first deck, the first one-pager, the first status update, the first email signature, the first personal brand page) so new hires can look as capable as they are expected to be. The line of thinking is: your paycheck says you're a professional; here is how you show it.
candidates.brand_connection: Canva already sells confidence in output: 'you don't need to be a designer'. This extends it to 'you don't need to be a seasoned pro to look like one'. It directly connects to workplace use, onboarding and team adoption.
expected_strengths: Names a real, under-addressed emotion (imposter feelings at the start of work)
Strong commercial link: new hires bring Canva into their teams, creating bottom-up B2B adoption
Platformable across content, partnerships with employers, universities and HR onboarding
Credible and useful rather than purely emotional
main_concerns: Less emotionally warm and celebratory than other angles
Could read as functional template marketing without a strong creative hook
Risk of reinforcing anxiety instead of relieving it

candidates.title: The Thank-You Economy
candidates.core_idea: Across many cultures, the first thing people do with the first paycheck is spend it on someone else: a parent, a teacher, a sibling. Canva makes the first paycheck about the people who made it possible. The campaign invites people to create a 'thank-you' for the person they spent it on (cards, videos, certificates, a 'return on investment' report for a parent), and tells the real stories of what first checks bought. The line of thinking: the first paycheck is the first dividend of everyone who believed in you.
candidates.brand_connection: Canva is a tool for expression and connection, with a strong presence in cards, gifts and personal messages. It positions the brand as warm and human, and gives a broad audience, including parents, a reason to engage.
expected_strengths: Culturally rich and globally resonant, with strong storytelling potential
Involves families and gives a second audience a role
Tear-jerking film potential with a strong product use at the heart
main_concerns: Familiar emotional territory that many brands (banks, insurers) have touched
Distant from B2B and productivity positioning

candidates.title: The First Invoice Club
candidates.core_idea: For freelancers, creators and gig workers, the 'first paycheck' is actually the first invoice they dare to send, and the hardest part is pricing and presenting themselves. Canva launches the First Invoice Club: a program and toolkit (invoice, rate card, proposal and portfolio templates) with mentors who share their own first invoice and what they charged. candidates.brand_connection: Canva already powers small businesses and solo entrepreneurs. This links a practical business need to a real emotional barrier (undervaluing yourself), positioning Canva as the business starter kit and feeding Canva's business and Pro offering.
expected_strengths: Strong B2B and small-business relevance with a direct conversion path to paid plans

reasons_for_selection: It rests on the sharpest, most original insight: the paycheck arrives before the feeling of being a professional, so there is a gap that Canva can close.

It is strategically grounded in Canva's core promise of giving people the confidence to produce work that looks capable, without needing to be an expert.

rejected.reason: Emotionally appealing and shareable, but sentimental and consumer-leaning, with privacy risks and a weak link to the workplace objective. Best used as a supporting ritual inside the chosen idea rather than as the platform.

Warm and culturally resonant, but the territory is already well trodden by financial and insurance brands, it does not assume a universal behaviour, and it is furthest from Canva's productivity and B2B role.

Commercially strong and insightful, but it addresses a narrower audience and reads as a utility program more than a broad cultural idea. Its best element, normalizing asking to be paid, could be a later extension aimed at freelancers.

revisions_after_selection.change: Reframed the tone from 'fix your imposter feelings' to 'your first paycheck is proof, now show it'. The campaign celebrates competence rather than diagnosing insecurity.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The original framing risked amplifying anxiety and sounding patronising to a young audience. A confident, celebratory tone fits Canva's optimistic personality.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a signature ritual from C1: a small 'first payday' moment in the product where new users can mark the day, for example a shareable 'Day One Pro' card, with no pay data shown.
revisions_after_selection.reason: A rite of passage gives the functional kits an emotional and social hook, and keeps the idea shareable without the privacy risk of showing payslips.

revisions_after_selection.change: Extended the audience definition to include first-time freelancers and gig workers, with invoice and rate-card templates in the kit.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Many first paychecks are now invoices rather than salaries, so the campaign would otherwise miss a large and growing group, and it borrows the strongest element of C4.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added an employer and university onboarding partnership as the main B2B channel, so that kits can be included in welcome packs and first-week programs.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It converts consumer attention into team-level adoption and gives the idea a clear commercial role, in line with the B2B brief.

final_proposal.title: Paid Professional
final_proposal.idea: Your first paycheck says you're a professional. Your first week often doesn't feel like it. Paid Professional closes that gap. Canva marks the first payday with a 'Day One Pro' kit: the first deck, one-pager, status update, email signature, and for freelancers, the first invoice and rate card. All of it is built so a beginner looks as capable as they already are. A shareable 'Day One Pro' card lets people celebrate the milestone without showing a single number. Real first-timers and their managers show the first thing they made, and employers and universities hand the kit out at onboarding. The paycheck is proof of the job. Canva helps you show it. Each new hire who adopts Canva on day one becomes a quiet champion for it inside the team.
follow_up_questions: What is the very first piece of work a new hire is judged on, and how could the brand make that moment less intimidating in your market?
How might the ritual of marking a first payday differ across cultures, and which local customs could become the campaign's most distinctive creative expressions?
Beyond templates, what product or partnership could make Canva part of a company's onboarding itself, so adoption starts on day one rather than being discovered later?
