task_understanding.focus: Luxury fashion's 'buy new, desire new' logic is under pressure from repair culture, resale and visible mending. Dior already has what most brands lack: ateliers, couture-grade skills and a heritage of pieces meant to last. But repair is usually treated as a back-of-house service, not as desirable. The opportunity is to make repair and reuse feel like the most Dior thing a person can do, a form of status and craft rather than a sustainability apology.
assumptions: Dior offers some repair and restoration services for leather goods and ready-to-wear, but they are little known and framed as after-sales care, not as a brand statement.

Dior's strongest assets for this topic are the petites mains (the ateliers), the codes of Christian Dior (lucky star, lily of the valley, wheat ear, bee, houndstooth) and icons like the Bar jacket and Lady Dior.
The core audience is two groups: affluent aspirational buyers aged about 25-45 who already shop resale and value provenance, and long-time clients who own pieces of emotional value.

Luxury customers distrust sustainability claims, and the sector has faced scrutiny over supply-chain and labour practices. Any campaign must be backed by real services and measurable facts, not by tone alone.
Repair must not read as 'your Dior is broken' or as a way to sell less. It needs to read as an added layer of value and identity.
Operational capacity for repairs is limited, so the idea should work as a pilot that can scale, with honest turnaround times.

candidates.title: The Second Signature
candidates.core_idea: Repair becomes the final act of design. Any authentic Dior piece mended at the atelier can carry a small embroidered mark, chosen by the owner, drawn from Dior's lucky codes (star, lily of the valley, wheat ear), placed where the repair was made. The artisan's initials and the date are stitched inside the lining. Marks accumulate, so a piece with three marks has lived three lives. The ambition is a new status code: 'Ask to see the mark.'
candidates.brand_connection: Christian Dior was superstitious and surrounded himself with lucky charms, so the codes carry personal meaning. The idea also puts the petites mains' hands at the centre and turns the craft promise of couture into something a customer can wear.
expected_strengths: Makes repair visible, desirable and shareable, which is the main barrier to repair in luxury.
Built from existing Dior codes, so it feels native rather than bolted on.
Highly platformable: owner stories, a mark library, collector culture, social content, boutique experiences.
Gives every repair a human signature, which responds to the demand for craft transparency.
main_concerns: Some clients will want repairs to be invisible, so an invisible option must remain.
Risk of being read as 'branding the damage' if not handled with taste.
Needs atelier capacity and clear pricing to avoid disappointing clients.

candidates.title: Handed Down
candidates.core_idea: A reuse-led emotional campaign about inheritance. Dior invites people to bring in a piece they received from a mother, aunt or friend. The atelier restores it and re-fits it to the new wearer. Short films capture the handover moment, with the garment's story and measurements passed on with it, like a recipe.
candidates.brand_connection: Dior is a house of lineage: founder, successive creative directors, generations of clients. The New Look itself reinvented what was already there.
expected_strengths: Strong emotional pull and film potential.
Moves reuse from resale transactions to meaning and memory.
Appeals to long-time clients and their children, widening the audience.
main_concerns: Can feel sentimental and familiar, closer to heritage advertising than a cultural spark.
Hard to scale beyond storytelling into a repeatable behaviour.
Less appealing for younger buyers without family Dior to inherit.

candidates.title: Open Atelier
candidates.core_idea: Make the repair bench a stage. A working repair atelier is opened to the public in flagship windows and online, with named artisans mending real clients' pieces in real time. Visitors can follow a repair from intake to return, and artisans explain every decision.
candidates.brand_connection: The petites mains are Dior's most trusted proof of quality. Showing them at work in public makes craft the star, not the logo.
expected_strengths: Demonstrates credibility through transparency rather than claims.
Strong for retail traffic, press and live content.
Gives the brand a stronger answer to questions about how its products are made.
main_concerns: Opens the house to scrutiny of working conditions beyond the Paris ateliers, so it must be backed by supply-chain facts.
Observational content can feel like a documentary rather than a campaign idea with a clear client takeaway.
Hard to translate into something owners themselves do or share.

candidates.title: The Hundred-Year Hem
candidates.core_idea: A provocative, long-horizon pledge: Dior designates a small group of icon pieces, starting with the Bar jacket, as repairable for 100 years, with the promise published and dated. Each piece gets a repair record that travels through its owners. The campaign is a countdown toward 2126, with the first owners acting as custodians.
candidates.brand_connection: Dior has already outlived the founder by decades. A century-long promise matches the idea of timeless design and its own archive.
expected_strengths: Bold and quotable: it reframes the product as an heirloom with a guarantee.
Differentiates Dior from fast and aspirational fashion on the strength of a real commitment.
Supports resale value and trust in pre-owned Dior.
main_concerns: A 100-year promise is a major legal and operational commitment.
Risk of over-promising and being held to account, which would be a high-stakes greenwashing failure.
More of a product guarantee than a cultural idea, so it needs a strong expression to travel.

reasons_for_selection: It tackles the real barrier, that repair is hidden and feels like a downgrade, by making it a visible mark of status.
It is built from Dior's own codes and the petites mains, so it could not belong to any other brand.
It is a behaviour as well as a message: people choose a mark, wear it and show it, which gives the campaign a life beyond media.
It scales gradually: the mark can start with a few icon pieces and a pilot atelier, then grow without a heavy long-term legal promise.
It naturally absorbs the best parts of the other ideas: the artisan's initials give transparency, and the accumulating marks create a story of ownership.

rejected.reason: Emotionally strong but conventional for a heritage house, and it relies on storytelling rather than a new behaviour or product. Its best element, the handover moment, can be used as film content within C1.

Credible and useful as a transparency layer, but it centres on observing craft rather than on what customers do. It also exposes the brand to wider supply-chain scrutiny that a campaign alone cannot answer. The artisan-naming element is kept in C1.

Bold, but a 100-year promise creates large legal and operational risk and turns the idea into a guarantee, not a cultural spark. It is better kept as a possible later chapter once repair capacity is proven.

revisions_after_selection.change: Extended eligibility from pieces bought new to any authentic Dior piece, including pre-owned and inherited.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The brief covers reuse as well as repair. This links the idea to the resale and inheritance behaviour already present in the audience and increases the value of pre-owned Dior.

revisions_after_selection.change: Made the visible mark opt-in, with an invisible-repair option kept as standard.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Not all clients want visible mending. Choice protects the premium service while making the visible version a personal statement.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added public reporting of real repair numbers and turnaround times, and credited the artisan with initials inside the lining.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Luxury audiences are sceptical of sustainability claims. Verifiable facts and named craftspeople make the idea credible and reduce greenwashing risk.

revisions_after_selection.change: Dropped any language about 'scars' or 'flaws' in favour of 'lives' and 'signatures'.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Keeps the tone in line with Dior's elegance and avoids implying that the product is fragile.

revisions_after_selection.change: Positioned the rollout as a pilot with a small set of icon pieces (Bar jacket, Lady Dior) in a few cities.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Atelier capacity is limited, and a controlled start allows honest delivery promises before scaling.

final_proposal.title: The Second Signature
final_proposal.idea: Dior turns repair into the house's most intimate signature. Any authentic Dior piece, including pre-owned or inherited, can be mended at the atelier. The owner may choose to cover the repair with a small embroidery from Christian Dior's lucky codes: a star, lily of the valley, wheat ear. Inside the lining, the artisan stitches their initials and the date. Each mark records another life, so the most loved pieces become the most prized. The campaign films real owners alongside the petites mains, then invites people to show their mark: 'Ask to see the second signature.' It starts as a pilot on the Bar jacket and Lady Dior, with real repair numbers and turnaround times published so the promise stays credible.
follow_up_questions: What would make a visible repair mark feel like a status symbol to a client rather than evidence of damage, and who should be the first people seen wearing it?
How could the mark system grow beyond the lucky codes, for example by letting clients co-design a mark, without losing the exclusivity and craft of the atelier?

Which proof points (turnaround time, repair volumes, artisan credits) would make a sceptical luxury client believe the promise, and how can they be shared without sounding like a sustainability report?

task_understanding.focus: Loneliness is increasingly a daily, low-grade absence of small human contact rather than only a crisis of deep relationships. Payments sit at the centre of that shift. Contactless, self-checkout, delivery and in-app buying have made everyday life smoother and quieter. The opportunity is for Mastercard to put its 'Priceless' belief (the moments that matter are not the transactions) to work by using the payment moment to create human connection, without profiling or monetising people's loneliness.
assumptions: Mastercard's long-standing 'Priceless' platform gives it permission to talk about what money cannot buy, and loneliness is a natural, current extension of it.
The audience is broad: urban adults 25-45 who live alone, work remotely or have moved cities, plus older adults. All of them have lots of low-stakes commercial interactions and few meaningful ones.
Research on 'weak ties' suggests brief, friendly encounters (the barista who knows you) meaningfully lift wellbeing. A realistic brand role is to enable those, not to claim to cure loneliness.
Privacy and trust are non-negotiable for a payments brand. Any idea that infers loneliness from spending data would be seen as creepy and would damage the brand.
Mastercard cannot run venues itself, so ideas must work through merchants, partners and the card network's existing touchpoints, such as terminals, cards and apps.
Contactless payment has arguably contributed to reduced human interaction. Acknowledging this honestly will make the campaign more credible than pure uplift.
A campaign should be platformable: able to grow across product, retail, PR and content, not a single stunt.

candidates.title: Statement of Us
candidates.core_idea: An opt-in, year-end 'people statement' that reframes your spending as a record of who you shared life with: dinners split, gifts bought, rounds paid for. It then nudges you to reconnect with the people who have dropped off. The bank statement becomes a diary of relationships rather than a ledger.
candidates.brand_connection: Mastercard owns the idea that value lies in experiences and people. This turns transaction data into a mirror of what the brand says matters.
expected_strengths: Strong, shareable insight: 'your statement knows who you've been with'.
Emotionally resonant and easy to personalise.
Natural year-end PR moment.
main_concerns: High privacy risk. It reads as surveillance of social life, which is dangerous for a payments brand.
Mastercard does not hold issuer-level customer relationships, so execution depends on banks.
It could leave people feeling worse by showing them how few people appear.

candidates.title: Unpayable
candidates.core_idea: A stance-led campaign. Mastercard publishes 'The Price of Company': what people now pay to feel less alone, such as rent-a-friend services, AI companions and tipping for a chat. It then creates a free 'Unpayable' mark for community hours, tables and benches where connection is deliberately not for sale.
candidates.brand_connection: It flips 'Priceless' into a provocation: a payments company saying some things should never be priced. This is bold and ties directly to the brand's core thought.
expected_strengths: Provocative and newsworthy, with a strong cultural point of view.
Research and report give credibility and PR reach.
A recognisable mark could become a platform asset.
main_concerns: Risk of seeming hypocritical or preachy for a company that profits from payments.
The mark needs partners and governance to mean anything.
Mostly a message, with limited everyday behaviour change.

candidates.title: Split with a Stranger
candidates.core_idea: Pop-up communal tables where the bill is only payable when two strangers tap their cards together on a shared terminal, and each pays half. Friction becomes the invitation to start a conversation.
candidates.brand_connection: It uses the tap, Mastercard's most recognisable interaction, as a social device, and makes the card the thing that brings people together.
expected_strengths: Highly visual and filmable, with a clear mechanic.
A playful way to dramatise connection through payment.

task_understanding.focus: Luxury fashion sells newness and desire, yet its most defensible sustainability story is durability: pieces made to be mended, not replaced. The opportunity is to make repair and reuse feel like the highest form of luxury, rather than a guilt-driven add-on, by rooting it in Dior's couture ateliers and their culture of making, fitting and remaking by hand.
assumptions: Dior's core equity is savoir-faire: the ateliers, the petites mains, and the couture tradition of fitting and altering garments for a specific body.
Luxury customers increasingly question overconsumption and 'quiet luxury' has shifted status toward longevity, provenance and craft over logos.
Resale and vintage Dior (Galliano-era, Saddle bag, Book Tote) already carry huge cultural cachet, but Dior captures little of that value or story.
Repair is currently seen in luxury as a back-of-store service, which is functional, invisible and slightly embarrassing, not a desirable experience.
The target audience is aspirational and established Dior buyers aged roughly 25-45, plus younger vintage hunters who love Dior but may never buy new.
Dior cannot appear to discourage purchasing, so the idea must grow desirability and loyalty rather than preach restraint.
Any claims must be credible and avoid greenwashing; the idea should be about craft and care, not carbon statistics.

candidate.title: Dior Second Fitting
candidate.core_idea: In couture, a garment is never finished at the first fitting; it is refined until it belongs to the body. 'Second Fitting' extends that ritual across the life of every Dior piece. Any Dior item, bought new, inherited, or found secondhand, can be brought to the atelier for a Second Fitting: repaired, re-cut, re-lined or reimagined by the same hands that make the collections. Nothing is hidden. Repairs are made visible as signature craft: a Dior-grey stitch, a re-embroidered patch, a dated atelier label inside the lining recording each fitting. A garment's life becomes a documented lineage of owners and atelier interventions, making older, mended pieces more valuable and more coveted than pristine ones. The campaign launches with a Paris atelier residency and a film in which a worn Saddle bag, a 1990s jacket and a grandmother's New Look skirt each receive a Second Fitting, with the new owner and the petite main who works on it. It then scales via a 'Second Fitting' label, a limited seasonal capsule made from reclaimed atelier fabric, and pop-up fitting rooms in key cities that welcome vintage Dior regardless of where it was purchased.
candidate.brand_connection: It builds directly on Dior's most ownable asset: the atelier and the couture practice of fitting. It elevates the petites mains from anonymous makers to cultural heroes, reinforces Monsieur Dior's idea of clothes made to last and to flatter an individual, and turns the heritage archive into a living service. It also lets Dior claim the booming vintage and resale culture on its own terms, without becoming a resale platform.
expected_strengths: Reframes repair as an upgrade and a status marker, not a sacrifice, which suits luxury psychology.
Highly ownable: only Dior has these ateliers, this archive and the couture fitting ritual.
Platformable across film, retail experiences, product (labels, capsules), social content, and PR.
Brings in younger vintage-loving audiences and creates new reasons to enter Dior stores and build lifelong relationships.
Visible mending and dated lineage labels create shareable, collectible proof, and organic social content.
Supports retention and lifetime value, since each fitting is a touchpoint with the client.
main_concerns: Atelier capacity: demand could outstrip skilled labour, so access, pricing and waiting times need careful design.
Risk of seeming elitist or tokenistic if repair is only for top clients or only a pop-up gesture rather than a standing service.
Servicing items bought secondhand or unauthenticated needs a clear authentication and policy stance.
Greenwashing scrutiny: must be paired with credible operational commitments on materials, durability and take-back.
Internal tension with a newness-driven business model; needs to be positioned as additive and loyalty-building.

final_proposal.title: Dior Second Fitting
final_proposal.idea: In couture, a dress is never finished at the first fitting. Second Fitting extends that ritual across a garment's whole life. Bring any Dior piece, new, inherited or found in a vintage shop, to the atelier, where the same hands that make the collections repair, re-cut or reimagine it. Repairs are worn proudly: a Dior-grey stitch, a re-embroidered patch, a dated label inside the lining recording every fitting, so a piece's history becomes its value. A film follows a worn Saddle bag, a 1990s jacket and a grandmother's skirt through the atelier, spotlighting the petites mains. Pop-up fitting rooms and a capsule from reclaimed atelier fabric carry it into the world. Luxury isn't what stays untouched. It's what is worth keeping.
follow_up_questions: How could the dated 'fitting label' become a collectible, tradeable record of a piece's life, and what would it mean for resale value?
Who should be the first faces of Second Fitting: celebrity owners, ordinary families with inherited pieces, or the petites mains themselves, and how does that choice change the story?
What would a democratic, standing version of this service look like beyond a Paris residency, so it avoids feeling like a one-off luxury gesture?

task_understanding.focus: The first paycheck is a rite of passage that nearly everyone remembers, but it is usually delivered in a confusing, undesigned document. Gross pay, deductions and net pay are a shock to first-time earners and a missed chance for the employers who issue them. The opportunity is for Canva to own the moment where work becomes real, using its core belief that clear, beautiful communication belongs to everyone, not only designers. This also gives Canva a way into the B2B workplace conversation (HR, small business owners, managers) through an emotional human moment.
assumptions: Canva's brand truth is that it makes visual communication simple and empowering for non-designers, and the campaign should demonstrate that truth rather than merely celebrate the topic.
The first paycheck is emotionally loaded (pride, independence, 'is this right?') and the gap between expected pay and actual pay is a near-universal, discussable and shareable experience.

The primary audience is first-time earners (teens, students, career starters, side-hustlers). The B2B audience is small business owners, HR and team managers who decide how new hires are welcomed and informed.
Canva is not a payroll or financial advice provider and should not act like one. Its role is clarity, presentation and celebration, not tax or legal guidance.
Gen Z and young millennials respond to honest, self-aware cultural commentary and to creating and sharing their own versions, more than to polished brand sentiment.
Canva's template ecosystem, Visual Suite (docs, charts, whiteboards, video) and Canva for Teams can act as the campaign's product proof.

candidates.title: The Paycheck, Explained
candidates.core_idea: Pay stubs are among the most important and least designed documents of adult life. Canva publicly redesigns the first-paycheck experience: a 'Pay Stub Makeover' that turns the gross-to-net shock into a clear, friendly visual story, plus free templates employers and first-timers can use to explain a paycheck in plain, visual language. The platform is 'Design is how things make sense.'
candidates.brand_connection: It dramatises Canva's core promise of making complex information clear and beautiful for anyone. It also gives B2B teams (HR, small business owners) a practical template use case, using charts, docs and brand kits.
expected_strengths: Taps a universal, slightly funny truth ('where did my money go?') that people already talk about, so it is naturally shareable.
Product-led proof: the campaign is the product in action.
Serves both the emotional consumer audience and the practical B2B audience.
Extends easily into formats such as makeover reveals, creator explainers, employer toolkits and OOH that mimics ugly pay stubs.
main_concerns: Risk of seeming to give tax or financial advice, which would need careful framing and disclaimers.
Payroll data is sensitive, so templates should use no real data.
Could feel dry if the emotional first-paycheck moment is not kept at the center.

candidates.title: First Paid Pixel
candidates.core_idea: Celebrate the first time someone is paid for something they made. Canva invites people to share the first design that earned them money (a lawn-care flyer, a bake-sale menu, a band poster) next to the first paycheck it produced, and builds a living archive of 'first paid work' that proves creativity can be a livelihood.
candidates.brand_connection: It positions Canva as the tool behind first creative incomes, linking to Canva Creators, the marketplace and the side-hustle economy.
expected_strengths: Emotional and aspirational, with strong user-generated content potential.
Showcases the range of what non-designers make with Canva.
Supports Canva's creator and marketplace business.
main_concerns: Narrows the topic to people paid for design-like work, so it excludes the many first paychecks that come from retail, food service or labor.
Could read as self-congratulatory.
Less relevant to the B2B and productivity positioning.

candidates.title: Welcome to Payday
candidates.core_idea: Flip the lens to employers. The first paycheck is the moment a new hire decides whether they belong, yet it usually arrives with silence or a PDF. Canva launches a 'First Payday Kit' for managers and small business owners: a personal note, a visual 'what this means' explainer, a team shout-out and a celebratory moment, all customisable in minutes. The message: 'Make the first paycheck feel like a first.'
candidates.brand_connection: Directly B2B, using Canva for Teams, brand kits and collaborative workflows to improve onboarding and culture.
expected_strengths: Clear commercial relevance and a concrete workplace use case.
Low-cost gesture for employers with an outsized emotional payoff.
Fits retention and culture conversations that buyers care about.
main_concerns: Employer-led emotion can feel corporate or performative if the new hire's voice is missing.
Less culturally disruptive and harder to make viral.
Depends on adoption by managers rather than first-time earners themselves.

candidates.title: Official
candidates.core_idea: The first paycheck is the moment imposter feelings meet proof: you now officially have a job. Canva makes 'Official' a ritual, a first-job identity kit generated the week the first paycheck lands: a business card, a LinkedIn banner, a name badge, a 'first day to first paycheck' recap video. The idea is that you stop pretending once you can show it.
candidates.brand_connection: Canva already powers personal and professional identity assets, and this ties them to a defining life moment.
expected_strengths: Emotionally resonant, built on a real insight about belonging and imposter syndrome.
Naturally creates personal, shareable assets.
Easy to scale across social, campus and early-career channels.
main_concerns: Overlaps with existing Canva resume and LinkedIn use cases, so it may feel familiar.
Focuses on self-presentation rather than the paycheck itself.
Less strong on the B2B or team angle.

reasons_for_selection: It is the most strategically ownable: only a brand whose purpose is making information clear and beautiful can credibly redesign the pay stub.
It starts from a sharp, widely shared tension (the gap between expected and actual pay) that people already joke about, which makes it platformable and shareable.
It works for all first-time earners, not just creatives, and also gives B2B buyers a practical reason to engage.
It demonstrates the product rather than just talking about the topic, so the idea is also the proof.
It can carry the emotional beat of the other directions (celebration, belonging) inside a clarity-led platform.

rejected.reason: Emotionally appealing but too narrow: it speaks mainly to people paid for creative work and leaves out most first-paycheck experiences. It also leans toward the creator economy rather than Canva's B2B and productivity focus.
Commercially sensible but less culturally sparky and dependent on employer adoption. Its strongest element (the personal welcome) is better used as an extension of the selected idea.
Insightful about belonging, but it moves away from the paycheck itself and overlaps with existing resume and LinkedIn behaviours, so it is less distinctive for Canva.

revisions_after_selection.change: Reframed the promise from 'understand your taxes' to 'understand your paycheck at a glance', limited to layout, plain language and visual explanation, with a clear note that Canva does not give financial advice.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Avoids regulatory and credibility risk and keeps Canva in its lane of clarity and design.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added an emotional opening beat: a 'First Paycheck Reveal' moment where first-timers see their stub transformed, with a keepsake version they can save or share.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Prevents the idea from becoming a dry explainer and restores the pride and nostalgia that make the topic memorable.

revisions_after_selection.change: Built in an employer layer: editable templates with placeholder data for HR and small business owners, including a short personal welcome note to the new hire.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Brings in the best element of C3, strengthens the B2B relevance and avoids handling any real payroll data.

final_proposal.title: The Paycheck, Explained
final_proposal.idea: Everyone remembers their first paycheck, and everyone remembers the shock: the number you were promised, then the number you got. It arrives on one of the least designed documents of adult life. Canva makes it make sense. The campaign launches with a Pay Stub Makeover: real first-timers hand over a confusing stub (with personal data removed) and watch it become a clear, friendly visual story, from 'what I earned' to 'where it went' to 'what's mine'. Free templates let employers add a personal welcome note, and let anyone redesign and save their own as a keepsake. The line of thought: design is how things make sense. It is not financial advice. It is clarity, made by Canva, for the moment work becomes real.
follow_up_questions: What other 'first-time adult documents' (a lease, a contract, a bill) are confusing in the same way, and could Canva own a wider territory of making adult life legible?
How could employers or payroll partners take part without Canva touching real data, and what would make a manager want to send a first-paycheck welcome note?
What is the most honest, funny or touching way to dramatise the first-paycheck shock, and who is the best voice to tell it (a creator, a parent, a first boss)?

task_understanding.focus: Loneliness is usually discussed as an emotional problem, but it often has a practical, invisible cause: money friction around being together. People turn down invitations, avoid hosting and drift from friends because they are unsure what a plan will cost or afraid of the awkward bill-split. Mastercard owns the moment where money meets human connection, so the opportunity is to remove the financial friction that keeps people apart and make saying yes easier, without ever preaching about loneliness.
assumptions: Mastercard's 'Priceless' platform ('there are some things money can't buy, for everything else there's Mastercard') gives it a credible, long-held link to shared experiences, and its role is to be the network that makes connection easier, not to be a friend.
Mastercard is a network, not a card issuer or a consumer app, so any product-led idea has to work through issuers, merchants and fintech partners, or be a pilot.

Cost anxiety is a real but under-voiced reason people decline plans. This should be validated with Mastercard's own research or a commissioned survey before launch, and no statistics are assumed here.

The audience is adults roughly 22-45 whose friendships thin out through life changes (new city, remote work, uneven incomes), plus the 'quietly isolated' who would never describe themselves as lonely.
Lonely people reject the label and are put off by pity-based messaging, so the work should be framed around invitations and belonging, not loneliness itself.
A finance brand entering an emotional topic must show behaviour and utility, not just sentiment, and must protect privacy and trust above all.

candidates.title: Cap It: the invitation with a price ceiling
candidates.core_idea: Reframe a hidden cause of isolation: people say no because they cannot see what saying yes will cost. 'Cap It' makes the price ceiling part of the invitation ('Dinner Friday. Cap: $25. Everyone's in.'). The host sets a per-person ceiling, partner venues offer 'capped' menus and experiences, and issuer partners can enforce or track the cap on shared plans. The ceiling is a social signal that announces 'you can afford this.'
candidates.brand_connection: It builds on Priceless by making shared experiences accessible, and it uses Mastercard's real assets: the merchant acceptance network, issuer relationships and payment rules. The brand's role is to enable the yes.
expected_strengths: Names a surprising, specific, human tension (the unspoken 'I can't afford it') instead of a generic loneliness message.
Platformable: invite templates, capped menus, 'Cap Night' events, creator and community hosting, a recurring seasonal moment.
Product-grounded and measurable (capped plans created, venues joined, invitations accepted).
Avoids pity and stigma, so it appeals to people who do not see themselves as lonely.
main_concerns: Requires issuer and merchant partners, so scale depends on their buy-in.
Risk of reading as a budgeting tool unless the emotional hook leads.
The cost-anxiety assumption needs research to confirm.

candidates.title: Table for One More: the open seat
candidates.core_idea: Dining alone is where loneliness is most visible. Restaurants add 'open seats' at shared tables, and a solo diner can choose to sit with others. Cardholders can also pay for an extra seat that a stranger can claim.
candidates.brand_connection: Priceless dining experiences and the idea that a meal is worth more than its cost. The tap becomes a gesture of hospitality.
expected_strengths: Highly visual and photogenic, with strong PR and social potential.
Simple to understand and emotionally warm.
Fits easily with Mastercard's existing dining and city partnerships.
main_concerns: Shared-table and stranger-matching concepts already exist, so novelty is limited.
Safety, comfort and operational burden for restaurants.
Could pathologise eating alone, which many people enjoy, and reinforce stigma.

candidates.title: Noticed: the routine nudge
candidates.core_idea: With explicit opt-in, a cardholder nominates someone they trust. If a regular pattern (the daily café, the weekly grocery run) stops for a set period, the trusted person gets a gentle prompt to check in. It turns payment patterns into a signal that someone has gone quiet.
candidates.brand_connection: Mastercard understands everyday routines at scale and could use that for good, in the spirit of its data-for-good positioning.
expected_strengths: Provocative, newsworthy and strategically sharp, with real benefits for isolated older adults.
Makes the brand's unique data capability emotionally meaningful.
main_concerns: Privacy and surveillance fears are severe for a financial brand, and trust damage would outweigh the benefits.
Mastercard does not hold cardholder-level relationships, so legal and operational barriers are heavy.
Risk of false alarms and of feeling intrusive or paternalistic.

candidates.title: Known By Name: the regular's welcome
candidates.core_idea: Being known by name is a quiet antidote to isolation. Local merchants use the name a cardholder chooses to be called when they tap, so the barista, shopkeeper or driver greets them by it. The campaign celebrates 'regular' culture and makes neighbourhood belonging a daily ritual.
candidates.brand_connection: Extends the thinking behind Mastercard True Name, where the name on the card is the name the person actually uses, into the moment of payment.
expected_strengths: Emotionally powerful and small enough to be believable.
Draws on an existing, credible brand asset and a values story.
main_concerns: Requires merchant point-of-sale changes and a clear privacy model.
Narrower reach: it addresses recognition, not the barrier to making and keeping friends.
Risk of blurring the True Name message, which has a specific inclusion purpose.

reasons_for_selection: It offers the most original and revealing insight: loneliness is often sustained by financial uncertainty around plans, not just by a lack of people.
It lets Mastercard act within its real remit (payments, acceptance, shared experiences) and delivers a concrete benefit rather than a sentiment.
It is the most platformable: one simple mechanic (the cap) can be expressed as an invite, a menu, an event, a creator format and an annual ritual.
It avoids stigma by never labelling the audience as lonely, and it avoids the privacy and trust risks that sink C3.
It is feasible as a phased pilot with a small number of issuer and merchant partners, then scalable.

rejected.reason: Warm and visual but familiar, since shared-table and stranger-dining formats already exist. It also risks stigmatising solo dining and carries safety and operational concerns, and it addresses a single moment rather than the underlying barrier.

The most provocative, but turning payment patterns into a welfare signal creates serious privacy, legal and trust risk for a financial brand. A single misstep would damage the brand more than the idea could help it.
A lovely and credible ritual, but it is narrower in impact, depends on merchant point-of-sale changes, and risks diluting the True Name inclusion story. It could work later as a supporting element.

revisions_after_selection.change: Lead the creative with the emotional moment of the unspoken 'I can't afford it' and the relief of a visible cap, rather than leading with the product mechanic.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Prevents the idea from reading as a budgeting tool and keeps it culturally relevant and on-brand for Priceless.

revisions_after_selection.change: Never use the word 'lonely' in consumer-facing creative; frame the platform around invitations, saying yes and showing up.
revisions_after_selection.reason: People who are isolated often reject the label, and a pity tone would repel the audience we want to reach.

revisions_after_selection.change: Make the cap a host-set, group-visible number that is never linked to any individual's finances or income.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Protects privacy and dignity, and ensures the cap lowers social risk instead of exposing who is struggling.

revisions_after_selection.change: Launch as a partner-led pilot (a few issuers, a set of capped-menu venues in two or three cities) with a single annual 'Cap Night' as the public moment.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Mastercard is a network and cannot ship a consumer feature alone, so a pilot proves the model and creates a repeatable cultural ritual.

revisions_after_selection.change: Commission a short research study to validate how often cost uncertainty causes people to decline plans, and use it as the campaign's opening proof point.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The core insight is currently an assumption; credible evidence strengthens the story and the PR.

final_proposal.title: Cap It
final_proposal.idea: Many people don't turn down plans because they don't want company. They turn them down because they can't see the cost, and they'd rather stay home than say so. Cap It puts the price ceiling into the invitation: 'Dinner Friday. Cap: $25. Everyone's in.' Partner venues offer capped menus and experiences, issuers make shared plans easy to track, and the cap is set by the host and never tied to anyone's finances. Mastercard launches it as a pilot in a few cities, built around an annual Cap Night when thousands of tables, hosted by friends, neighbours and creators, say yes at a price everyone can meet. We never say 'lonely'. We make saying yes cheaper, easier and a little braver, because the best things in life are priceless, but showing up shouldn't be out of reach.
follow_up_questions: Which other invisible frictions (time, logistics, embarrassment, travel cost) stop people from seeing one another, and could Mastercard remove one of them in a similarly simple way?
How could the cap become a shared cultural symbol, like a badge, a hashtag or a phrase people use in everyday invitations, so that it spreads without Mastercard's help?
Who should host the first Cap Nights (community groups, local creators, workplaces, neighbours), and how would each change the tone and reach of the platform?

task_understanding.focus: Canva is seen as a design tool for 'designers-adjacent' people, but its real growth lies in becoming the first professional tool people reach for when they start earning money from their own skills. The first paycheck is a rite of passage, and for a growing share of Gen Z and young millennials it no longer comes from an employer. It comes from a side hustle, a freelance gig, a first client, or a small shop. The opportunity is to own the moment when 'making things' turns into 'getting paid for things', and to position Canva as the tool that makes a beginner look like a business from the first invoice.
assumptions: Canva's core base is non-designers (students, small business owners, freelancers, marketers), and its growth depends on moving them from casual use to professional, paid use, including Canva Pro and Teams.
For many young people the first paycheck is a mix of identity, pride and anxiety (imposter syndrome, 'do I deserve this?'), and not only about money.
The first paycheck increasingly comes from self-directed work (a freelancer's first invoice, an Etsy sale, a creator brand deal) as well as from a first job, so the campaign should honor both.
Young earners often feel they look 'amateur' and underprice themselves because their materials (invoice, portfolio, pitch, logo) don't look professional.
Many people photograph, frame or share their first paycheck or first payment notification, so there is an existing cultural ritual to build on.
The audience is skeptical of corporate 'hustle culture' messaging and responds better to warmth, humor and honesty than to motivational clichés.
Canva has strong template and community infrastructure (creators, Canva Create, template marketplace) that can scale a participatory campaign globally with local adaptations.

candidate.title: The First Invoice
candidate.core_idea: Reframe the first paycheck as the moment you first send a professional document that says 'I'm worth paying'. Canva launches 'The First Invoice', a campaign and template collection built around the very first thing a new earner makes: an invoice, a rate card, a thank-you note to the first client, a 'first paycheck' frame. The campaign invites people to design and share the document that got them their first money, and celebrates it like a graduation. A hero film follows several people (a 19-year-old dog walker, a 40-year-old career changer, a teen selling stickers) whose first invoice is a little messy, then shows how a polished one changes how they see themselves and how clients treat them. Canva turns the real first invoices of its community into a public 'Museum of First Invoices', with each entry showing the amount, the story and the template used. Every first-time Canva Pro user who sends their first invoice gets a small keepsake: a printable 'framed first paycheck' that they can design in the app. Local versions swap in the invoice and payment conventions of each market.
candidate.brand_connection: Canva's promise is that anyone can design, and that design is not a luxury but a form of confidence. The first invoice is the most underrated piece of design in a young person's life: it decides whether you are taken seriously, and it is something people usually build from a blank doc with shame. It lets Canva move from 'make a poster' to 'help me get paid', which supports its B2B and small-business push (Pro, Teams, brand kits, Canva for Business) with an emotionally real entry point. It also reinforces the brand truth that looking professional is a skill you can borrow, not a privilege.
expected_strengths: Finds a small, specific, human object (the first invoice) inside a huge cultural topic, which makes the idea ownable and avoids generic 'money and hustle' messaging.
Moves Canva toward higher-value, professional use cases and creates a natural funnel to Pro, brand kits and business features.
Highly participatory and shareable: people love showing their 'first' and the Museum creates a long-lived UGC archive.
Easily scalable via templates and creators, and adaptable by country, currency and trade (tutors, photographers, bakers, developers).
Emotional and slightly funny rather than preachy; the contrast between messy first invoice and polished one is a strong storytelling device.
Inclusive of different life stages, so it avoids being only about teenagers with a first job.
main_concerns: Invoices sound unglamorous; the creative work must make them feel emotional and visual rather than administrative.
Canva is not an invoicing or payments platform, so there is a risk of overpromising (tax, legal, payment processing). Partnerships or clear scope are needed.
Sharing income amounts is sensitive; the Museum needs optional anonymity and clear consent and moderation.
The campaign could be read as encouraging unpaid-to-underpaid gig work; tone needs to respect fair pay and avoid glorifying hustle.
Invoice formats and norms vary widely by country and by employment type, which adds localization cost.

final_proposal.title: The First Invoice
final_proposal.idea: Everyone remembers their first paycheck. Nobody remembers the thing they made to earn it. Canva turns the first invoice into the new rite of passage. A hero film follows a teenage sticker seller, a dog walker and a career changer as they send their first, slightly embarrassing invoice, then their first polished one, and notice how clients, and they themselves, respond differently. Canva releases a collection of First Invoice templates, rate cards and thank-you notes, and invites people to share the document that got them paid, with the amount optional. The best entries become a living Museum of First Invoices, and every new earner can design a keepsake 'framed first paycheck'. The message: you don't need to feel professional first. You need to look like someone worth paying, and Canva helps you borrow that confidence until it becomes yours.
follow_up_questions: What other 'first' documents or objects in a working life (the first business card, the first pitch deck, the first 'out of office') carry as much emotion as the first invoice, and could be their own chapters?
How could the campaign celebrate people whose first paycheck came from an employer rather than a side hustle, without losing the 'first invoice' focus?
What would make a person proud, rather than exposed, to publicly share what they earned, and how might the Museum protect and honor that?

task_understanding.focus: Loneliness is rarely about having no one. It is about having no easy first move. Reaching out feels like asking for something: it needs a plan, a cost and a social debt, so 'we should catch up' dies in the group chat. Payments are where plans become real. The opportunity is for Mastercard to use its role in removing friction from money to remove the friction from connection, with Priceless as the emotional frame: the best things in life are experiences with people, not purchases.
assumptions: Mastercard's brand equity is Priceless (value found in moments, not price), plus recent purpose work on inclusion (True Name, Touch Card). Loneliness fits as 'what money can't buy, but can help start'.
As a network and not a consumer app, Mastercard works through issuers, fintech partners and merchants, so ideas should be launchable as partnerships or pilots.
Loneliness is a high-stakes, stigmatised topic. The brand should never label or diagnose people as lonely, and it must not look as if it profits from pain.
Privacy and trust are core to the category. Any use of spending data must be opt-in, aggregated or avoided entirely.

The core audience is 25-45 urban and suburban adults with plenty of acquaintances but thin real-world contact (remote workers, new movers, new parents), with a secondary audience of older adults. Both are digitally connected and socially hesitant.
Cashless, contactless and self-checkout life has quietly removed many tiny human interactions. Mastercard is partly implicated, so the brand should show some self-awareness.

candidates.title: The Slow Lane
candidates.core_idea: Reclaim the micro-conversations that frictionless payment erased. Partner with retailers and cafés to open 'Slow Lanes': checkout lanes where the tap is the start of a chat, with staff trained and rewarded for conversation, and a custom 'hello' sound for the Mastercard sonic mark. The campaign's provocation is that the most advanced payment brand is asking for a little friction back.
candidates.brand_connection: Mastercard acknowledges its own role in speed and convenience, then uses its acceptance network and sonic identity to restore the human moment in payments. It is a bold admission and a clear Priceless point of view.
expected_strengths: Surprising, self-aware stance that earns press and cultural conversation
Draws on a real behavioural truth: the checkout chat is a lonely person's only conversation of the day
Strong use of sonic branding and physical retail environments
main_concerns: Hard to scale beyond pilots and dependent on merchant staffing and goodwill
Could read as a stunt, or even irritate time-poor shoppers
Reaches people already out in the world, not the most isolated

candidates.title: On Me
candidates.core_idea: Make the first move free. 'On Me' is a pre-paid invitation: a small virtual card tied to a specific place and time ('Coffee at Rosa's, Thursday 4pm, on me') that you send to someone you've been meaning to see. The recipient taps to accept, and the cost, the plan and the awkwardness of asking are already handled. When they accept, they receive their own 'On Me' to pass on to someone else, so one invitation can start a chain of meetings.
candidates.brand_connection: It sits at the heart of what Mastercard does: moving money to make something happen. It turns payment from a transaction into a gesture, which is Priceless in action, and it drives real spend at local merchants.
expected_strengths: Attacks the actual barrier (the first move) with a product-shaped answer
Highly platformable: pass-it-on chains, merchant partnerships, city launches, user stories
Naturally social and shareable, with clear behavioural data on meetings that happened
main_concerns: Competes with peer-to-peer payment apps and gift cards, so the difference must be the invitation, not the money
Risk of feeling like 'buying friendship' or putting the recipient in debt
Needs issuer and merchant partners to work, and funding for the pilot

candidates.title: Regulars
candidates.core_idea: Celebrate and manufacture belonging at the neighbourhood level. Mastercard launches 'Regulars', a recognition programme for local cafés, barbers, bakeries and bars that make people feel known. Merchants get a Regulars mark, and cardholders get a small, personal 'we know your order' moment, including a card showing the name they choose to be called by. The campaign tells the stories of the places where someone is greeted by name.
candidates.brand_connection: It builds on Mastercard's small-business support and its True Name belief that being seen as who you are is a form of dignity. It places the brand in the third places where community happens.
expected_strengths: Warm, emotionally rich storytelling with real merchants
Supports small businesses, which is brand-aligned and credible
Easy to localise by city and neighbourhood
main_concerns: Closer to existing small-business and loyalty programmes, so less distinctive
Rewards people who already go out and risks feeling like a loyalty scheme
Slow to build meaningful scale

candidates.title: Connection Budget
candidates.core_idea: People budget for rent, groceries and subscriptions but never for seeing each other. In partnership with banks, Mastercard introduces an opt-in 'Connection' category in money apps: a small monthly pot reserved only for shared experiences, such as coffees, dinners, tickets and trains to visit family. The pot nudges users to spend it before the month ends, and unspent money rolls into a 'next time' gift for someone else.
candidates.brand_connection: It uses Mastercard's role in financial tools and issuer partnerships to treat connection as something worth planning and funding, the Priceless idea turned into a budgeting habit.
expected_strengths: Reframes social spending as essential, not indulgent
Fits issuer and fintech app ecosystems and generates measurable behaviour
Clear, simple concept that is easy to explain
main_concerns: Tracking social spending feels surveillant and clashes with privacy expectations
Money is rarely the main barrier to seeing people, so it may miss the real insight
Dependent on bank partners' product roadmaps and slow to launch

reasons_for_selection: It targets the true behavioural barrier, the awkward first move, rather than a symptom such as the lack of venues or budgets.
It is a product-led idea that only a payments brand can credibly own, which turns Priceless from a sentiment into a mechanism.
The pass-it-on chain gives it built-in momentum, a clear campaign narrative, and a way to show real outcomes (meetings that happened).
It scales from a single-city pilot with a few merchants to a national platform, and it drives measurable benefit to local businesses.

rejected.reason: A bold and surprising stance, but it depends on retail staff and shopper patience, is hard to scale, and mainly reaches people who are already out in public. Its best elements, the human moment and the sonic 'hello', can be folded into On Me as the sound of an accepted invitation.

Warm and credible but too close to existing small-business and loyalty programmes, and it recognises belonging that exists rather than helping people create it. Better as a supporting merchant layer than as the main idea.

The budgeting insight is clever, but it assumes money is the barrier, and categorising and tracking social spending raises privacy concerns that clash with a trust-based brand. It is also slow to launch and weaker on emotion.

revisions_after_selection.change: Make the invitation about a specific place and time with the cost already covered, not a cash transfer.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Money sent to a person feels like charity or debt. An invitation to a coffee feels like a gift, which avoids the 'buying friendship' risk and separates On Me from peer-to-peer payment apps.

revisions_after_selection.change: Never use the word 'lonely' in the product or in messages to recipients. The invitation says things like 'Thinking of you', and the campaign tells stories of reconnecting.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Naming loneliness stigmatises users and makes people less likely to send or accept an invitation. The brand should lead with warmth and keep the topic in the campaign story, not in the interface.

revisions_after_selection.change: Add a pass-it-on mechanic: each accepted invitation gives the recipient one On Me to send to someone else.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It turns recipients into senders, removes the sense of obligation to repay the sender, and gives the campaign natural momentum.

revisions_after_selection.change: Launch in one city with independent local merchants and one issuer partner, and use Mastercard's sonic logo as the 'accepted' sound.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It keeps the pilot feasible and credible, supports small businesses, and builds a distinctive sensory brand asset that carries ideas from C1 and C3.

revisions_after_selection.change: Measure success by invitations accepted and meetings that happened, with no personal spending data used.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It protects privacy and trust, and gives a more meaningful outcome than transaction volume.

final_proposal.title: On Me
final_proposal.idea: Most lonely people aren't short of contacts. They're short of an easy first move. 'We should catch up' dies because reaching out feels like asking. On Me removes the ask. Send someone a pre-paid invitation to a specific place and time: 'Coffee at Rosa's, Thursday 4pm. On me.' They tap to accept, and Mastercard's sonic logo plays as a small 'hello'. After the meeting, they receive their own On Me to pass to someone else, so one invitation can start a chain of reunions. It never says 'lonely' and never sends cash, only a reason to show up. Launch in one city with independent cafés and a single issuer partner, then tell the stories of the chains. Priceless, made practical.
follow_up_questions: What other moments of social hesitation (new neighbours, former colleagues, old friends, family you've drifted from) could an invitation with the cost already covered unlock?
How could the pass-it-on chain become a visible, city-wide story without exposing anyone's private connections?
What would a credible role for the brand look like outside payments, such as pairing On Me with community groups or care organisations, without turning loneliness into a marketing opportunity?

task_understanding.focus: Luxury fashion's status system runs on newness, yet younger affluent buyers increasingly read longevity, provenance and care as the smarter flex. Dior owns a rare asset for this shift: ateliers full of petites mains, and a heritage of pieces built to last. The opportunity is to make repair and reuse feel like the most desirable, most Dior thing a client can do. It should not read as a compliance gesture or a eco-footnote to the next collection drop.
assumptions: Dior's equity rests on couture craftsmanship, Parisian ritual and desirability, so the campaign must feel like luxury and not like a thrift or sustainability-NGO message.
Dior already offers repair and restoration services, but they are low-profile, transactional and rarely culturally visible.
The core audience is affluent aspirational and established clients aged roughly 25-55, including secondhand and vintage Dior owners who are not yet full customers.

Luxury audiences are skeptical of greenwashing, and the sector has faced public scrutiny of supplier labour practices (including reports about Dior's Italian subcontracting), so claims must be modest and backed by action.
Repair can add revenue and loyalty, and can raise the desirability of new pieces by making them heirloom-worthy, rather than cannibalizing sales.
The client wants one platformable idea that works across retail, social, PR and product, not a one-off sustainability stunt.

candidates.title: The Signed Mend
candidates.core_idea: Make visible repair a new status mark. Mended Dior pieces are restored with a discreet, couture-grade signature stitch, such as a cannage-pattern darn or a tone-on-tone thread, so a repaired piece reads as proof of a life lived in Dior. Repair becomes a coveted detail, like a patina on a leather trunk.
candidates.brand_connection: Draws on Dior's cannage motif, atelier technique and the idea of the couture signature, turning craft into a visible code of the house.
expected_strengths: Gives repair a distinct visual language that can appear in editorial, street style and collaborations.
Turns a service into a status object, which suits luxury psychology.
Easy to execute in product and photography.
main_concerns: Visible mending is already a familiar trend (kintsugi, Patagonia Worn Wear, visible-mending craft culture), so originality is limited.
Some clients want invisible repair, so the mark could feel like a stigma.
Risks becoming an aesthetic gimmick, with people damaging pieces on purpose.

candidates.title: Made to Be Remade
candidates.core_idea: Design a capsule where pieces carry generous seam allowances, replaceable components and lifetime alteration promises, so they are built to be refitted as bodies, tastes and generations change. The campaign tagline concept is that Dior fits the life you actually have, not just the body you had on the day you bought it.
candidates.brand_connection: Couture is fundamentally about fit to one body. The idea extends that tailoring ethos across time and life stages.
expected_strengths: A real product and service innovation that gives the campaign substance.
Strong link to couture methods and the Bar jacket silhouette.
Opens a long-term relationship with clients through alterations.
main_concerns: Needs major design, production and service changes, so it is slow and expensive.
Reaches only new capsule buyers, not existing owners or secondhand audiences.
Low immediate cultural spark compared with an event or provocation.

candidates.title: The Return Collection
candidates.core_idea: The creative director builds a runway show from clients' own old Dior pieces. Clients return their worn pieces, which the ateliers reinterpret and send down the runway on the clients themselves, with the story of each piece told alongside it.
candidates.brand_connection: Taps Dior's archive culture and runway theatre, turning a show into an act of reuse and putting real clients inside the house's fashion narrative.
expected_strengths: Highly shareable and emotionally rich, with strong PR potential.
Elevates reuse as creative authorship, not charity.
Gives clients status as co-authors.
main_concerns: Event-based and episodic, with limited year-round behaviour change.
Reaches only a small number of clients directly.
May be seen as a gimmick, or as a cover for the main collections continuing as normal.

candidates.title: Fermé pour réparations
candidates.core_idea: On one day a year, Dior closes its flagship to new sales and hangs a sign: Closed for repairs. The boutique floor and windows become working ateliers where petites mans mend clients' Dior pieces in public view. The rest of the Dior boutique network joins in, so the gesture travels around the globe.
candidates.brand_connection: Puts the petites mains in the shop window instead of the newest bag. It flips a luxury house's most valuable retail space from selling newness to honouring care, in a distinctly Parisian voice.
expected_strengths: Bold, simple and visual, and instantly understood without explanation.
Recurring ritual that can become a durable, ownable platform.
Generates PR, social content and footfall while giving the repair service real visibility.
Humanizes the ateliers and reveals the craft behind the price.
main_concerns: A closure day could be dismissed as a stunt if nothing changes the rest of the year.
Short-term sales loss and operational complexity across many boutiques.
Scrutiny of supply-chain practices could make the gesture look hypocritical.

reasons_for_selection: It has the strongest cultural spark: a luxury house closing its own shop to repair things reverses category convention and is understood in one sentence.
It is platformable: a recurring ritual, with repair stories, atelier livestreams and a year-round appointment service all growing from it.
It uses a real Dior asset, the petites mains, and makes craft visible instead of just talking about it.
It includes secondhand and vintage owners, widening the audience beyond current clients without diluting the brand.
Its main risk, credibility, can be managed through specific revisions, while the other ideas have structural weaknesses (limited originality, high cost, narrow reach).

rejected.reason: Visible mending is a well-worn trend, so the idea lacks originality and may not feel distinctively Dior. It is also a design detail, not a campaign platform, and could be absorbed into C4 as a service option.
Substantive but slow and expensive, with a narrow reach limited to new capsule buyers. It has low immediate cultural spark and would be better treated as a longer-term product roadmap.
Emotionally strong but a one-off event with limited year-round behaviour change and limited direct reach. It risks being a showpiece that sits beside business as usual.

revisions_after_selection.change: Turned the closure into a fixed annual ritual with a year-round appointment service behind it, instead of a single stunt.
revisions_after_selection.reason: A one-day gesture invites accusations of performance. A recurring ritual with a lasting service shows commitment and builds the platform.

revisions_after_selection.change: Opened the day to any Dior piece of any age and origin, including vintage and secondhand finds.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Widens the audience to aspirational and younger owners, and signals that Dior pieces are meant to circulate and last, which strengthens their desirability.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a card signed by the individual artisan who repaired each piece, and named the petites mains in communications.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Addresses the anonymity of luxury labour and gives the campaign a human, craft-centred story that is hard to dismiss as greenwashing.

revisions_after_selection.change: Dropped broad sustainability claims and instead frame the campaign around craft, time and care, and publish transparent repair figures and supplier commitments alongside it.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Luxury audiences and media are sceptical of green claims, and past scrutiny of supplier labour practices means the gesture must be backed by verifiable action.

final_proposal.title: Fermé pour réparations
final_proposal.idea: Once a year, Dior hangs a sign on Avenue Montaigne: "Fermé pour réparations." For one day, nothing new is sold. The boutique becomes a working atelier, and the windows, usually home to the newest bag, show petites mains mending clients' Dior: a grandmother's Bar jacket, a cracked Lady Dior handle, a thrifted find. Anyone can bring any Dior piece, of any age, from anywhere. Each returns with a card signed by the hand that mended it. Boutiques worldwide follow in their own time zones, so the closure travels around the globe. The message: the most Dior thing you can own is not the newest piece but one worth keeping. The ritual then lives on through atelier livestreams, repair stories and a year-round appointment service.
follow_up_questions: What other deliberate pauses or closures could a luxury brand use to signal its values more powerfully than any advertisement?
How could a repaired piece become a status symbol instead of a flaw, and who should be the first people seen wearing one?
What would Dior need to change in its own operations and supply chain for a day like this to feel earned rather than staged?

task_understanding.focus: The first paycheck is a rare moment of pure identity: the first time work becomes money and 'I make things' becomes 'I'm professional'. Canva's opportunity is to own the less-told half of that moment. Before the money is spent, a first-job worker has to prove they belong, and the proof is often a deck, a one-pager, a schedule, a poster, a pitch. The campaign should connect Canva to the first-job milestone for Gen Z and early-career workers, and widen Canva's image from a design tool for creatives to the tool a first job quietly runs on, so that the next generation of workplace buyers and team admins carries the habit into their careers.
assumptions: The audience is early-career workers (roughly 18-26) in their first real job, including part-time, internships and gigs. Many already know Canva from school, but don't yet see it as a 'work' tool.
Canva's B2B growth depends on bottom-up adoption: individuals bring it into teams, and teams pull in Canva for Teams or Enterprise. Early-career employees are a likely seed of that adoption.

The first paycheck is usually framed around money (spending, saving, budgeting), which is crowded with banks and fintechs. Canva has no credibility to speak about money itself, so it must speak about what the work was.
Many first jobbers feel imposter syndrome and are asked to make visual or communication work without training. They are often the 'one who knows Canva' in the office.

The first paycheck is a memory people already keep and share: photos of the first check, a stub, a first-purchase story. That makes it highly shareable and nostalgic across generations, including the managers who buy software.
Canva's tone is warm, accessible and democratic, and the campaign should keep that tone rather than becoming corporate.
The campaign should work globally, so the paycheck must be treated as a universal ritual (cash, bank notification, payslip, mobile transfer) rather than a US-style paper check.

candidates.title: The First Thing You Made
candidates.core_idea: Reframe the first paycheck as payment for the first thing you made at work. Invite people to revisit their first work creation (a flyer for the shop, a menu, a slide for the boss, a rota) and the paycheck it helped earn. People share the artefact next to the pay moment, and Canva lets them recreate or remix it as a 'first paycheck' keepsake. The idea: every career starts with something you made.
candidates.brand_connection: Canva's promise is that anyone can make things. It ties the milestone to creation, not consumption, and positions Canva as present at the beginning of working life rather than only at the design stage.
expected_strengths: Emotionally rich and nostalgic across ages, so it reaches both first jobbers and the managers who remember theirs.
Highly user-generated: every participant produces a shareable artefact.
Strongly on-brand and easy to platform across social, creators, schools and employers.
main_concerns: Risk of drifting into generic nostalgia with a weak B2B link.
Requires people to have kept or remember the artefact; some made nothing visual.
Could read as a template campaign rather than an insight-led one.

candidates.title: Proof You Belong
candidates.core_idea: Name the real first-paycheck tension: you got paid, but do you feel like you belong? Show that new hires earn their place through small visible work, like the deck nobody else wanted to make. Canva becomes the tool for that 'proof of belonging', and the campaign celebrates the unglamorous first deliverable as the true initiation. The reveal: your first paycheck is the company's way of saying 'we believe you', and the first thing you make is you saying 'I believe it too'.
candidates.brand_connection: Directly aligns Canva with workplace confidence and professional presence, pushing it from creative tool to career tool, which supports team and enterprise adoption.
expected_strengths: Grounded in a true, underserved insight (imposter syndrome in the first job).
Strong B2B relevance: it speaks to new hires and to the managers who onboard them.
Platformable into onboarding kits, templates for first-week work, and employer partnerships.
main_concerns: Imposter syndrome can feel heavy and may clash with Canva's upbeat tone.
Risk of seeming to say new workers need Canva to be good enough.
Less obviously tied to the paycheck itself as an icon.

candidates.title: The Payslip Redesign
candidates.core_idea: The payslip is the most important document most people receive, and one of the worst designed: confusing, cold, full of codes. Canva redesigns the first payslip into something a person actually understands and wants to keep, with plain language, clear visuals and a keepsake version. It is a bold provocation: if design can make a first paycheck feel like an achievement, why are the documents of work so bad? Employers can adopt Canva-designed payslip and offer-letter templates.
candidates.brand_connection: Applies Canva's core belief that good design should be accessible to a real, everyday, overlooked object. It demonstrates design as clarity, not decoration.
expected_strengths: Surprising, memorable and highly ownable: nobody in the category talks about payslip design.
Strong PR potential and a clear product extension via HR and payroll templates.
Directly serves B2B buyers in HR and internal communications.
main_concerns: Payslips are tied to payroll systems and regulation, so real adoption is complicated.
Could feel like a stunt without emotional pull for the first jobber.
Risk of straying into territory where Canva has limited credibility (HR and finance).

candidates.title: Pay It Forward Deck
candidates.core_idea: Invite people to make something for the next first jobber with their own first paycheck story: a one-page guide, a welcome poster, a 'what I wish I knew' card for new hires. Experienced workers design advice for newcomers, and Canva connects them to schools, youth programmes and employers. The paycheck becomes the start of a chain of mentorship, not just a reward.
candidates.brand_connection: Uses Canva's community, templates and nonprofit and education footprint to turn shared knowledge into design, reinforcing a collaborative and generous brand.
expected_strengths: Generates a large pool of useful, authentic content built from real stories.
Good fit for Canva's social-impact credentials and education relationships.
Bridges generations and gives managers a reason to take part.
main_concerns: Advice-sharing campaigns are common and may feel familiar.
Relies on participation from two sides at once.
The first paycheck is a backdrop rather than the central tension.

reasons_for_selection: It is built on the sharpest and most true insight: the first paycheck confirms you were hired, but belonging is earned through the first thing you visibly make.
It connects the milestone to Canva's actual commercial role in work (decks, docs, visuals) and to the bottom-up path into teams and enterprise, which the B2B category needs.
It is platformable: onboarding templates, a first-week toolkit, creator stories, employer partnerships and a recurring 'first paycheck season' around graduation and summer jobs.
It avoids the money territory dominated by banks and fintechs and gives Canva a distinct point of view.
Its main risk (heavy tone) can be solved through execution by celebrating the small win rather than dwelling on the anxiety, and by borrowing the warmth and nostalgia of C1.

rejected.reason: Emotionally appealing and highly shareable, but the insight is softer and the B2B link is weak. It risks becoming a generic nostalgia or template campaign. Its best element, the keepsake artefact, is folded into the recommended idea.

A clever provocation with strong PR potential, but it depends on payroll systems and regulation Canva doesn't control, and it speaks more to HR than to the first jobber. It could work later as a supporting stunt but is a weaker core idea.
Generous and brand-aligned, but advice-sharing and pay-it-forward mechanics are familiar, depend on two-sided participation, and treat the paycheck as backdrop rather than the central tension.

revisions_after_selection.change: Reframed the tone from 'overcoming imposter syndrome' to 'celebrating the first small win', using humour and warmth about the unglamorous first task (the slide, the rota, the sign).
revisions_after_selection.reason: An anxiety-led tone could feel heavy and imply that new workers are not good enough on their own, which clashes with Canva's optimistic, empowering voice.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a shareable keepsake: users pair their first work creation with their first pay moment in a simple 'first paycheck, first make' format.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Borrows the nostalgia and user-generated strength of C1 so the idea has a clear public participation mechanic and a stronger link to the paycheck as an icon.

revisions_after_selection.change: Made the manager and employer a visible second audience, with a prompt for managers to share the first thing a new hire made for them.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Managers are the B2B buyers and influencers; including them turns the campaign into a team ritual and supports Canva for Teams adoption.

revisions_after_selection.change: Replaced paper-check imagery with a universal pay-moment device (notification, cash, transfer, payslip) in all creative.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The campaign must work globally, and the paper check is not the norm in most markets.

final_proposal.title: First Paycheck, First Make
final_proposal.idea: Your first paycheck says they hired you. The first thing you make says you belong. Canva celebrates the unglamorous first deliverable (the slide, the rota, the shop sign) as the real initiation into work. People share their first pay moment next to the first thing they made, and managers share what their new hire made for them. Canva supplies a first-week kit of templates for the things new hires are always asked to produce, plus a keepsake format that turns that first make into a memory. Each graduation and summer-job season, the ritual returns. It repositions Canva from a design tool to the quiet confidence behind every first job, and seeds team adoption from the bottom up.
follow_up_questions: Which first-job tasks are so universal (the slide nobody wants to make, the team rota) that they could become recognisable cultural symbols of starting work?
How could the campaign give managers a real role without turning it into corporate onboarding content?
What would a 'first paycheck season' look like in markets where pay moments are digital or informal, and what rituals already exist there?
