task_understanding.focus: Loneliness is rarely caused by a lack of people. It comes from a lack of reasons to meet them. Mastercard sits inside the daily rituals of exchange, including paying, splitting, owing and treating. Payment technology has also removed many of life's small human touchpoints, such as the chat at the till, the cash handed over and the 'I'll get the next one'. The opportunity is to put reasons for human contact back into money moments, so that Mastercard's 'Priceless' belief (the best things money can't buy) works as a behaviour and not just a tagline.
assumptions: Mastercard's strongest territory is 'Priceless': the idea that human connection is the real value behind transactions. It also holds credible equity in inclusion (True Name), local community (Priceless Cities, small business support) and sonic identity.
A payments brand must not appear to monetise, surveil or diagnose loneliness. Any idea must be opt-in, privacy-safe and free of transaction-data profiling.
Lonely people often avoid the label, so the idea should work for everyone and not stigmatise a 'lonely' segment.

The core audience is adults 22-45 in urban, digitally native settings. They are socially networked but time-poor, and they let friendships drift because organising a meetup takes effort, not because they lack friends.
Cultural context: remote work, self-checkout, delivery apps and tap-to-pay have made daily life frictionless, and many people feel that frictionlessness has a social cost.
The campaign should be platformable across product (a feature or pilot), content, partnerships and PR, and should not rely on a charity donation mechanic, which would be a category cliché.

candidates.title: The Slow Lane
candidates.core_idea: Reintroduce deliberate human friction at checkout. Mastercard partners with retailers and cafes to create 'Slow Lanes' staffed by people, where tapping is the end of a short chat and not a replacement for it. It is framed as a counter-trend to self-checkout.
candidates.brand_connection: Mastercard is the invisible infrastructure that made payments instant, so it is credible, and brave, for it to champion the moments speed erased. The sonic 'tap' sound becomes a hello.
expected_strengths: Visually simple and highly PR-able
Taps into a widely felt cultural nostalgia for neighbourhood commerce
Supports small business partners
main_concerns: Depends on retailer buy-in and operations
Limited scale and reach
Risks reading as a one-off stunt or as anti-technology for a technology company

candidates.title: Open Seat
candidates.core_idea: Mastercard Priceless experiences, such as dinners and events, are usually sold as pairs. 'Open Seat' lets cardholders gift a spare seat to a neighbour or an acquaintance, or hold an open place at a shared table at partner restaurants.
candidates.brand_connection: It extends Priceless Cities and the experiences platform, turning the cardholder's access into hospitality for others.
expected_strengths: Builds on existing assets
Generous and warm in tone
Easy to run through partner venues
main_concerns: Stranger-meeting raises safety and moderation issues
Skews towards premium cardholders
Close to existing social-dining platforms, so less ownable

candidates.title: Known By Name
candidates.core_idea: An opt-in tap experience where the terminal or receipt shows the cardholder's chosen name, so merchants can say 'Hi, Sam' on every visit. Being known by name is the first antidote to anonymity.
candidates.brand_connection: It extends the True Name platform, which respects the names people choose, into a daily ritual of belonging.
expected_strengths: Emotionally resonant
Leverages a proven and credible Mastercard asset
Embedded in a product behaviour
main_concerns: Requires terminal and merchant changes at scale
Raises privacy and 'being watched' concerns
Impact on loneliness is indirect and small

candidates.title: Owe Me One
candidates.core_idea: Reframe the debt between friends as a bond worth keeping. In a peer-to-peer payment moment (splitting a bill, covering a coffee), a new option, 'Settle in person', replaces the money transfer with a scheduled meetup. The payer says 'I'll get you back' and the app sets a shared date. A payments brand deliberately choosing not to complete a transaction is the provocation: sometimes the most human way to pay someone back is with your time.
candidates.brand_connection: It is Priceless in practice. Mastercard owns money movement, so it can credibly say what money moves toward. Time with people is the one currency that cannot be sent digitally.
expected_strengths: Built on a true behavioural insight: owing a friend gives a reason to see them
Counter-intuitive and ownable for a payments brand
Platformable across product pilot, content, partnerships (cafes, restaurants) and social ('who do you owe one?')
Does not label anyone as lonely, so there is no stigma and it appeals to everyone
main_concerns: Needs a product or pilot partner, or a credible prototype
Could be seen as gimmicky if there is no real usage
Meetups may not happen, so there must be a graceful fallback to normal payment

reasons_for_selection: It is rooted in a sharp, true insight: loneliness often comes from the lack of a reason to meet, and everyday debts create that reason.
It sits at the centre of what Mastercard does (moving money between people) while arguing for something money cannot buy, which is a strong and fresh expression of Priceless.
Choosing not to complete a transaction is surprising and provocative but strategically grounded.
It avoids the stigma of naming loneliness and works as a mass behaviour, so it can scale from a pilot to a cultural habit.
It is highly platformable: a feature, a social phrase ('owe me one'), partner venues and user-generated stories.

rejected.reason: The Slow Lane is charming and PR-friendly, but it depends on retailer operations, has limited reach, and sets a payments company against the technology it built. It reads as a stunt rather than a platform.
Open Seat is warm but raises stranger-safety issues, skews premium, and is less ownable because it resembles existing social-dining services. It also does not rest on a payment behaviour.
Known By Name makes strong use of True Name, but it needs significant hardware and merchant change, raises privacy concerns around being recognised, and has only an indirect effect on loneliness.

revisions_after_selection.change: Remove the word 'loneliness' from consumer-facing messaging and lead with the warmth of owing a friend one ('the debt worth keeping').
revisions_after_selection.reason: People avoid the lonely label, and a stigma-free invitation is more likely to be used and shared.

revisions_after_selection.change: Limit 'Settle in person' to people already in the user's contacts, with both parties confirming the plan, and use no transaction data to suggest who might be lonely.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This protects privacy and safety and avoids any impression that Mastercard is profiling or surveilling users.

revisions_after_selection.change: Add a no-shame fallback: if the meetup has not happened after an agreed window, the app offers a normal payment or a rescheduled date.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It makes the feature practical for people with busy lives and reduces the risk that the idea fails when plans slip.

revisions_after_selection.change: Launch as a limited pilot and cultural moment (for example a prototype with a P2P partner and partner cafes) rather than as a full product rollout.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It lowers delivery risk, proves usage and generates real stories for the wider campaign.

task_understanding.focus: Loneliness is rarely a lack of people. More often it is a lack of easy, low-risk reasons to be together. Mastercard's Priceless platform has long argued that the best moments can't be bought, but money often decides whether they happen at all. The opportunity is for Mastercard to own the practical, human gap between wanting company and actually getting it: the small, awkward, sometimes costly act of reaching out.
assumptions: Mastercard is a network, not a bank, so any idea must work through issuers, merchants and partners and cannot rely on owning the customer relationship.
Priceless ('there are some things money can't buy') gives Mastercard permission to speak about human connection. The campaign must still show a role for payments, not just sympathy.

The audience is broad: adults 25-45 in cities who are socially stretched, plus people who have moved, changed jobs, become parents or retired and lost their routines. Loneliness is not only an issue for older people.
Many lonely people stop initiating. They fear rejection, fear imposing, and fear the cost of an outing. The invitation is the bottleneck, not the number of people around.
A finance brand talking about loneliness faces a credibility and sensitivity risk. It must act, avoid exploiting the emotion, and avoid using personal spending data in ways that feel intrusive.
Local merchants such as cafes, restaurants, studios and venues have quiet off-peak hours and a commercial incentive to be part of the answer.
Budget and partner capacity favour a pilot in a few markets before any global rollout.

candidates.title: The Covered Invite
candidates.core_idea: Make reaching out free and easy to accept. Any cardholder can send a digital invitation to a coffee, a meal or a class, and Mastercard covers the guest's first item at participating local merchants. The invite says, in effect, 'It's covered. Just come.' It removes the two main reasons people don't send or accept invitations: cost and the feeling of being a burden.
candidates.brand_connection: It turns Priceless into a mechanism. Mastercard pays for the seat so the moment can be priceless. It uses what a payments network actually does (moving value between a person, a merchant and a guest) and gives merchants off-peak footfall.
expected_strengths: Clear, simple behavioural insight: people stop inviting, not just stop attending.
Platformable: invites can be themed (new neighbour, old friend, colleague, 'first one back') and run seasonally, for example in the holidays.
Gives merchants and issuers a reason to join, and creates shareable invite moments.
Measurable through invites sent, accepted and redeemed.
main_concerns: Funding and redemption mechanics must be capped and fraud-proofed.
Needs a merchant network and issuer buy-in in each market.
Could read as a discount promotion if the tone isn't human enough.

candidates.title: Priceless Regulars
candidates.core_idea: Loneliness eases when you are known somewhere. Mastercard backs the 'third places' (barbers, cafes, diners) where staff recognise you, by helping small merchants host low-pressure regular hours and by celebrating the people who have been regulars for years. Regular status becomes a form of belonging.
candidates.brand_connection: Mastercard supports small businesses and sees the daily routines of local commerce. Being a regular is a payments-adjacent behaviour that is also deeply human.
expected_strengths: Warm, culturally resonant, with strong storytelling potential from real regulars and owners.
Supports Mastercard's small-business credentials.
Easy to execute locally.
main_concerns: Passive and nostalgic: it celebrates connection but doesn't help people who don't yet have a regular place.
Less ownable, since many brands could do a 'support local' story.
Weak mechanism for reaching people who are actually isolated.

candidates.title: The Quiet Index
candidates.core_idea: Use aggregated, anonymised Mastercard Economics Institute data to publish a city-by-city picture of solo versus shared spending, and use it to show where social life is thinning out. The findings are given to city governments and community groups as a tool for investing in places and events that bring people together.
candidates.brand_connection: It leverages Mastercard's data and economic insight, a true asset that few competitors can match, and positions the brand as a serious cultural contributor.
expected_strengths: Credible, newsworthy and PR-friendly, with strong earned-media potential.
Differentiated: only a payments network could produce it.
Offers a B2B and public-policy angle.
main_concerns: Spending data is a blunt proxy for loneliness and could be criticised as inaccurate.
Risk of feeling like surveillance of private lives, which clashes with trust in a financial brand.
Informs but doesn't directly change anyone's experience of loneliness.

candidates.title: Someone Real
candidates.core_idea: Romance and friendship scams prey on loneliness. Mastercard works with issuers so that when payment patterns suggest someone is being groomed, they get a call or message from a trained human who talks with them rather than just blocking the card. The campaign tells the story that protecting people from scammers also means noticing when they are lonely.
candidates.brand_connection: It builds on Mastercard's security and fraud-prevention credentials, a genuine product truth, and links them to an emotional human reality.
expected_strengths: Strong product truth and clear societal harm.
Provocative reframing of fraud as an emotional issue, not only a technical one.
Can drive meaningful issuer collaboration.
main_concerns: Narrow audience (scam victims), and it risks stigmatising lonely people as vulnerable.
Relies on issuers to deliver the human intervention, which Mastercard does not control.
Privacy and regulatory complexity in detecting this behaviour.

reasons_for_selection: It addresses a real behavioural barrier, the act of reaching out, and gives people a concrete way to act.
It makes Priceless tangible: the brand pays for the seat so the moment can be priceless. This is a strong, ownable use of Mastercard's role.
It works for a broad audience and is not limited to one age group or vulnerability.
It has built-in commercial logic for merchants and issuers, so it can scale beyond a one-off stunt.
It is easy to pilot, measure and extend into recurring seasonal and thematic campaigns.

rejected.reason: Emotionally appealing but passive and less ownable. It celebrates existing belonging rather than helping people who lack it, and many brands could run a similar 'support local' story.

Credible and PR-rich, but spending data is an imperfect proxy for loneliness and the idea risks feeling like surveillance. It informs without changing individual experiences. It could work later as a supporting proof point.
A strong product truth, but too narrow, dependent on issuers' interventions, and open to stigmatising lonely people as targets. Better kept as a separate security-led initiative.

revisions_after_selection.change: Cap the covered amount at a small first item (such as a coffee or a class drop-in) and limit each person to a few invites per month.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Keeps the economics sustainable and prevents abuse, while keeping the gesture about connection rather than freebies.

revisions_after_selection.change: Guests do not need a Mastercard. They redeem through a simple code or QR.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The invitee is often the person most in need of a nudge, and requiring a card would exclude them and read as a sales tactic.

revisions_after_selection.change: Invitations are sent manually by the cardholder. No use of spending or contact data to suggest who to invite.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Avoids any perception of surveillance, which would undermine trust in a financial brand.

revisions_after_selection.change: Focus participating merchants on independent, off-peak venues, and let them set the quiet hours.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Makes the program commercially attractive for small businesses and encourages relaxed, low-pressure settings.

revisions_after_selection.change: Add a no-pressure invite format with an easy decline ('no worries, keep it for later').
revisions_after_selection.reason: Reduces the fear of rejection that stops people from inviting, which is the core insight.

final_proposal.title: The Covered Invite
final_proposal.idea: Lonely people rarely lack company so much as the nerve to ask for it. Inviting feels like imposing, and accepting feels like a cost. The Covered Invite removes both. Any Mastercard holder can send a simple digital invite to a coffee, a meal or a class at a participating independent venue. The invite carries one line: 'It's covered. Just come.' Mastercard pays for the guest's first item, who doesn't need a Mastercard, and either side can say 'maybe later' with no awkwardness. Merchants fill quiet hours, and the brand shows what Priceless means in practice: money clears the way so the moment itself can be priceless. Themed waves such as new neighbours, old friends and the first week back can keep the platform running through the year.

How could the invitation itself become a cultural object that people want to share, keep or answer, rather than a voucher?
What would make a local merchant feel like a host in this idea rather than a redemption point?

candidates.title: The Slow Lane
candidates.core_idea: Reintroduce deliberate friction. Partner with retailers to create a 'Slow Lane' checkout where tap-and-go is replaced by a staffed, unhurried exchange. A short sonic cue and signage tell customers that this lane is for talking.
candidates.brand_connection: Mastercard is the brand of effortless payment, so being the one to say 'sometimes don't rush' is a surprising, self-aware flip. The sonic logo becomes a 'take your time' signal.
expected_strengths: Highly visual and shareable, with a clear cultural tension between speed and humanity.
Directly confronts the effect of the brand's own category (frictionless payment).
Easy for press and social media to understand.
main_concerns: Operationally heavy, and retailers may resist anything that slows throughput.
Risks reading as a gimmick or as anti-technology messaging from a technology company.
Limited reach, since it only touches people who visit participating stores.

candidates.title: Priceless Pending
candidates.core_idea: A 'suspended payment' system for companionship. Cardholders pre-pay a coffee, a meal or a seat at a communal table that anyone can claim, with a note, as a way to say 'someone thought of you'. Claims are made by tapping at participating venues.
candidates.brand_connection: It makes generosity a payment behavior and fits the Priceless idea that the best purchases are gifts of presence.
expected_strengths: Emotionally warm and simple to explain.
Builds on a real tradition (caffè sospeso) with a modern payment mechanism.
Scales through merchants and an easy opt-in.
main_concerns: Charity-like and not new, so it may feel borrowed and generic.
Frames lonely people as recipients and risks stigma.
Depends on issuers and merchants to build the plumbing.

candidates.title: Regulars
candidates.core_idea: Treat 'being a regular' as an antidote to loneliness. Using only aggregated, anonymized, business-level patterns, Mastercard identifies neighborhoods where repeat-visit culture at local third places (cafés, barbers, pubs, laundromats) is fading. It then partners with those businesses, chosen through community nomination, to create 'Regulars' rituals: a reserved communal table, a weekly regulars' hour, and a staff 'welcome back' practice. Participating businesses get a Regulars mark, and the brand's sonic logo becomes the sound of being recognized.
candidates.brand_connection: It uses Mastercard's unique asset, its understanding of commerce at scale, for human ends. It supports small business, extends Priceless into everyday life instead of rare luxury, and gives the transaction a role in belonging.
expected_strengths: Grounded in a revealing insight: for many people the most consistent human contact is being known by a shopkeeper.
Platformable across cities and categories, with a built-in local rollout and content stream (regulars' stories).
Proof of a real contribution to community and small business, not just messaging.
Reframes a payment as an act of belonging.
main_concerns: Any hint of data use around loneliness can feel invasive, so the privacy architecture must be explicit.
Needs credible measurement so the work doesn't look like a branding exercise.
Depends on local business participation and staff buy-in.

candidates.title: Together Points
candidates.core_idea: A rewards mechanic that gives boosted benefits only when spending is shared, such as two cards paying at the same table or a bill split among friends, to encourage people to do things together.
candidates.brand_connection: It plays on loyalty and rewards, an area Mastercard already works in, and on the social ritual of splitting the bill.
expected_strengths: A concrete product behavior that is easy to test.
Taps into a familiar financial ritual (splitting).
Easy for issuers to adopt.
main_concerns: Commodifies friendship and could feel transactional or patronizing.
Excludes people who are already isolated and have no one to split with.
Needs issuer cooperation and may feel like a standard promotion.

reasons_for_selection: It has the strongest insight: being a 'regular' is an unrecognized form of belonging, and Mastercard sits at the point where it happens.
It uses what Mastercard is uniquely placed to offer (commerce understanding, merchant reach, small-business commitment) and is not a borrowed charity format.
It is a platform: a repeatable program, a recognizable mark and a sound, with local stories that can keep producing content.
It helps people who are not looking for help, since a table and a familiar face are non-stigmatizing.
Its main risk, data sensitivity, can be addressed through design choices.

rejected.reason: A strong provocation, but operationally fragile, limited in reach and in tension with the retailer's priorities. It points at the problem but does little to create ongoing connection. Its best element, the sonic cue, is reused in C3.
Warm but familiar, and it casts lonely people as recipients. It also lacks a distinctive Mastercard truth beyond being a payment mechanism.
It turns friendship into a points mechanic, which risks cynicism, and it leaves out the people who are most isolated. It reads as a promotion rather than a cultural idea.

revisions_after_selection.change: Removed any individual-level identification. Insight now comes only from aggregated, anonymized, business- and neighborhood-level repeat-visit trends, and this is stated publicly in the campaign.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Using personal spending to infer loneliness would break trust and undermine the idea.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added community nomination: neighbors nominate the places that make them feel known, and the data is used only to validate and prioritize.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Keeps the program human and participatory and avoids a top-down 'we found your lonely neighborhood' tone.

revisions_after_selection.change: Made the sonic logo 'welcome back' cue opt-in for merchants and a subtle sound rather than a mandated one.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Protects authenticity and avoids forcing staff into scripted warmth.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added an independent academic partner to measure outcomes (repeat visits, reported neighborhood connection) and a pilot-first rollout in a small number of cities.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Gives the campaign credibility and a basis for scaling responsibly.

revisions_after_selection.change: Dropped the language of 'fighting loneliness' from consumer-facing communication in favor of celebrating regulars.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Avoids stigma and keeps the tone celebratory.

final_proposal.title: Regulars
final_proposal.idea: For many people, the most dependable human contact is being known at the corner café, barber or laundromat. Contactless payment has quietly made that contact optional. Regulars turns it back into something worth protecting. Neighbors nominate the places that make them feel known. Using only aggregated, anonymized trends, Mastercard helps identify where repeat-visit culture is fading and backs those businesses with a communal table, a weekly regulars' hour and a Regulars mark on the door. When a regular taps, a soft version of Mastercard's sonic logo becomes the sound of 'welcome back'. Local stories of regulars become the campaign. Independent researchers measure the effect on belonging. Priceless was never about what you buy. It is about being known where you buy it.
follow_up_questions: Which everyday places in your own life make you feel known, and what small ritual would protect them from disappearing?
How could the brand show its use of data for belonging in a way that visibly strengthens trust instead of triggering suspicion?
What would a 'regular' ritual look like in non-physical places, such as online communities, so the idea reaches people who can't easily leave home?

task_understanding.focus: The first paycheck is the first moment a person is treated as a professional, and it is also the first time many people have to present themselves as one: a name on a payslip, a new LinkedIn headline, a first invoice, a first pitch. The opportunity for Canva is to own the 'first' of professional identity, so that the first thing people make as working adults is made in Canva. That builds early habit and loyalty among the next generation of Canva users, who will later bring it into teams and paid plans. It also pushes Canva's B2B story beyond templates toward the start of a career.
assumptions: The audience is mainly 18-27-year-olds starting first jobs, internships, freelance work or side hustles, including Gen Z entering the workforce. Their future workplace buying influence is the long-term B2B value.
The first paycheck is emotionally ambiguous. It brings pride and a feeling of arrival, but also anxiety, impostor feelings and an underwhelming number after tax and deductions.
Canva already has strong awareness among students and educators, so the campaign should move it from 'school project tool' to 'professional identity tool' rather than build basic awareness.
Canva should not give financial advice. Its credible territory is making, designing and presenting, not budgeting or investing.
People share milestone moments on social platforms, especially the ones that feel like a rite of passage, so a shareable ritual is realistic.
Canva has a free tier that lowers the barrier to participation, and the campaign can show paid features without hard selling.
The budget is lean, so ideas should rely on earned and social reach, product-led mechanics and partnerships rather than heavy media.

candidates.title: The First Payslip, Redesigned
candidates.core_idea: The payslip is the most important and ugliest document of early adulthood: dense, grey and confusing. Canva makes it beautiful and understandable. Users upload or recreate their first payslip and get a Canva template that turns the rows (gross, tax, net) into a clear visual, while personal details stay private. It becomes a shareable keepsake, 'the receipt of my first day as a grown-up'.
candidates.brand_connection: Canva's core promise is making complex, intimidating things simple and beautiful. A payslip is a perfect example of an intimidating document. It stays in Canva's lane of visual communication and does not drift into financial advice.
expected_strengths: Very clear, instantly understandable product demonstration
Taps a real pain point (nobody understands their payslip) with an emotional payoff
Highly shareable as a keepsake or flex
main_concerns: Payslips contain sensitive data, so privacy and trust risks are high
Could be read as financial education, which is outside Canva's credibility
Payslip formats vary by country, which makes scaling complex

candidates.title: First Pay, First Make
candidates.core_idea: A ritual campaign that invites people to spend a small part of their first paycheck on something they make to mark the moment: a framed poster, a thank-you card to the person who backed them, a personal brand mark, a printed business card. Canva Print and templates turn the paycheck into a first act of authorship. The platform idea is 'Make something with your first pay'. It reframes the paycheck from something you spend into something you create with.
candidates.brand_connection: Canva is a making tool, and Canva Print links digital creation to physical objects. The campaign positions Canva as the place where milestones become artefacts, and it nudges people toward print and paid features naturally.
expected_strengths: Simple, ownable ritual that can recur every year and in every market
Connects directly to monetisable products (print, Pro)
Emotional and visually rich content for social sharing
main_concerns: Asking young people to spend their first pay may feel tone-deaf when money is tight
Ritual needs seeding by credible voices to avoid feeling forced
Risk of being generic gifting or scrapbooking content

candidates.title: The Person Behind the Paycheck
candidates.core_idea: The first paycheck only exists because someone took a chance on you. Canva invites people to design a thank-you for that person: the parent who paid for the bus fare to interviews, the teacher who wrote a reference, the first boss. Canva creates a 'First Thank-You' tool that turns the gratitude into a card, video or poster, and the stories are collected into a public wall of thank-yous.
candidates.brand_connection: Canva has always been about empowering others to express themselves. Gratitude gives it an emotional, human role, and sending designed cards drives engagement across collaboration and sharing features.
expected_strengths: Highly emotional and likely to travel as a feel-good story
Appeals to both the new worker and the older generation, widening the audience
Easy to produce through real stories
main_concerns: Gratitude-card campaigns are a well-trodden category convention
Link to B2B and professional identity is weak
Emotional but not very surprising

candidates.title: Net Pay Is Not Your Net Worth
candidates.core_idea: A provocative stance on the quiet disappointment of the first paycheck, when the number you were promised shrinks after tax. Canva gives young workers a way to show what their first job gave them that the payslip does not list: skills, a portfolio, a first client, a name. A 'Second Payslip' template lets people design the unofficial statement of everything they earned beyond money, which becomes the seed of a visual CV.
candidates.brand_connection: Canva is already the go-to tool for CVs, portfolios and personal branding. The campaign links the paycheck moment to Canva's career-identity products and reframes value as visible, designable proof of skill.
expected_strengths: Insight-driven and emotionally honest, since it names the deflation of the first net pay
Clear bridge from the paycheck to CV and portfolio tools, supporting the B2B pipeline
A platformable device (the Second Payslip) with easy user-generated content
Playful, shareable format that avoids financial advice
main_concerns: Could read as consoling people about low pay, which is a sensitive tone to get right
Needs a sharp visual identity so the template does not feel like another CV tool
Requires careful localisation as tax and pay norms vary by country

reasons_for_selection: It is built on the most revealing human truth of the four: the first paycheck is both a milestone and a small letdown, and no brand speaks to that second feeling.
It sits squarely in Canva's credible territory (CVs, portfolios, personal branding) and avoids the privacy and financial-advice risks of C1.
It connects the paycheck to a clear B2B-relevant outcome: young professionals who build their professional identity in Canva and carry the habit into their teams.
The Second Payslip is a simple, ownable, platformable device that can run as user-generated content, creator partnerships, templates and employer or university tie-ins.
It is more surprising and less category-conventional than the gratitude cards of C3 or the gifting ritual of C2.

rejected.reason: Strong demonstration, but handling payslips raises privacy and trust concerns, drifts toward financial education, and varies too much by country to scale on a lean budget.
A neat ritual with good monetisation links, but asking people to spend their first pay may feel tone-deaf, and the idea is closer to generic gifting content with a weaker B2B link.
Emotionally appealing but a familiar gratitude-card convention that is less surprising and weakly tied to professional identity and the B2B opportunity.

revisions_after_selection.change: Renamed the working idea from a slogan-like 'Net Pay Is Not Your Net Worth' to the platform name 'The Second Payslip' and kept the original line only as an internal stance.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The line could sound like consolation for low pay. A named, playful device is more ownable and easier to turn into a template and repeatable campaign.

revisions_after_selection.change: Made the Second Payslip celebratory and specific, with lines like 'Gross: one first client' or 'Deductions: zero fear of public speaking', rather than a general reflection on value.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Specific, funny entries keep the tone proud rather than sympathetic and are easier for people to copy and share.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a clear path from the Second Payslip into a one-click visual CV or portfolio page and a team or workplace version.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The idea must deliver on the B2B objective and turn a viral moment into an ongoing professional use of Canva.

revisions_after_selection.change: Designed the template to be entirely self-authored, with no upload of real payslips or financial figures.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This removes the privacy risk and avoids any perception that Canva is giving financial advice.

final_proposal.title: The Second Payslip
final_proposal.idea: Your first paycheck arrives with a small letdown: the number after tax is never the number you imagined. The payslip lists only what you were paid. It doesn't list what you earned. Canva launches The Second Payslip, a template for designing the unofficial statement of everything your first job gave you. Gross: one first client. Bonus: a portfolio piece. Deductions: zero fear of presenting. Creators, new graduates and employers share their own, and with one click it becomes a visual CV or portfolio. The campaign turns a deflating moment into proof of professional identity, built in Canva, and it makes the first payslip the start of a habit that follows people into their teams.
follow_up_questions: What would the line items on your own Second Payslip say, and which of them are the surprising ones that make people want to share?
How could employers, universities or first-job communities adopt the Second Payslip as an onboarding or graduation ritual?
Could the Second Payslip become an annual format, such as a yearly or promotion edition, that keeps people in Canva throughout a career?

task_understanding.focus: Luxury fashion sells newness and desire, yet its most defensible sustainability claim is durability: a Dior piece is built to outlive trends and owners. The opportunity is to make repair and reuse feel like the highest expression of luxury rather than a sustainability apology. Today repair is hidden in back-of-house ateliers, and resale is dominated by third parties who capture the value and the story. The campaign should move repair from a service people are embarrassed to need to a status ritual people proudly show off, while giving Dior ownership of the second, third and fourth life of its pieces.
assumptions: Dior's craft heritage (haute couture ateliers, the Bar jacket, Lady Dior, the 30 Montaigne address) is its strongest credibility asset for repair, and it is currently under-leveraged in consumer-facing communication.
Luxury shoppers increasingly distrust overt 'eco' messaging and respond better to craft, provenance and emotional value than to guilt or statistics.
Younger affluent audiences (Gen Z and millennials) already buy pre-owned luxury and value pieces with a visible history, but they associate Dior's own repair with cost, waiting time and intimidation.

Dior can offer repair, refurbishment and certified resale through its own channels, or could plausibly expand these services, without diluting brand exclusivity if access is framed as privilege of ownership.
The client brief on 'repair and reuse' is intended for a consumer-facing campaign with cultural reach, not only a CRM or service announcement.
Brand safety matters: the campaign must not imply Dior products are fragile or that overconsumption is acceptable because repair exists.

candidate.title: The Second Fitting
candidate.core_idea: Dior reframes every repair as a 'second fitting': the same ritual of care, measurement and craft that created the piece, now applied to its next chapter. Each repaired or refurbished item leaves the atelier with a discreet, numbered 'Fitting Card' (and a tiny hand-stitched mark inside the lining) recording what was mended, by which atelier hand, and who has worn it. Visible mending becomes a signature: Dior atelier 'scars' in couture-grade gold thread, enamel or re-embroidery that are deliberately beautiful rather than invisible. The campaign platform is built on the line of thinking that a Dior piece is never finished, only fitted again. It runs in three layers: (1) a film and photographic series showing real clients, from a grandmother with a 1970s Dior suit to a 22-year-old with a resale Saddle bag, at their second fittings at 30 Montaigne and in regional ateliers; (2) a 'Dior Lives' certified-return and resale route in which pieces returned to Dior are re-fitted, re-carded and re-released with their lineage visible, so provenance becomes the new luxury; (3) a seasonal runway moment where a capsule of archive pieces, borrowed back from clients, is shown with their visible repairs as the finale, making the mend the hero of the show. Social participation comes from clients sharing their 'fitting card' histories, creating a living archive of Dior lives rather than a hashtag.
candidate.brand_connection: Dior's identity is rooted in the atelier, the hand and the idea of transformation, from Monsieur Dior's New Look reshaping the silhouette to the couture fitting as an intimate act. 'The Second Fitting' extends this directly: repair is not an add-on service but a continuation of couture. It turns the 30 Montaigne mythology and the petites mains into the face of sustainability, and it gives Dior ownership of provenance, which resale platforms cannot replicate. It also fits Dior's long-standing play with memory, femininity, and legacy (heirloom pieces, archives, the House's own museum), positioning durability as emotional inheritance rather than technical virtue.
expected_strengths: Converts a perceived weakness (repair as a sign of wear or cost) into a status marker, with visible mending as a new luxury codes.
Authentic: draws on real ateliers, real craftspeople and real client histories rather than invented eco narratives.
Platformable across film, retail, product, runway, CRM and social, and can run for years with new stories each season.
Recaptures resale value and brand control from third-party platforms by giving pieces certified lineage that only Dior can issue.
Emotionally rich and culturally resonant with the rising appreciation of vintage, heirlooms and 'quiet luxury' provenance.
Gives craftspeople visibility, supporting talent and heritage narratives that also help with employer brand.
main_concerns: Operational capacity: ateliers may not scale to meet demand, and long wait times could damage the promise and the brand.
Risk of being read as greenwashing if new-product volumes and marketing intensity are not addressed alongside it.
Visible repair may clash with some clients' expectations of perfection, so the aesthetic must be carefully designed and optional.
Pricing and access: repair must feel generous but not cheapen exclusivity, requiring clear tiers and possibly complimentary first repairs for key lines.
Authenticity and counterfeit risk: Fitting Cards and marks must be secure so they cannot be forged to inflate fake pieces.

task_understanding.focus: The first paycheck is a big emotional milestone that usually arrives as one of the worst-designed documents in a person's life: a dense payslip, or a silent direct-deposit notification with no ceremony. The gap between gross and net pay causes shock, confusion and anticlimax. The opportunity is for Canva to show what design does for work, which is turning confusing, unloved information into something people understand and feel proud of. The campaign should reach first-time earners and the employers, HR teams and payroll platforms who create that moment, and make Canva part of the story of someone's first working day.
assumptions: Canva's brand promise is that anyone can make something that looks and communicates well, so a bad everyday document is a natural thing for it to fix.
The audience is two-sided: Gen Z and early-career workers (the emotional audience) and HR, People and payroll teams (the B2B buyers who can distribute the idea at scale).
Many first paychecks now arrive by direct deposit, so the old ritual of holding and framing a check is gone and people may feel its absence.
The most common first-paycheck emotions are pride, surprise at tax deductions, and uncertainty about what the numbers mean. Plain-language clarity will be welcome and not patronising.
Canva should not give financial or tax advice or process payroll. Its role is visual communication, templates and creative tools, so partnerships are needed for anything involving real pay data.
People share milestones socially, and first-paycheck content is already a recurring social format that Canva can enter without inventing the behaviour.
Privacy matters: any idea that touches real payslips must keep sensitive data safe.

candidates.title: The Payslip, Redesigned
candidates.core_idea: Canva redesigns the first payslip so it explains itself: a visual 'where did my money go' breakdown in plain language that doubles as a keepsake. Employers and payroll providers can adopt it through Canva for Teams templates, and individuals can restyle their own version to share, with sensitive numbers redacted.
candidates.brand_connection: It shows Canva's core belief that design is a form of clarity. It turns the most boring document in working life into proof of what good design does, and puts Canva into HR and payroll workflows, which is the B2B route.
expected_strengths: A clear, demonstrable before-and-after that is easy to show in a single image.
Solves a real pain point (deduction shock) and not only a celebration moment.
Gives B2B buyers a concrete reason to use Canva in onboarding and internal comms.
Easily extended into explainers for tax, benefits and pension statements.
main_concerns: Risk of seeming to give financial guidance if the explanations get too specific.
Dependent on payroll partners or employers to reach real payslips.
Needs a privacy-safe way to handle personal pay data.

candidates.title: Frame It Forward
candidates.core_idea: Revive the ritual of framing the first check, in a digital form. People use Canva to design a 'first paycheck' piece in which the amount is replaced by a thank-you to whoever helped them get there (a parent, mentor, teacher), then send it to that person.
candidates.brand_connection: Canva is already where people make cards, tributes and keepsakes. The idea links design to gratitude and relationships, and makes Canva the tool for emotional milestones.
expected_strengths: Highly emotional and shareable, with a built-in recipient who may become a new Canva user.
Simple to execute with templates and a social prompt.
Avoids financial topics completely.
main_concerns: Little connection to Canva's B2B and productivity positioning.
Close to existing 'thank-you card' territory, so it may not feel distinctive.
Mostly a seasonal template push and not a platform.

candidates.title: Payday One Kit
candidates.core_idea: Canva gives employers a complete 'Day One to Payday One' onboarding kit: a designed welcome, a first-month calendar, a payslip explainer and a first-paycheck moment for new hires, all customisable and brand-aligned.
candidates.brand_connection: It positions Canva as the tool for HR and people teams, extending its work-related offering beyond marketing into employee experience.
expected_strengths: Directly aimed at B2B buyers with clear commercial value.
Easily measured through template use and team sign-ups.
Builds on assets Canva already has (presentations, docs, brand kits).
main_concerns: Feels like a product bundle more than a cultural idea, so it risks being unremarkable.
Gives little emotional pull for new employees themselves.
Overlaps with many HR-software onboarding offers.

candidates.title: Paid in Design
candidates.core_idea: Canva becomes the source of the first paycheck for young creatives by commissioning real, paid micro-briefs from small businesses and nonprofits. The first-time earners are then featured, and their payment is shown alongside the work they made.
candidates.brand_connection: It links Canva's creator community and marketplace to a real economic outcome, so that design skill literally becomes income.
expected_strengths: Provocative and credible, since Canva is giving a first paycheck and not only talking about one.
Generates strong stories and authentic creator content.
Supports Canva's creator and education ecosystem.
main_concerns: Operationally heavy: sourcing briefs, payments, contracts and legal compliance across markets.
Reaches a narrow audience of aspiring designers and not all first-time earners.
Reputation risk if payment, quality or fairness goes wrong.

reasons_for_selection: It is the clearest link between Canva's product truth (design makes things understandable) and the topic's real tension (a big moment wrapped in a confusing document).
It works for both audiences: new earners get clarity and a keepsake, and employers and payroll platforms get a reason to adopt Canva.
It is visual and demonstrable, so the idea can be understood in one before-and-after image.
It can grow into a platform, with the same approach applied to other confusing documents such as tax forms, benefits letters and contracts.

rejected.reason: Emotionally warm but generic and closer to a seasonal card template than a campaign platform. It has little tie to Canva's B2B and productivity position.
Commercially sensible but reads as a product bundle with no cultural spark. It works better as a distribution layer for C1 than as the lead idea.
Bold and credible but operationally and legally heavy, and it reaches only a narrow group of aspiring designers. It is better kept as a later extension or a separate initiative.

revisions_after_selection.change: Lead with clarity ('understand it') before celebration ('keep it'), so the explainer is the core and the keepsake is the reward.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Deduction confusion is the more distinctive and useful problem, and it avoids drifting into the generic gratitude territory of C2.

revisions_after_selection.change: Build the idea on payroll-provider and employer partnerships and keep all explanations to describing what each line is, never advising on tax or money choices.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Canva does not run payroll and should not be seen as giving financial advice, and partners provide real-world reach.

revisions_after_selection.change: Add an auto-redact feature to the shareable version so amounts and personal details can be hidden before posting.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Pay data is sensitive, and privacy by design protects trust while still allowing the social milestone sharing.

revisions_after_selection.change: Fold in the employer onboarding kit from C3 as the B2B delivery route.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It gives HR teams a straightforward way to adopt the idea at scale and ties the campaign to Canva's workplace business.

final_proposal.title: Payday, Explained
final_proposal.idea: Your first paycheck is a milestone delivered as a spreadsheet. Canva redesigns it. Working with employers and payroll providers, we turn the first payslip into a clear, human page: what you earned, what went where, and what each line means, in plain language and a layout you'd actually want to look at. It arrives with a 'first payday' keepsake you can personalise and share with the numbers blurred out. The campaign shows the before and after, a dense payslip next to a designed one, and invites people to restyle other confusing documents. For HR teams it comes as a Canva onboarding kit. The message: when information is designed well, people feel capable, and a first paycheck should feel like a beginning.

How could employers and payroll providers be encouraged to adopt the redesigned payslip so that it reaches people without them having to ask?
What would a new earner want to keep or share from their first payday, and how can the keepsake feel personal and not like a corporate template?

task_understanding.focus: Luxury's most credible sustainability act is also its oldest: making things last. Dior has a huge opportunity to reframe repair and reuse as the ultimate expression of luxury (value that deepens with time) rather than a bolt-on eco program. The challenge is to make repair desirable and visible, not a quiet service for broken things, and to do so without triggering greenwashing suspicion or cheapening the dream.
assumptions: Dior's equity rests on couture craft, the ateliers, and iconic pieces (Bar jacket, Lady Dior, Saddle bag, J'Adore) that already carry decades of history, so repair is a natural extension of the brand rather than a departure from it.

The client wants a campaign that builds brand love and cultural relevance, not just announces a service; behavior change (more owners using Dior repair and resale-adjacent services) is a secondary goal.
Luxury consumers, especially younger ones, increasingly buy vintage and pre-owned, and they distrust sustainability claims from fashion houses; proof and craft will beat promises.
Dior cannot undermine the new-product aspiration or the exclusivity of its codes, so reuse must be framed as inheritance and continuity, not discounting.
The audience spans heirloom-minded long-term clients and Gen Z/Millennial aspirants who treat clothes as identity, story and social content.
Dior can make operational commitments (expanded atelier repair, authenticated reuse pathways, archive access) that back the campaign with real product truth.

candidates.title: The Second Signature
candidates.core_idea: Every repair at a Dior atelier ends with a visible, deliberate mark: a hand-stitched signature from the artisan who restored the piece, in a Dior-designed mend (a gray thread, a gold seam, a re-embroidered bee). Repair is reframed as co-authorship: the piece now has two signatures, the house's and the hand's. The campaign celebrates mends as status, the way a patina on a Bar jacket is proof of a life lived.
candidates.brand_connection: Dior is built on named hands and the atelier mystique ('les petites mains'). Making the artisan's signature visible turns the hidden labor of couture into the hero, and extends the house's obsession with detail to the afterlife of a garment.
expected_strengths: Turns repair from a flaw-fixing service into a status symbol and collectible mark.
Highly visual and shareable: the mend becomes the new logo-adjacent detail people show off.
Honors the artisans, giving internal and external pride and authenticity.
Scalable platform: artisan portraits, mend codes, limited editions of signature thread, social UGC of mended pieces.
main_concerns: Visible mends could feel like a fashion gimmick, or clash with owners who want an invisible repair.
Requires operational capacity and consistent quality across ateliers.
Risk of being read as 'damaged goods as luxury' unless art direction is flawless.

candidates.title: Inherited by Design
candidates.core_idea: Dior positions its pieces as built to be passed on. Each item can be registered in a digital 'lineage', a living record of owners, repairs, and moments. The campaign tells stories of Dior pieces changing hands across generations and contexts, ending with the line that a Dior piece is never finished, only continued. Reuse becomes inheritance and sisterhood, not secondhand.
candidates.brand_connection: Monsieur Dior's own sense of legacy, the Bar jacket's 1947 revolution, and Dior's archive all make time and inheritance natural territory. The brand already trades on iconic pieces that outlive trends.
expected_strengths: Emotionally resonant and easy to understand.
Protects exclusivity by framing reuse as lineage and authenticated provenance.
Supports a real product layer (digital passport, authenticated resale or transfer, repair history) that adds resale value.
Rich storytelling material from real clients and archive pieces.
main_concerns: Heirloom narratives are familiar in luxury (Patek's 'begin your own tradition') and could feel derivative.
Less surprising and less youth-facing than other options.
Digital passport mechanics risk becoming a tech initiative that overshadows the story.

candidates.title: Dior Lost & Found
candidates.core_idea: A pop-up and digital series in which Dior invites the public to bring in the one dead, torn or forgotten Dior piece in their wardrobe (a bag with a snapped strap, a jacket from a mother's closet) and the atelier gives it a public, theatrical restoration or reinvention. The campaign is a cultural event: live-streamed transformations, designers reimagining pieces, and unclaimed pieces reborn into a collection.
candidates.brand_connection: Dior's ateliers are theatrical and its creative directors love reinterpretation, so reworking existing pieces plays to both the craft and the fashion-show spectacle.
expected_strengths: Strong earned-media and event potential, with great before/after content.
Democratizes access to the atelier, inviting people who don't normally feel Dior is for them.
Real stories supply authentic emotional hooks.
main_concerns: Operationally heavy, with large costs per participant and limited reach.
Could read as a one-off stunt without a lasting platform.
Risk of queue chaos and brand dilution if the experience is not tightly curated.

candidates.title: The Anti-Collection
candidates.core_idea: For one season, Dior announces a runway show built entirely from existing Dior pieces: archive, client-owned, and repaired garments, recut and restyled by the house. No new fabric, only new meaning. The 'collection' is a provocation that the most luxurious thing a house can do is refuse to make more. Clients lend pieces, and the show's credits list each garment's original year and owner.
candidates.brand_connection: Dior's runway is its biggest cultural stage, and reworking the New Look's own legacy of reinvention (a silhouette that rewrote fashion) shows the house at the top of its creative power while committing to craft over volume.
expected_strengths: Bold, headline-grabbing, and clearly differentiated from any other house.
Gives the topic the biggest stage in fashion and creative credibility.
Provides rich creative content: archive plus client stories plus reimagined silhouettes.
main_concerns: Commercial tension: a no-new-product season conflicts with revenue and merchandising realities.
Could be seen as a one-time gesture rather than a lasting repair and reuse platform.
Complex logistics around borrowing, insuring and altering client and archive pieces.

reasons_for_selection: It turns the problem (repair feels like admission of damage and a hidden service) into a desirable object of status, which is the real barrier to repair and reuse in luxury.
It is deeply rooted in Dior's actual product truth: the artisans, the ateliers, and the obsession with the hand.

It is platformable: every repair is a new piece of content, artisan portraits create an ongoing series, and limited signature threads, mend codes and co-signed pieces extend it into retail and culture.
It is ownable and surprising: it makes the evidence of wear a brand asset, which few houses have attempted.
It is scalable and operationally credible without requiring a one-off event or a disruption to the commercial calendar, and it can later absorb elements of C2 and C3.

rejected.reason: Emotionally solid, but heirloom and legacy storytelling is a familiar luxury trope, so it is less surprising and ownable. Its digital passport mechanic is better treated as a supporting layer than as the core idea.

Strong event energy, but the idea is an activation more than a durable platform, with high per-participant cost, limited reach and control risks. Its public-restoration spirit can live inside C1 as a launch moment.

revisions_after_selection.change: Offered clients a choice between a visible signature mend and an invisible mend, with the signature option framed as an opt-in 'co-signed' status rather than a default.

task_understanding.focus: The first paycheck is a rite of passage with a hidden problem: it's the first time a person's worth is expressed as a number they didn't set, on a document (the payslip) that is confusing and badly designed. Canva's opportunity is to move from 'the tool for making things' to 'the tool for making your case' in the workplace. That ties a nostalgic, universal moment to Canva's push into work-grade presentations, docs and team plans, and speaks to early-career people who will bring their tool habits into the companies they join.
assumptions: Canva is already widely known and liked by students and early-career people, but is perceived as a 'make a poster or social post' tool more than a serious work tool; B2B growth depends on changing that.

The first paycheck is emotionally loaded (pride, relief, confusion, a little disappointment about taxes and deductions), and people already share it culturally through screenshots, framed cheques and parent phone calls.

The core audience is 18-27 year olds starting first jobs, internships and freelance work, who are tomorrow's team leads and software buyers. A secondary audience is managers, HR and team admins who influence workplace tool adoption.
Most early-career people feel they lack the language, confidence or format to ask for more, and visual communication is something Canva can credibly make easier.
A campaign can't make claims about salary outcomes. It must give people tools and confidence, not promises, and it must work across markets with different pay norms and currencies.
The budget favours a social-first, creator-led and template-driven platform over heavy production or complex partnerships.

candidates.title: First Dollar Frame
candidates.core_idea: Canva turns the first paycheck into a keepsake. It offers a library of templates for framing, celebrating and sharing the first payment (a 'first earned' certificate, a thank-you card to the people who helped, a milestone poster). Users post their stories under a shared format.
candidates.brand_connection: Canva makes personal moments beautiful and shareable in minutes, so it fits naturally with a celebratory, nostalgic moment.
expected_strengths: Emotionally warm and instantly understandable
Highly shareable and UGC-friendly
Low production complexity and easy to localise
main_concerns: Sentimental keepsake is a familiar category trope, so it is not surprising
Skews consumer and does little for B2B or workplace positioning
Behaviour would be a one-off moment rather than a lasting habit

candidates.title: Made It. Got Paid.
candidates.core_idea: A campaign celebrating first paychecks that came directly from something someone designed in Canva: a bakery menu, a wedding invite, a club poster, a logo for a neighbour. Real stories become a series that shows how a creative skill turns into first income, plus a prompt for people to price and package their first gig.
candidates.brand_connection: Shows Canva as an engine of economic opportunity, tied to its creator marketplace and freelancer use cases.
expected_strengths: Authentic proof of Canva's value with real people
Inspires side-hustle and freelance audiences
Strong creator and community collaboration potential
main_concerns: Skews toward freelancers and sole traders rather than company employees and teams
Risk of sounding like a 'get rich with design' claim
Stories are hard to scale consistently across markets

candidates.title: The Payslip, Redesigned
candidates.core_idea: The first payslip is the most important document most people receive and one of the worst designed. Canva redesigns the payslip, offer letter and onboarding pack into clear, human formats, working with employers and payroll partners so a first paycheck can finally be understood (what tax is, what deductions mean).
candidates.brand_connection: Canva's promise is that design makes complexity clear. It is also a direct B2B route into HR and people teams, which already create documents at scale.
expected_strengths: Genuinely useful, and a revealing cultural observation about a neglected document
Clear B2B entry through HR and onboarding workflows
Likely to earn press as a public-good design intervention
main_concerns: Needs payroll and HR partnerships, with legal and compliance constraints that vary by country
Utility is real but emotional pull is weaker than the moment deserves
Slow to launch and hard to scale globally

candidates.title: The Number You Didn't Design
candidates.core_idea: The first paycheck is the first number someone else set for you. The campaign invites early-career people to make the next one theirs by turning their value into a visual case: a 'Worth Deck' built from the first payslip, with slides for impact, growth and the ask. It reframes visual communication as a career skill, and Canva becomes the place where people prepare to speak up.
candidates.brand_connection: Builds on Canva's Presentations, Docs and Teams products and positions Canva as the tool for persuading at work, not just decorating. It connects emotional first-job culture to workplace adoption.
expected_strengths: Strong, provocative insight with real tension and ownable territory
Platformable: templates, creator content, campus programmes and employer toolkits can all extend it
Directly supports the B2B and work-tool positioning
main_concerns: Could be read as encouraging entitlement or ignoring the reality of pay negotiation power
Moves beyond the literal first paycheck toward the second

reasons_for_selection: It has the sharpest insight of the four: a first paycheck is a number you didn't set, which creates real tension and a clear call to action.

rejected.reason: Warm but predictable, and it keeps Canva in the 'celebration and decoration' box. It doesn't advance the B2B or workplace positioning.

Useful and a smart B2B door, but dependent on payroll partnerships and legal variation, which makes it slow and hard to scale. Better kept as a later extension or proof point than as the lead idea.

revisions_after_selection.change: Anchor the campaign in the literal first payslip as the starting point (each line becomes a slide), rather than launching with a general 'ask for a raise' message.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Keeps the idea tied to the client's topic and gives it a vivid, filmable ritual instead of drifting to a generic career-advice message.

revisions_after_selection.change: Reframe the 'ask' from salary demand to 'make your value visible', with templates for impact timelines, learning goals and next-role proposals as well as pay conversations.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Reduces entitlement risk, works in markets and jobs where negotiation isn't possible, and avoids implying outcomes Canva can't guarantee.

revisions_after_selection.change: Add a manager and HR kit ('Receive it well') with templates for feedback, review conversations and growth plans.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Makes the campaign a two-sided workplace idea, protects against it feeling adversarial, and adds a direct B2B and team-plan hook.

revisions_after_selection.change: Add a disclaimer-free but careful principle: no salary figures or benchmarks in Canva-owned content; blur and anonymise any shared payslips.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Protects user privacy and avoids legal and credibility risks around pay data across regions.

final_proposal.title: The Number You Didn't Design
final_proposal.idea: Your first paycheck is the first number someone else designed for you. Canva helps you design the next conversation. Canva releases the Worth Deck kit: impact timeline, wins one-pager, learning plan and the ask. A companion 'Receive it well' kit gives managers templates for review and growth conversations, so the idea works for teams, not against them. Run it at first-job and graduation moments through creators, campuses and LinkedIn. The message: visual communication is a career skill, and Canva is where it's built. It is not about demanding more, but about making your value impossible to overlook.

How could managers and HR teams become co-authors of the campaign rather than its audience, so it builds adoption inside companies?
What would a Worth Deck look like in cultures where negotiating pay is taboo, and how should the idea change there?

task_understanding.focus: Make repair and reuse a desirable expression of Dior's couture savoir-faire rather than a sustainability obligation. The opportunity is to move the category from 'buy less' guilt to 'keep what's irreplaceable' pride, and to show that the most luxurious thing a piece can have is a long, human history.
assumptions: Dior's core equity is the atelier: the 'petites mains', the New Look silhouette, the Avenue Montaigne heritage and the Conservatoire archive. Craft is more credible and more ownable for Dior than generic eco-messaging.

Dior is assumed to already offer some repair, alteration or after-care for its leather goods and ready-to-wear. The campaign would elevate and scale this service, not invent capabilities the house lacks. Real service scope must be confirmed with the client.
The client wants cultural relevance and brand desirability, not a compliance-style sustainability report. Claims must stay verifiable to avoid greenwashing accusations.

The audience is twofold. Aspirational and established luxury clients (28-55) want longevity, provenance and emotional value. Gen Z and Millennial culture-watchers are comfortable with resale, vintage and visible mending, and distrust brand 'purpose' talk.
Repair and reuse in luxury can read as contradictory, since luxury sells newness. The campaign must resolve that tension, not hide it.
Tone should stay elevated, tactile and emotional, never preachy or discount-coded.

candidates.title: The Second Signature
candidates.core_idea: Every Dior piece repaired in the ateliers receives a small, numbered embroidered mark by the artisan who mended it, a 'second signature' inside the lining or hem. Repair becomes authorship: the piece now carries two hands and two chapters. The campaign tells these stories through close-up films of the repairers, the objects, and the owners' memories.
candidates.brand_connection: It puts the petites mains in the foreground, the part of Dior that cannot be copied by fast fashion. It echoes the couture tradition of signed, numbered work and makes the Dior label mean 'made and remade by hand'.
expected_strengths: Resolves the luxury-versus-repair tension: a repaired piece becomes more valuable and more personal, not less.
Highly platformable: films, artisan profiles, collectible marks, social 'show your second signature' content, a possible capsule of pieces mended by named artisans.
Gives resale and pre-owned a provenance logic, since the mark records the piece's history.
Credits craftspeople, which feels honest and humanizing.
main_concerns: Operational scale: marks on every repair may be impractical and need a clear scope.
Artisan consent, credit and labor considerations must be handled carefully.
Risk of seeming to romanticize damage unless framed around care and longevity.

candidates.title: Dior Lineage
candidates.core_idea: A provenance system and ceremony for second-life Dior. Each piece gets a digital and physical 'lineage card' recording its owners, repairs and occasions. Certified pre-owned pieces are re-presented in boutiques as 'second owners welcome', with a story rather than a discount.
candidates.brand_connection: It leans on Dior's archive and heritage-keeping mindset, treating every garment as a future archive piece.
expected_strengths: Strong business logic: authentication, resale control and brand-led reuse.
Appeals to collectors and resale-savvy younger buyers.
Scalable through digital infrastructure.
main_concerns: Moves toward a platform or tech product and away from emotion and craft.
Resale could be seen as diluting exclusivity or cannibalizing new sales.
Competitors already run authentication and passport programs, so it is less ownable.

candidates.title: Dior Mends Anything
candidates.core_idea: A limited 'open atelier' event in Paris and a few global cities where the public brings any beloved broken object, such as a torn teddy bear, a grandfather's coat or a cracked handbag of any brand, and Dior artisans mend it with couture technique, free. The objects and their stories become an exhibition and film series.
candidates.brand_connection: It democratizes access to the atelier and shows that Dior's craft is about care and attention, not just products.
expected_strengths: Provocative, emotional and highly shareable.
Humanizes the house and generates earned media.
Surprising, since a luxury brand is giving away its most valuable asset, skilled time.
main_concerns: Does not directly encourage repair of Dior products or lasting behavior change.
Capacity constraints could create long queues and disappointment.
May read as a one-off PR stunt unless connected to a durable service.

candidates.title: The Handover Fitting
candidates.core_idea: Focus on the moment a Dior piece is passed down: from mother to daughter, between friends, to a new owner. The atelier offers a 'handover fitting' that re-tailors and restores a beloved piece to its new wearer's body and style. The campaign collects and stages handover stories across generations.
candidates.brand_connection: It builds on the New Look and the idea of Dior as a family of silhouettes that outlive trends, linking couture tailoring to personal inheritance.
expected_strengths: Deep emotional pull and universal storytelling.
Makes reuse feel like love, not austerity.
Re-tailoring is a service Dior can plausibly deliver.
main_concerns: Skews toward existing owners and heirloom-worthy pieces, limiting reach with new audiences.
Sentimental territory is crowded in luxury advertising, so the execution risks cliché.

reasons_for_selection: It has the sharpest insight: in an age of machine-made sameness, the visible human hand is the true luxury, and repair is where that hand shows most clearly.
It is the most ownable for Dior because it elevates the petites mains and the atelier, which no mass competitor can claim.
It reframes repair as added value, which resolves the central contradiction between luxury and reuse.
It is a platform, not a one-off. The mark, the artisan stories, the objects and the owners' memories can run for years and extend into resale, collaborations and exhibitions.
It is strategically grounded in an existing service and can scale in stages, starting with leather goods and couture-adjacent pieces.

rejected.reason: Commercially sensible but infrastructure-led and emotionally cool. It is less distinctive because authentication and passport programs already exist in the category, and it risks diluting exclusivity. Its provenance logic is better used as a supporting layer for C1.

Bold and highly shareable but disconnected from Dior's own products and long-term repair behavior. Capacity limits and the risk of reading as a stunt make it better as a single activation within the platform than as the core idea.
Emotionally strong but sits in a crowded sentimental territory and centers on alteration more than repair. Its best element, the handover moment, is folded into the recommended idea instead.

revisions_after_selection.change: Made the second signature optional and tied to a clear scope, starting with leather goods and select ready-to-wear. Owners can choose an invisible repair or a signed one.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Not every client wants a visible trace, and operational limits mean full rollout is unrealistic at launch.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added artisan consent, named credit and recognition as a core principle, so artisans choose to sign and are featured in the campaign.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The idea depends on the artisans' authorship. Using their names without agreement would undermine the authenticity of the campaign.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a 'handover' moment from C4: when a signed piece is passed to a new owner, the owner can request the artisan's note or a return visit.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It strengthens the emotional layer and extends the idea toward reuse and inheritance, not just repair.

revisions_after_selection.change: Extended eligibility to authenticated pre-owned Dior pieces, with a lineage record, where verified.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It widens the audience beyond first owners, links repair to reuse, and avoids elitism, while borrowing the useful provenance logic of C2.

revisions_after_selection.change: Reframed communications to avoid celebrating damage. The message is care and continuity, not 'break it so we can fix it'.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It prevents an irresponsible reading, keeps the sustainability claim credible and avoids greenwashing criticism.

final_proposal.title: The Second Signature
final_proposal.idea: A Dior piece is made once, but it can be signed twice. When an artisan in the Dior ateliers repairs a bag, jacket or dress, they can stitch a small numbered mark of their own into the lining: a second signature. The piece now carries two hands and two chapters, so repair becomes authorship, not erasure. The campaign follows the petites mains, the objects they mend and the people who bring them back, in intimate close-up films and tactile content. Marks are optional and credited with the artisan's consent. Pieces can be passed on, and authenticated pre-owned items can carry their lineage forward. Dior's message: the rarest luxury is not newness, it is a piece that has been loved, mended and handed on by human hands.

Where else in luxury or culture is the maker's hand hidden, and what would happen if Dior invited other crafts, such as jewelry or fragrance, to sign their second chapters?
