task_understanding.focus: Loneliness is rarely a lack of people. More often it is a lack of reasons and rituals to meet the people already in your life. Digital and contactless payments have removed many small human exchanges, and peer-to-peer payments have made it easy to settle up and move on. The opportunity is for Mastercard to put its payments expertise to work on connection, so that money becomes an excuse to meet instead of a way to avoid contact. The campaign should do this without trivialising loneliness or turning it into a sales pitch.
assumptions: Mastercard's 'Priceless' platform gives it permission to speak about what matters beyond money, so a loneliness message can feel authentic if it is grounded in how people actually pay and share.
Mastercard is a B2B2C network, so any consumer-facing idea must be deliverable through issuer, fintech and merchant partners, not through its own app.

The core audience is adults aged 25-45 with busy, scattered, digitally mediated social lives. They have friends and family, but see them less and less. A secondary audience is older adults who are isolated after life changes.
Loneliness is stigmatised, so people will not self-identify as lonely. The idea must work through everyday behaviour and positive framing, not diagnosis.
Any use of transaction data must be aggregated, anonymised and opt-in to protect trust, since a financial brand is held to a higher privacy standard.
Credibility comes from a real product or behaviour change, not from a purely emotional film.

candidates.title: Keep the Tab Open
candidates.core_idea: Settling up is the fastest way to end a social loop: once the money is sent, there is no reason to see each other again. This idea reverses that. A 'Pay me back in person' option on split-bill and payment-request flows turns a debt into an IOU of shared time (one dinner, two coffees, a Sunday walk). Both people see an open tab and get a light nudge to book it. The tab closes when it is redeemed in real life.
candidates.brand_connection: It builds on the most basic payments behaviour, settling up, and gives it a human twist. It extends 'Priceless' by suggesting some debts are better left unpaid in money, and it positions Mastercard as the brand that understands the social role of money.
expected_strengths: Built on a sharp, counterintuitive insight: efficiency in payments quietly erodes relationships.
Platformable across a product feature, partner integrations, a launch film, merchant tie-ins and user-generated 'oldest tab' stories.
Works through ordinary behaviour, so nobody has to admit to being lonely.
Provocative for a payments brand to say 'don't settle up' while staying strategically on-brand.
main_concerns: Needs issuer or fintech partners to build the feature, which slows rollout.
Some may read 'unpaid debts' as financially irresponsible or awkward between friends.
Risk of fading into a gimmick if the nudges are weak or feel nagging.

candidates.title: Open Table
candidates.core_idea: Participating restaurants and cafés create shared 'open tables' where solo diners can opt in to sit with others. When two strangers share a table and pay with Mastercard, the brand covers the first round or dessert. The aim is to make eating alone a doorway to company by choice.
candidates.brand_connection: It turns Priceless-style experiences into a tangible, merchant-based product and shows Mastercard bringing people to local venues.
expected_strengths: Highly visual and easy to photograph and share.
Gives merchants a reason to join by driving footfall.
Strong experiential and PR potential in Priceless Cities.
main_concerns: Sitting with strangers is intimidating for the people who most need it.
Safety, moderation and scalability are operational burdens.
Similar shared-table and supper-club concepts already exist, so it is less ownable.

candidates.title: Save the Regulars
candidates.core_idea: For many people the barista, the corner shop owner or the barber is their most regular human contact. Using aggregated, anonymised insights on repeat-visit patterns, Mastercard identifies and supports local 'third places' that act as everyday social infrastructure. It funds them, trains staff in small-talk and noticing, and gives 'Regular' status to customers via a window sticker and a loyalty perk.
candidates.brand_connection: Links to Mastercard's small-business support and merchant network. It makes the brand the guardian of the places where everyday community happens.
expected_strengths: Emotionally resonant: celebrates the unsung people who notice you.
Combines social purpose with a business benefit for small merchants.
Gives the brand a clear territory in community resilience.
main_concerns: Close to existing small-business support programmes, so it may feel familiar.
Data use could feel intrusive if explained badly.
Impact is local and slow to scale globally.

candidates.title: The Connection Index
candidates.core_idea: Mastercard publishes an annual, anonymised and aggregated index of city 'social infrastructure', based on how much people spend on shared experiences versus solo, convenience-led ones. It identifies neighbourhoods drifting toward isolation and shares findings and funding with city governments and charities to help rebuild places to gather.
candidates.brand_connection: Draws on Mastercard's economic research and data credibility to put the brand in the loneliness conversation as a source of insight.
expected_strengths: Newsworthy and credible, with strong earned media potential.
Gives policymakers and NGOs something actionable.
Differentiates by using the unique asset of payment data.
main_concerns: Risk of seeming surveillance-like or creepy for a financial brand.
Cold and abstract, with little emotional pull for ordinary consumers.
Spend does not equal loneliness, so the methodology could be challenged.

reasons_for_selection: It has the sharpest, most surprising insight: the efficiency of payments can remove the reasons people meet, and Mastercard can be the brand to fix it.
It is rooted in a product truth (settling up) and a behaviour everyone recognises, so it feels authentic for a payments brand.
It is the most platformable. The same idea powers a feature, a launch film, a cultural movement about 'oldest tabs', merchant tie-ins and partner activations.
It avoids the stigma of loneliness by working through everyday friendships and giving people an easy excuse to reconnect.
It stays provocative but strategically grounded because it extends 'Priceless' instead of departing from it.

candidates.core_idea: Revive the old ritual of framing the first dollar earned. Canva offers beautiful templates to turn a first paycheck into a keepsake: a poster, a thank-you card to the person who helped you get here, a 'what I'll remember' collage. Users and creators share their frames under one hashtag-free, ritual-led banner.
candidates.brand_connection: It uses Canva's strength in personal, celebratory design (posters, cards, collages) and makes a ritual out of a template.
expected_strengths: Warm and highly shareable.
Taps a real cultural ritual that people already half-remember from parents and family.
Low production cost and easy to scale through templates.
main_concerns: Weak B2B link, and it leans on Canva's consumer side.
Sharing pay amounts raises privacy and comparison issues.
Close to ordinary 'celebrate with a template' marketing, so differentiation is limited.

candidates.title: Receipts of Firsts
candidates.core_idea: A cultural archive of what people bought with their first paycheck, told as designed receipts. Creators, public figures and ordinary people turn their first-paycheck purchase (rent deposit, a gift for mum, a bad sneaker choice) into a visual 'receipt'. candidates.brand_connection: It shows how design makes personal stories expressive and gives Canva a role as the storytelling tool of everyday life.
expected_strengths: Charming, human, and likely to generate user stories.
Strong editorial and PR potential with recognisable contributors.
A fresh visual format.
main_concerns: The B2B and productivity link is thin.
It reads as nostalgia content without a clear product behaviour.
It could be more of a content series than a lasting platform.

candidates.title: The First Paycheck You Sign
candidates.core_idea: Flip the lens to the person giving the first paycheck: the founder or small-business owner running payroll for their first hire. Founders say this is more nerve-wracking than their own first earnings, because it makes the business real. Canva creates a 'first hire kit' (offer letter, welcome pack, team handbook, a thank-you note on first payday) and tells the stories of founders who made that moment count.

Rich founder storytelling and a useful template kit.
main_concerns: Narrower audience, and less emotionally universal than the employee side.
Founder-hero storytelling is a familiar format.
It drifts from the first-paycheck feeling most people have.

reasons_for_selection: It has the sharpest insight: the payslip is the most emotionally loaded and worst-designed document in work life, and it is a gap only a design brand could credibly fill.
It connects the consumer-facing emotional moment (a first-time earner) with the B2B buyer (HR and onboarding teams) in one platform.
It is a real platform: template packs, a redesign challenge, partner integrations and an annual first-payday moment.
It demonstrates Canva's product truth, that clear design changes how people feel, rather than just decorating a milestone.

rejected.reason: Warm but generic. It celebrates the moment without revealing anything new, has a weak B2B link, and the privacy risk of sharing pay amounts limits the idea. Its keepsake element is absorbed into C1 as a small component.
Charming editorial content, but it lacks a clear product behaviour and a B2B tie. It is more of a content series than a platform, and could be done by almost any brand.

Strong B2B relevance and a fresh angle, but the audience is narrow and the emotional resonance is lower than for the first-time earner. Its 'first hire' kit idea is kept as a possible later extension of C1's employer templates.

revisions_after_selection.change: Reframed the idea from 'redesigning the payslip' to designing the communication layer around it: a decoder, a welcome note and a keepsake, with payroll providers and employers staying in charge of the numbers.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Canva is not a payroll provider. This avoids legal, accuracy and financial-advice risk and keeps the idea credible and implementable.

revisions_after_selection.change: Made employer and HR templates in Canva for Teams the main commercial route, with first-time earners as the emotional storytellers.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Keeps the campaign aligned with the B2B category and gives it a measurable business outcome (team and workspace adoption).

revisions_after_selection.change: Used anonymised, fictional sample payslips in all public activity and asked for no real pay data.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Pay is private and sensitive. This protects trust and avoids comparison or shaming dynamics.

revisions_after_selection.change: Led the campaign story with the human moment (the first-time earner's confusion and pride) and made the redesign challenge the proof point, not the headline.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The emotional hook is what makes the idea feel culturally relevant rather than like a document-formatting exercise.

final_proposal.title: Payday, Designed
final_proposal.idea: Your first paycheck is the moment work becomes real, and it arrives as a document built to be ignored. Canva takes on the most important, least designed page in working life. We show first-time earners squinting at lines like 'PAYG' and 'deductions' and feeling a bit lost on their proudest day. Then Canva gives teams a Payday Kit: a plain-language visual decoder that explains each line, a welcome-to-payday note from the team, and a keepsake worth keeping. Payroll providers still own the numbers; Canva owns how it feels. A student challenge redesigns the payslip with fictional data, and HR teams adopt the best versions as templates. First payday becomes an onboarding ritual that says: we made this clear because you matter.
follow_up_questions: Which other 'first-time' documents (a lease, a first contract, a first invoice) are just as emotional and badly designed, and could Canva become the brand that fixes them as a series?
How could employers measure the effect of a well-designed first payday on how new hires feel about the company, and could that evidence help sell Canva to HR leaders?
What would a payroll provider need to see to co-create this with Canva, and what might they gain from making the payslip a brand moment?

task_understanding.focus: Luxury's repair and reuse conversation is dominated by resale platforms and 'circularity' reports, which treat a Dior piece as a commodity with a second price. The opportunity for Dior is to make repair and reuse feel like the highest form of luxury: an act of devotion and craft that proves a Dior piece is built to be kept, mended and passed on, rather than a sustainability concession. The campaign should shift status from 'newest' to 'longest loved'.
assumptions: Dior (LVMH) has real assets for this topic: Paris ateliers, couture-trained artisans (petites mains), archives from 1947 onward, the Bar jacket, Lady Dior and Saddle bag as heirloom icons, and an existing repair and after-care service.
The client wants credible, non-greenwashed engagement with repair and reuse that protects brand desirability and pricing rather than discounting it.
Luxury consumers already repair and inherit pieces, but quietly; the behavior is under-celebrated and rarely shown in fashion advertising.
Younger affluent audiences (Gen Z and millennials) are comfortable with vintage and resale and are skeptical of sustainability claims from luxury houses, so proof beats promise.
Dior's emotional territory is femininity, romance, craftsmanship and Parisian heritage, which pairs naturally with ideas of memory, inheritance and care.
Budget and operations can support a scaled-up repair service and limited-edition activations, but not unlimited free repair for every product globally.

candidates.title: The Mended Is the Beloved
candidates.core_idea: Reframe visible repair as the ultimate luxury signal. Dior ateliers offer a 'signature mend': a repair that is deliberately beautiful and visible (golden-thread stitching on a Bar jacket, a hand-painted edge on a Lady Dior), inspired by kintsugi-like logic but rooted in couture technique. Owners wear their repair as proof of a long relationship with a piece. Campaign imagery celebrates scars, patina and wear in the way fashion usually celebrates newness.
candidates.brand_connection: Draws on Dior's couture hand-work, its fixation on detail, and the romance of the atelier. The repair becomes an extension of the design, not an apology for damage.
expected_strengths: Visually striking and ownable; creates a new status marker people can show off.
Inverts a category convention (perfection and newness) in a way that feels surprising yet brand-true.
Highly platformable into social content, editorial, in-store ateliers and UGC.
main_concerns: Visible repair aesthetic may clash with some clients' desire for flawless pieces.
Kintsugi-style references risk feeling borrowed or cliché if not grounded in Dior's own craft language.
Needs enough atelier capacity to deliver the service credibly.

candidates.title: Passed On, Dior
candidates.core_idea: Make inheritance the campaign hero. Dior creates an official 'Passing On' ritual: a piece is repaired, refreshed, and re-registered with a discreet new lineage tag stitched inside that records each owner's name and the year, forming a living provenance. The campaign tells real stories of pieces moving between generations and strangers, and lets clients pass a piece to a new owner through Dior-certified reuse.
candidates.brand_connection: Leverages Dior's 75+ year archive and its identity as a house of heirloom icons. Provenance is already a luxury currency; Dior owns the chain of custody rather than outsourcing it to resale platforms.
expected_strengths: Emotionally rich and deeply human; stories carry the campaign.
Gives Dior control of the reuse market and brand experience rather than ceding it to third parties.
Provenance tags create a long-term loyalty and data asset.
main_concerns: Heirloom storytelling is a familiar luxury trope and could feel sentimental without a sharper twist.
Operationally heavy: tagging, authentication and resale logistics.
Risk of cannibalizing new sales if not framed carefully.

candidates.title: Atelier Open Late
candidates.core_idea: Turn repair into a live cultural event. Dior opens its Paris atelier workshops (and pop-up ateliers in other cities) as public 'mending sessions' where petites mains repair clients' own beloved pieces on the spot, side by side with the owners, while they tell the story behind the damage. The campaign documents these sessions as a serialized film and live-streamed 'repair hours', making the artisans the stars.
candidates.brand_connection: Spotlights the invisible craftspeople behind Dior's mythology and makes craft transparency a reason to believe in the brand's longevity claims.
expected_strengths: Makes hidden labor visible, building trust and authenticity.
Strong earned media and content potential; scalable via city pop-ups.
Low risk of greenwashing criticism because the action is tangible.
main_concerns: Limited reach if it remains an event rather than a sustained platform.
Perceived as elitist if access is narrow.
Throughput is low; waiting lists could frustrate clients.

candidates.title: The Second Debut
candidates.core_idea: Treat reuse as a fashion-show moment. Each season, Dior's creative director reworks returned, damaged or unsellable archive and client pieces into a small runway-quality 'second debut' capsule, shown within the main show. Pieces are credited with their original year and previous life, and the campaign positions reinvention as the house's creative frontier. Clients can also commission a 'second debut' of their own old piece.
candidates.brand_connection: Connects to Dior's tradition of reinvention (the New Look itself was a rupture) and gives the creative director a bold, culturally visible role in the topic.
expected_strengths: Generates fashion-press attention and positions reuse as creative, not charitable.
Aligns with the house's creative authority and runway spectacle.
Strong hook for celebrity and influencer participation.
main_concerns: Capsule scale is small, so impact on actual repair and reuse behavior may be limited.
Could read as a one-off marketing stunt or upcycling trend-chasing.
Depends heavily on the creative director's buy-in and calendar.

reasons_for_selection: It makes repair itself desirable and visible, changing what status looks like rather than just describing Dior's care services.
It is the most surprising and least clichéd of the four, and it rests on a real product truth: Dior's hand-craft can make a repair as beautiful as the original.
It is highly platformable: a service (signature mends), a visual language (wear and patina in imagery), a social behavior (wearing your mend), and room to absorb the best parts of C2 and C3.
It supports luxury pricing and desirability, because repair is framed as couture-level craft that deepens attachment, rather than as discounting or a sustainability concession.
It is operationally credible at launch scale, beginning with iconic pieces and flagship ateliers.

rejected.reason: Emotionally strong but the heirloom narrative is a well-worn luxury trope, and the provenance-tagging infrastructure is operationally heavy. Its best element, a lineage record, is better used as a later extension of C1.
Great for transparency and craft credibility but it is primarily an event format with limited reach and throughput. It works better as an activation channel for C1 than as the core idea.

Fashion-forward and attention-grabbing but small in scale and tied to a seasonal creative moment, so it risks looking like upcycling-as-stunt and does little to change everyday repair and reuse behavior.

revisions_after_selection.change: Rooted the visible mend in Dior's own craft vocabulary (house codes such as cannage, toile de Jouy, Bar-jacket pique, Dior-grey and gold thread) rather than a generic kintsugi reference.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Avoids a borrowed, cliché cultural reference and makes the mend unmistakably Dior and ownable.

revisions_after_selection.change: Made the visible mend optional: clients choose between an invisible restoration and a 'signature mend'.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Respects clients who want flawless pieces, lowers the adoption barrier and protects the brand from seeming to promote damage.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a discreet inside-label record of the mend (year and atelier), borrowing the provenance idea from C2.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Adds lasting value and resale desirability to a mended piece, reinforcing that repair raises rather than lowers worth.

revisions_after_selection.change: Planned launch with a limited set of icons (Bar jacket, Lady Dior, Saddle) at flagship ateliers, with artisan-led films borrowed from C3.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Keeps the promise operationally credible, avoids greenwashing criticism and gives the artisans a human face.

final_proposal.title: The Mended Is the Beloved
final_proposal.idea: Fashion worships the new. Dior celebrates the kept. The campaign launches the Signature Mend: a Dior atelier repair that can be deliberately visible, stitched in house-code thread on a Bar jacket or painted along the edge of a Lady Dior. A small label inside records the year and the hands that mended it, so a repaired piece becomes more valuable, not less. Campaign imagery flips luxury's visual rules, shooting worn, mended, loved pieces with the same reverence as a runway debut, and artisan-led films show the petites mains at work. Owners are invited to wear their mends as proof of a long relationship. Repair stops being a quiet chore and becomes Dior's newest status symbol.
follow_up_questions: What would a mended piece have to look like for a client to feel proud to be seen in it, and what would make it feel like a flaw instead?
Beyond Dior's iconic bags and jackets, which everyday or lower-priced products could carry a Signature Mend and bring younger audiences into the idea?
How might the 'wear your mend' behavior spread culturally, for example through celebrity wardrobes, vintage communities or other houses, without becoming a trend that peaks and fades?

task_understanding.focus: The first paycheck is a rite of passage that people mark with pride, screenshots and framed checks. For Canva's B2B and small-business audience (freelancers, side-hustlers, solo founders, early-career creatives), getting paid for the first time depends on something they have to make themselves: a credible-looking document. The opportunity is to connect Canva with the moment a person stops being an amateur and becomes someone who gets paid, and to show that Canva helps get them there.
assumptions: The audience is an emerging professional: a Gen Z or young Millennial freelancer, side-hustler, creator or micro-business owner. Salaried new hires are a secondary audience.
Canva is already seen as friendly and easy for creating, but less as a tool for professional credibility and for getting paid. That is the perception gap to close.

The first paycheck means different things to different people: a payroll deposit for some, a self-issued invoice finally paid for others. The self-employed version is under-served culturally and closer to Canva's product truth.
Canva has invoice, proposal, portfolio and pitch-deck templates, but we should not assume it processes payments. The campaign should not depend on payment data.
Impostor syndrome and 'am I a real professional yet?' anxiety are strong emotional drivers at this life stage.
Success is measured by business-template usage, new-user acquisition among freelancers and small businesses, and organic social sharing, not just awareness.

candidates.title: Frame It
candidates.core_idea: The first paycheck is the most emotionally loaded document of your early career, yet it arrives as an ugly stub or a bank notification. Canva turns it into a keepsake: templates and a print-ready tool to design and frame your first paycheck, your first receipt or your first dollar, with the hard-earned number as the hero.
candidates.brand_connection: Plays to Canva's core strength of making beautiful things easy, and to its print and personal-design offerings. It shows Canva can make an ordinary object feel special.
expected_strengths: Warm, highly shareable and easy to understand.
Fits the existing habit of posting first-paycheck moments.
Strong visual output for social and OOH.
main_concerns: Skews consumer and sentimental, so the B2B and productivity link is weak.
A one-off gimmick with little reason to return to the product.
Risk of sharing real income figures, which raises privacy concerns.

candidates.title: Paid Before You Were Ready
candidates.core_idea: For freelancers and side-hustlers, the first paycheck doesn't arrive. You have to request it with a document that must look professional before you've earned any credibility. Canva closes this 'look-pro gap' with a first-invoice kit and a ritual: a designable PAID stamp that people apply to their first paid invoice and share as a badge of becoming a professional.
candidates.brand_connection: Directly ties Canva's business templates (invoices, proposals, portfolios, pitch decks) to a deeply felt milestone. It positions Canva as the tool that gets you paid, not just a tool for making posts.
expected_strengths: Built on a real, under-told insight: nobody pays the amateur, and you need to look paid to get paid.
A ritual (the PAID stamp) that can spread as a UGC platform and become a sticker, an element and a community wall.
Moves Canva's perception towards professional credibility and commercial value.
Works across product, social, creator and small-business partnerships.
main_concerns: Narrower than the broader 'first paycheck' idea, since it centres on self-employed people.
Must not imply Canva handles payments.
The ritual only works if people actually adopt it.

candidates.title: The Stub, Explained
candidates.core_idea: Gross, net, tax, deductions: the first paystub shocks and confuses new workers. Canva publishes visual, template-driven explainers and a 'decode my first paystub' kit so young people understand what they're looking at, and employers can share it in onboarding.
candidates.brand_connection: Uses Canva's strength in visual communication and education, and its workplace and HR use cases such as onboarding decks and internal comms.
expected_strengths: Genuinely useful and likely to be saved and shared.
Opens a B2B route through HR and onboarding teams.
Credible as a utility.
main_concerns: Drifts into financial and tax advice, outside Canva's authority.
Tax rules vary by region, so the content is hard to scale and keep accurate.
Low emotional spark and a dry tone for a brand known for joy.

candidates.title: Paid to Make
candidates.core_idea: Celebrate people whose first paycheck came from something they made in Canva, such as a template, a logo or a social kit. The campaign uses real first-payout stories from Canva's creator and freelancer community to show that making things on Canva can become income.
candidates.brand_connection: Draws on Canva's creator marketplace and its community of people who design for others. The brand becomes an enabler of livelihoods.
expected_strengths: Authentic, human stories with strong proof points.
Aspirational for the target audience.
Supports creator recruitment as well as user acquisition.
main_concerns: Risk of sounding like an income claim or a get-rich pitch.
Depends on a small set of success stories, which feels like a typical testimonial campaign.
Less scalable as a platform beyond storytelling.

reasons_for_selection: It has the sharpest and least obvious insight: for the self-employed, the first paycheck begins with a document they design, so credibility has to come before income.
It places Canva's business templates in a high-emotion moment, which changes how the brand is perceived and drives usage in a commercially valuable category.
The PAID stamp is a simple, ownable ritual that makes the idea platformable. It can live as a product asset, a social mechanic, a creator challenge and an OOH motif.
It is strategically grounded in a real product truth (templates for invoices and proposals) without promising anything Canva doesn't offer.

rejected.reason: Warm and shareable, but sentimental and consumer-leaning. It doesn't advance Canva's B2B and productivity role, and it risks being a one-time gimmick.
Useful but off-territory. It moves Canva toward financial advice, is hard to localise and keep accurate, and lacks the emotional spark needed for a campaign.
Credible but resembles a standard testimonial campaign. It risks sounding like an income promise and offers less room to build a participatory platform.

revisions_after_selection.change: The PAID stamp is a self-applied, user-controlled ritual, with no connection to payment verification or payment data.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Canva shouldn't imply it processes or confirms payments. A self-applied stamp keeps the claim honest and the mechanic simple.

revisions_after_selection.change: Shared stamped invoices hide the amount and client details by default, so people can post the milestone without revealing income.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Income is sensitive, and privacy by default removes a major barrier to sharing.

revisions_after_selection.change: The audience is widened from freelancers to include side-hustlers, solo founders and anyone issuing their first invoice, with a nod to salaried first-timers through the shared 'first PAID' wall.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Avoids feeling too narrow against the broad client topic of the first paycheck and increases the reach of the ritual.

revisions_after_selection.change: The campaign leads with the emotional insight (looking professional before you feel professional) rather than the invoice template.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Prevents the work from reading as a template promotion and keeps it culturally relevant.

final_proposal.title: Paid Before You Were Ready
final_proposal.idea: Nobody pays the amateur, yet you can't feel professional until someone pays you. For freelancers and side-hustlers, the first paycheck starts with a document you design yourself. Canva steps into that gap with a First Invoice Kit and a new ritual: the PAID stamp. When your first invoice is settled, you stamp it in Canva and share it, with the amount hidden by default. The stamp becomes a badge of 'I'm a professional now', a shareable sticker and a community wall of first PAIDs. Creators show the invoice they sent while still doubting themselves, then the stamp. Canva becomes the tool behind the moment you become a pro, not only a tool for making posts.
follow_up_questions: What other 'proof of professionalism' moments (a first business card, a first pitch, a first client email) could the stamp ritual extend to?
How could the PAID stamp work as a physical or cultural object, such as a real rubber stamp, a bell or a desk trophy, so it travels beyond screens?
Which partners (payment platforms, freelance marketplaces, coworking spaces, creator communities) could make the first-PAID moment more meaningful without Canva claiming to handle payments?

task_understanding.focus: The first paycheck is one of the few universal, emotionally loaded 'firsts' of adulthood, and it is a design problem nobody talks about. It arrives as a plain, ugly document (a payslip full of deductions, codes and acronyms) at the exact moment a person feels they have become an adult. The opportunity for Canva is to own the moment when people first make something to mark, understand or share their working life, and to reposition Canva from a 'design tool' to the tool people use to give shape to the milestones of their working identity, starting at the beginning. This also seeds early-career lifetime value, since first-job workers become the future team leads and Canva for Work buyers.
assumptions: Canva's primary growth lever in B2B is bottom-up adoption: individuals who learn Canva early (school, first job) bring it into teams and companies later.
The audience is 18-26-year-olds starting their first paid job (including part-time, gig and internship work), plus the parents, partners and friends who celebrate with them.

The first paycheck triggers mixed emotions: pride, confusion about taxes and deductions, anxiety about money, and a desire to mark the moment. Many people feel the gap between the gross figure they expected and the net figure they received.
Canva should not give financial advice or pretend to be a bank; its credible territory is making things clear, visual and shareable.
Gen Z and young millennials are fluent in social-native, screenshot-ready formats and respond to honesty and humour more than to aspirational polish.

The campaign needs to work globally, so it must flex across currencies, payslip formats and cultural attitudes to money (for example, in some cultures a first paycheck is given to parents, in others spent on treating friends).
Budget and production should favour platform-style ideas built on templates and user-generated content, which fit Canva's product strengths.

candidates.title: The Payslip Remix
candidates.core_idea: Turn the least loved document of adult life into something you can understand and own. Users upload or recreate their first payslip in a Canva tool that translates every line (gross, tax, pension, deductions) into plain-language, designed visuals: a clear 'where your money went' graphic. The campaign shows that the problem with payslips is design, not money. Users share their 'remixed' payslips, with figures optional or masked.
candidates.brand_connection: Directly demonstrates Canva's core belief that clear design makes complex things understandable and that everyone can be a designer. It shows the product making information visual, which is the same skill used in presentations, reports and dashboards at work.
expected_strengths: Strong, simple, demonstrable insight: payslips are badly designed and confusing.
Solves a real pain point, so the idea is useful rather than just promotional.
Template-driven, so it scales globally and generates user content.
Naturally links to the work use case (turning complex data into clear visuals).
main_concerns: Handling of personal financial data creates privacy risk and requires careful product design.
Payslip formats vary by country, making accuracy and localisation hard.
Could drift into financial advice territory, with legal and trust implications.

candidates.title: Frame the First One
candidates.core_idea: The first paycheck is the new graduation photo. Canva makes the keepsake of the moment: a 'First Paycheck' ritual kit, with templates for a framed mock-cheque, a thank-you card to whoever helped you get here, a milestone post, and a printable certificate for the fridge. The idea is that people mark graduations and birthdays but let their first earned money slip by unnoticed.
candidates.brand_connection: Positions Canva as the tool for marking life's moments, extending its existing strength in cards, invitations and celebratory design to a milestone nobody has yet claimed.
expected_strengths: Warm, emotional and highly shareable; easy for families to join in.
Easy to execute with templates and print partnerships.
Low legal and privacy risk because no financial data is needed.
main_concerns: Feels closer to a seasonal template pack than a platform; risks being sweet but forgettable.
Weak link to the B2B and work value proposition.
Digital payments mean there is no physical cheque to frame, so the ritual needs a new anchor.

candidates.title: Pay It Forward Deck
candidates.core_idea: Insight: for many people the first paycheck is not spent on themselves; it is spent on someone else (parents, siblings, a round of drinks). The campaign invites people to design a 'thank-you presentation' for the first person they spend it on: a short, personal Canva deck or video, 'Where my first paycheck went and why.' Canva also lets users nominate the people who helped them get their first job, and funds a small design-skills grant for each story shared.
candidates.brand_connection: Uses Canva's presentation and video tools in an emotional, human way, and links to Canva's purpose of empowering the world to design, with a giving mechanism that builds on its existing social impact commitments.
expected_strengths: Culturally rich and globally relevant, since gratitude and family obligation appear in many cultures.
Emotional storytelling that creates natural PR and social content.
Gives a purpose-led angle that differentiates from a purely product-led campaign.
main_concerns: Grant mechanics add complexity and cost.
Risk of seeming performative if the giving element is thin.
Presentation format is less native to social platforms than short-form content.

candidates.title: Day One Brand
candidates.core_idea: A provocative reframe: your first paycheck is the first time you become a brand of one. The campaign argues that getting paid means someone has bought your skills, so you should present yourself professionally from day one. Canva offers a 'Day One' identity kit: a personal logo, a simple one-page portfolio, a LinkedIn banner, a CV refresh, and a signature, all designed the week the first pay lands. The campaign line of thought is 'You've been paid. You're a professional. Look like it.'
candidates.brand_connection: Connects Canva's design tools directly to career identity and workplace credibility, and plants the habit of using Canva for work materials at the earliest stage of a career, which feeds Canva for Work growth.
expected_strengths: Clearest commercial and B2B link: builds early-career habit and professional use.
Timely, practical and easy to measure through template use and sign-ups.
Taps into an aspirational but achievable identity shift.
main_concerns: Personal branding for the young can feel pressuring and cliché, and is already a crowded space.
Less emotional and less surprising than the other directions.
May exclude people in gig or non-office jobs who do not see themselves as 'brands'.

reasons_for_selection: It is built on the sharpest and most surprising insight: the first paycheck is a rite of passage delivered in a document that looks like a spreadsheet from 1998. The problem to solve is design, which is exactly Canva's territory.
It offers genuine utility, which earns attention and trust better than a purely sentimental gesture, and it gives the campaign a product demonstration rather than just a message.

It has the strongest platform potential: a repeatable format ('remix your payslip') that can run across markets, creators, employers and schools, and be extended to other confusing work documents such as contracts, offer letters and benefit statements.

It connects to the B2B story: if Canva can make a payslip legible, it can make a quarterly report, onboarding pack or internal comms legible, and it introduces new workers to Canva at the moment they join an organisation.

rejected.reason: Emotionally pleasant but too close to a seasonal template pack, with limited differentiation, a weak work and B2B link, and no real physical anchor in a digital payments world. It works better as a supporting element than as the lead idea.

Culturally insightful and emotionally strong, but the grant mechanic adds cost and complexity, the risk of performative giving is real, and the product role is less distinctive. It is better kept as a later chapter or content series.

The most commercially direct, but the 'personal brand' space is crowded and cliché, the tone can feel like pressure on young workers, and it lacks the surprise and emotional truth of the selected idea.

revisions_after_selection.change: Make the payslip remix a template-and-explain experience that works without uploading real payslip data: users start from a sample payslip or type in their own numbers locally, and sharing masks figures by default.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Privacy and trust are the main risks for an idea involving financial documents; removing mandatory upload keeps the idea usable and safe.

revisions_after_selection.change: Position the tool as 'making it clear', not 'telling you what to do', and add pointers to local official or independent sources for tax and deduction definitions instead of giving advice.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Avoids financial advice liability and keeps Canva in its credible lane of clarity and visual communication.

revisions_after_selection.change: Add a localisation layer built with local creators and payroll or finance educators in each launch market, and a format that works for gig and part-time earnings statements too.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Payslip formats differ by country and not every first earner has a formal payslip, so the idea needs to flex to remain accurate and inclusive.

revisions_after_selection.change: Fold the emotional ritual from C2 into the share step: a 'My First Pay, Made Clear' card that people can send to the person they would thank.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Adds warmth and shareability to a utility-led idea and addresses the concern that the concept could feel purely functional.

final_proposal.title: Pay Slip, Made Clear
final_proposal.idea: Your first paycheck is a milestone delivered in the ugliest document you will ever own. Canva redesigns it. With the Payslip Remix, first-time earners drop in their numbers, or start from a sample, and get a clear, beautiful picture of what they earned, what went where, and what each strange acronym means, with sources for the facts rather than advice. Figures are masked by default for sharing, so people post their 'First Pay, Made Clear' card with pride, not exposure. Local creators and finance educators adapt it for each market, including gig and part-time pay. The campaign's point: confusion is a design failure, not a personal one. The same skill that clarifies a payslip clarifies a report, a deck or a plan, and Canva will be there when the career catches up.
follow_up_questions: Which other confusing 'first' documents of working life (offer letters, contracts, benefits summaries, tax forms) could become the next chapter of this platform?
How could employers or schools become partners so the tool reaches people at their first payday without Canva ever handling sensitive data?
What would make a young earner proudly share this card, and what is the line between a proud milestone and an uncomfortable disclosure of income?

Luxury buyers increasingly worry about the credibility of 'green' claims, and younger luxury audiences are heavily engaged in resale, vintage and archive culture, so repair and reuse matter to them and are already part of how they relate to the brand.
Many owners hold Dior pieces they love but no longer wear because of fit, damage or changing taste. They do not know Dior can renew these pieces or fear it would be costly or intimidating.
Dior wants to protect brand desirability and exclusivity. The campaign must not cheapen the brand or look like a discount or second-hand play.
The client has or can scale a repair, alteration or aftercare service, and can give atelier staff public credit. Where capacity is limited, access may be staged or limited-edition.
Audience: existing Dior clients, aspirational Gen Z and Millennial luxury fans, and inherited-piece owners (daughters, granddaughters, collectors), across fashion, bags, and shoes.

candidate.title: The Second Signature
candidate.core_idea: Every garment Dior repairs or renews receives a 'Second Signature': a small, visible, hand-stitched mark made by the specific atelier artisan who worked on it, with their initials and the date, in a signature Dior thread (for example, a dove-grey or a gold stitch tucked at the hem, lining or strap). The mark is not hidden. It is the new status symbol: proof that this piece has lived, been loved, and been mastered twice. The campaign reframes repair as co-authorship: the original designer wrote the first chapter, the artisan and the owner write the second. Platform elements: (1) Atelier Open Hours, where owners bring a piece and meet the artisan who will work on it; (2) a film and photo series of real owners and their pieces ('Mended by Hand', with generations, stories and Second Signatures in close-up); (3) a collectible Second Signature registry in the Dior app, logging a garment's lineage of owners and repairs, which also enhances resale and provenance value; (4) a limited run of runway looks or capsule pieces deliberately designed with 'repair-ready' details (visible darning, replaceable collars, re-weavable panels) that invite future Second Signatures; (5) an archive call-out inviting owners to bring in decades-old pieces for a once-a-year 'Reawakening' show where the best are displayed.
candidate.brand_connection: Dior was founded on the atelier and the idea that clothing is made by hand, with deep respect for the garment and the woman wearing it. The New Look itself was about reshaping silhouettes with extreme craft. The Second Signature extends this: the atelier is not only where new things begin but where they continue. It turns Dior's heritage of craftsmanship, archive and couture fitting into a sustainability behaviour (keep, repair, pass on) without sacrificing desire. It also gives the petites mains the visibility they deserve and makes longevity a luxury marker, not a compromise.
expected_strengths: Makes repair aspirational: a visible mark of care and craft turns a potential 'flaw' into a status signal, which is the real barrier in luxury.
Grounded in a real brand asset (the atelier) and real people (named artisans), which makes the claim credible and hard for fast fashion to copy.
Highly shareable and visual: close-up of the stitch, the artisan's hands, the owner's story. Works as film, social, in-store and PR.
Creates ongoing client relationships and traffic (repeat visits, provenance registry, app engagement) and strengthens resale value, which supports long-term brand equity.
Scalable in tiers: from small leather goods and shoes to couture; from flagship ateliers to pop-up repair salons in key cities.
Gives the 'repair-ready' capsule a design story, so the campaign also influences product design and not only communications.
main_concerns: Operational capacity: atelier time is scarce, so demand could exceed supply, and long waits or limited access could frustrate clients or feel exclusionary. Needs a clear phased rollout and pricing logic.
Risk of being read as greenwashing or as encouraging less purchasing if not paired with transparent commitments (repair guarantees, lifetime service, data on garments kept in use).
Pricing and accessibility: if repair is expensive, the message becomes 'only the rich can mend'. Consider pricing tiers or a limited free offer for heirloom pieces.
Brand sensitivity about visible marks on garments, which some clients may not want. Offer opt-in discreet or visible options.
Artisan privacy, consent and labour considerations when naming individuals publicly; needs fair credit and compensation.
Authenticity of provenance registry data, and the risk that it fuels counterfeit or resale gaming without strong verification.

final_proposal.title: The Second Signature
final_proposal.idea: What if the most coveted detail on a Dior piece wasn't the logo, but a stitch? When a garment is repaired or renewed in a Dior atelier, the artisan who worked on it adds a small, visible hand-stitched mark with their initials and the date: the Second Signature. Repair becomes co-authorship, proof a piece has been loved, mastered twice, and passed on. The campaign opens the ateliers through Open Hours where owners meet the hands that mend their pieces, a film series of real garments and the stories behind them, and a digital lineage registry that records each piece's life across owners. A small capsule of 'repair-ready' designs invites future signatures. Dior doesn't ask people to buy less; it makes keeping, mending and inheriting the new height of luxury.
follow_up_questions: What would make a visible repair mark feel more desirable than a pristine, untouched garment for a Dior client, and how could the brand test that before launch?

How could the Second Signature be offered at different price points or access levels without diluting its status, and who should be prioritised first: heirloom owners, loyal clients, or younger archive fans?
Beyond clothing, which other Dior categories (fragrance bottles, jewellery, shoes, bags) could carry their own version of a second-life ritual, and what would the equivalent of the stitch be?

task_understanding.focus: Luxury fashion's circularity story is usually told through recycling programs, resale platforms and sustainability reports, which feel clinical and cold. Dior has an opportunity to make repair and reuse feel like the most desirable, romantic and status-rich act in luxury: proof that a Dior piece is not bought for a season but kept, mended and passed on. The campaign should shift repair from an apology for wear to the highest expression of craft and love, without undermining the desire to buy new.
assumptions: Dior's core equity is couture savoir-faire, the Paris ateliers, Monsieur Dior's heritage and the idea of the made-by-hand, so repair is a natural extension of craft rather than a bolt-on sustainability message.
The client wants a brand-building idea with cultural pull, not a service announcement; any repair offer (e.g., atelier repair, restoration, care) already exists or can be scaled to support the idea.
The audience spans two groups: aspirational younger luxury buyers (Gen Z and millennials) who shop resale, vintage and archive, and established clients who own pieces with emotional history.
Luxury consumers distrust overt green claims; the idea must be emotional and aesthetic first, and credible and specific on practice second.
Visible mending, vintage dressing and 'archive' culture are already positive cultural signals, so the idea can ride an existing shift instead of inventing one.
Dior must avoid anything that signals its products are fragile or that discourages new purchases; the message is longevity as luxury.

candidates.title: Dior Scars: The Mended Is the Beloved
candidates.core_idea: Reframe the visible repair as the new luxury signature. Dior atelier artisans mend beloved pieces with deliberately beautiful, couture-level repair marks (embroidered patches over a tear, gold-thread darning on a Saddle bag corner, a re-lined Bar jacket with the owner's handwriting stitched inside). Each mend is a signed 'Dior scar' that proves a piece has been lived in. The campaign is told through portraits of the piece and the person, not the model.
candidates.brand_connection: Turns the atelier's hand skills into the hero. Echoes Dior's embroidery, toile de Jouy, and petites mains heritage. Positions Dior as the house that makes imperfection more valuable than newness.
expected_strengths: Visually striking and photographable; the mend becomes a collectible, shareable design element.
Plays on kintsugi and visible-mending culture while staying distinctively couture.
Creates a sought-after status marker that a new item cannot buy, driving repair demand.
main_concerns: Risk of implying products break easily if not framed as love, not damage.
Visible mending may clash with the polished perfection some clients expect.
Could be perceived as borrowing from kintsugi or craft traditions without nuance.

candidates.title: The Second Wearer
candidates.core_idea: Celebrate the handover. Dior pieces carry a 'wearer's ledger' (a discreet, atelier-sewn label or digital record) that logs each owner and each repair across decades. The campaign stages real handovers: a grandmother's 1960s Dior coat reworked for her granddaughter, a stranger's vintage bag certified and re-gifted. Pieces become characters with a biography, and a new generation is invited to be the next chapter.
candidates.brand_connection: Draws on Dior's long history and the idea of a house that dresses generations. Gives archive and vintage a living, emotional frame, not a resale one, and fits Dior's storytelling about its founder and heritage.
expected_strengths: Highly emotional with strong human stories and PR potential.
Positions reuse as inheritance, not second-hand, which protects brand value.
Builds a provenance layer that could support authentication and trust.
main_concerns: Heavily narrative; risks feeling sentimental or familiar (heirloom stories are a luxury trope).
Requires tracking infrastructure and owner consent.
Could weaken the appeal of buying new if not balanced.

candidates.title: Repair Couture Week
candidates.core_idea: Stage repair as a runway event. During Paris Fashion Week, Dior runs an open atelier where couture artisans repair, restyle and re-cut audience-submitted garments live, and the results are shown in a 'show' with the owners walking. Submissions come from the public (any Dior piece, any condition), and the best transformations are exhibited. Repair becomes a spectacle with a calendar moment.
candidates.brand_connection: Uses Dior's strongest asset, the show, and gives the atelier a stage. Connects to its history of spectacle and craft theatre, and to creative director-led reinterpretation.
expected_strengths: High-visibility, event-driven and media-friendly.
Shows craft transparently and demystifies the atelier.
Generates content with real stakes and unpredictable transformations.
main_concerns: One-off event can feel like a stunt without a lasting service behind it.
Limited scale; only a few pieces can be repaired.
Risk of reading as a publicity exercise and not a commitment.

candidates.title: Wear It Till It Tells
candidates.core_idea: Invert the fashion promise of 'new season' with a provocation: Dior invites people to wear a piece until it has a story worth telling. A campaign counter-programs the 'outfit repeat' shame, with celebrities and everyday clients proudly re-wearing the same Dior piece over years, shown in a time-lapse portrait series with the piece aging beside them. Dior stores offer a lifetime 'care and repair' passport that marks each milestone (first mend, first resole, first re-lining).
candidates.brand_connection: Aligns with Dior's timeless icons (Bar jacket, Saddle bag, J'Adore Dior pumps), which already outlast trends. Makes the House's classics the evidence for a different relationship to clothing.
expected_strengths: Clear, bold, cultural stance against disposability and outfit-repeat shame.
Easy to extend into social, retail and ambassador content.
Supports repeat engagement through a passport and care touchpoints.
main_concerns: Anti-newness messaging may conflict with commercial seasonal goals.
Time-lapse concept needs long timelines or careful staging to feel authentic.
Risks being seen as hypocritical if the brand keeps a rapid collection cadence.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a choice of mend styles, from invisible to boldly visible, so clients decide how much the repair shows.

final_proposal.title: Mended by Dior
final_proposal.idea: Make the mend the new luxury signature. Dior's atelier artisans repair beloved pieces, a torn Bar jacket, a worn Saddle bag corner, a loved scarf, with couture-level stitching, embroidery or gold thread, and sign each one with a small hand-sewn mark. task_understanding.focus: Loneliness is rarely about having nobody. It is about having no easy, low-pressure reason to be with someone. Mastercard can act at the point where intention turns into a plan, because a payment is often the moment a plan becomes real. The opportunity is to make showing up together cheaper, easier and more natural, and so give 'Priceless' a purpose beyond the moment itself.
assumptions: Mastercard's 'Priceless' platform is built on experiences and connection, so loneliness is a credible topic if the brand acts and does not just comment.
Many lonely people want company but find the first step awkward. Cost, effort and fear of rejection get in the way more often than a lack of opportunities.

The audience is broad: young adults in new cities, remote workers, recent retirees and people who have lost a partner. The first campaign should target adults 25-40 and their friends and family, because they are active planners and gift-givers.
Using customer transaction data to infer who is lonely would damage trust, so the campaign should not do this.
The idea must work through payment products or the acceptance network, which are things only Mastercard can offer.
A pilot in one or two cities with local merchants and community partners is realistic, and it can scale if it works.

candidates.title: Priceless Seats
candidates.core_idea: On slow nights, partner restaurants set aside communal tables for people who want to eat with others. Diners book a seat with a Mastercard and are matched with a small group. Eating alone is one of the most common lonely moments, and a table is a simple, familiar place to fix it.
candidates.brand_connection: It builds on Mastercard's dining heritage and Priceless Cities. The card becomes the ticket to a shared table.
expected_strengths: Easy to understand and visual.
Helps merchants fill quiet nights, so partners have a reason to join.
Builds on assets Mastercard already has.
main_concerns: Social dining apps and supper clubs already exist.
Sitting with strangers can feel intimidating, so it may appeal mainly to confident people.
It leans toward the brand's usual restaurant territory and is less surprising.

candidates.title: Two-Tap
candidates.core_idea: A gift card that only works when two people tap it together, either by pairing two cards or by one card used alongside a companion's. You give someone an invitation, not money. The payment itself requires company, so it turns a gift into a plan that cannot be spent alone.
candidates.brand_connection: It uses the core product truth of tap-to-pay and puts it to a new use. The card proves that connection is the point of the transaction, which is a modern expression of Priceless.
expected_strengths: A clear product mechanic that is easy to explain and to demonstrate.
Gives friends and family a way to help someone without saying 'you seem lonely'.
Works as a gift in any season and spreads through word of mouth.
Can be extended with local cafés, cinemas, classes and clubs.
main_concerns: It needs technical development and merchant onboarding.
A person with no one to invite could feel excluded.
The framing must avoid stigma.

candidates.title: The Everyday Hello
candidates.core_idea: For some people, the only daily conversation is a shop or café transaction. Mastercard trains and equips small-business staff to turn the tap into a short, genuine exchange, and recognises merchants who do it well as 'Priceless Regulars' places'.
candidates.brand_connection: It positions Mastercard as the network that supports small businesses and the human side of commerce.
expected_strengths: Warm, human and credible with small-business partners.
Low cost to run and easy to scale across many local shops.
Highlights an overlooked source of daily contact.
main_concerns: Hard to measure and relies on staff behaviour that the brand cannot control.
Forced friendliness could feel patronising.
Less ownable, since any brand could sponsor it.

candidates.title: The Lonely Economy Index
candidates.core_idea: Use aggregated, anonymised spending patterns, such as group versus solo purchases and the rise of single-portion and delivery spending, to publish a city-level index of social connection. Then fund local fixes in the lowest-scoring neighbourhoods.
candidates.brand_connection: It draws on Mastercard's data and insights business to show that payments reveal how people live.
expected_strengths: Generates press and city-government interest.
Gives the brand authority and a rigorous insight base.
main_concerns: Even anonymised data may feel invasive for a card brand.
Reads as a report, not an experience, so it creates less emotional engagement.
Spending is a weak proxy for loneliness, so the conclusions could be challenged.

reasons_for_selection: It is the only candidate that uses the payment mechanic itself, so it is clearly something Mastercard can do and others cannot.
It solves the real barrier, which is the awkwardness of the first invitation. A gift that needs two people gives both a reason to go.
It lets family and friends act without labelling anyone as lonely, which avoids stigma.
It is simple to explain, demonstrate and share, and it can grow into a platform with new places, groups and partners.
It carries less privacy risk than the data-led option and is more distinctive than the dining option.

rejected.reason: Useful and easy to execute, but the concept is familiar from supper clubs and social dining apps, and it relies on people being comfortable sitting with strangers. It could become one use case inside Two-Tap.
Warm and cheap, but it depends on staff behaviour the brand cannot control, is hard to measure, and could feel forced. It lacks a product element that is ownable.
Offers credibility and press, but using spending data on loneliness risks feeling intrusive, the proxy is weak, and it creates little emotional connection. It might work later as supporting research.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added an 'Open Pair' option where a card can be matched with a companion through community partners such as libraries, charities and clubs.
revisions_after_selection.reason: People with no one to invite could otherwise feel excluded by a mechanic that requires two people.

revisions_after_selection.change: Positioned the card as an invitation to do something ('Your plans are on us') and not as a loneliness remedy. Loneliness is the context, not the label printed on the product.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Naming loneliness on the gift could embarrass the recipient and reduce gifting.

revisions_after_selection.change: Limited the first launch to one or two cities with a capped card value and a local merchant network of cafés, cinemas, classes and community venues.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Keeps technical and merchant complexity manageable and allows the pilot to be tested before scaling.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a simple measure: percentage of cards redeemed by two people and the share of pairs who book a second plan.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Shows whether the idea creates repeat connection and gives the campaign an evidence base.

final_proposal.title: Two-Tap: The Card That Only Works With Company
final_proposal.idea: Loneliness often lasts because the first invitation feels awkward. Two-Tap is a Mastercard gift card that only works when two people tap it together. You are not giving money, you are giving a plan that cannot be spent alone. Friends and family can send one without saying 'you seem lonely'. An 'Open Pair' option matches a card with a companion through libraries, charities and local clubs, so no one is left out. Launch in one or two cities with cafés, cinemas, classes and community venues, and measure how many pairs redeem the card and make a second plan. Priceless has always been about moments that money cannot buy. Two-Tap makes the payment itself ask for one.
follow_up_questions: Which everyday places (a laundromat, a barbershop, a park kiosk) could offer a Two-Tap plan that feels natural and not staged?
How could the pairing be designed so that being matched with a stranger feels safe and easy, not like a social test?
What would a second and third plan look like, so that one invitation grows into a lasting habit of meeting up?

Small merchants will participate if the cost to them is near zero and the benefit is loyalty and community goodwill.

candidates.core_idea: Mastercard admits that making payment effortless also removed small human exchanges, and creates deliberate 'slow lanes' at partner merchants: checkout lanes and counters where paying is explicitly the start of a conversation, with no rush, no queue pressure and a human greeting.
candidates.brand_connection: Mastercard shaped the frictionless world through contactless and tap-to-pay. Owning the downside and offering a counter-move is a rare, honest brand stance. It reframes 'Priceless' as time spent, not speed gained.
expected_strengths: Provocative, self-aware stance that earns press and cultural conversation.
Simple, visible physical symbol (a lane sign) that can scale across markets.
Starts from a real product truth rather than a borrowed social cause.
main_concerns: Contradicts the speed and convenience associations of the category and could confuse the brand message.
Operationally hard for retailers, since slow lanes cost throughput.
Can feel gimmicky and does not address the recognition people want, only the time.

candidates.title: Known By Name
candidates.core_idea: Turn the silent tap into a moment of recognition. Cardholders opt in to share the name they like to be called with merchants they choose. When they tap, the terminal shows that name and the person behind the counter says it out loud. Regulars are celebrated as the social glue of neighbourhoods, and small businesses get tools and a window mark to make being known part of the service.
candidates.brand_connection: It extends True Name, the belief that a name is identity, from the card to the counter. It uses Mastercard's actual position in the transaction, the moment of tap, and supports small businesses. It makes 'Priceless' concrete: being known is something money can't buy but a payment can help start.
expected_strengths: Grounded in a real behaviour (the regular), so the insight is human and the mechanism is simple.
Platformable: real regulars' stories, a neighbourhood programme, merchant toolkit, in-store marks and earned media.
Gives the brand a role at the moment of payment rather than only in advertising.
Credible for Mastercard without overclaiming, since it restores one small piece of connection.
main_concerns: Privacy sensitivities: names on terminals must be strictly opt-in, merchant-specific and revocable.
Requires terminal or acquirer cooperation, so the first version may need to be a pilot or a simple behavioural tool.
Risk of being read as surveillance or loyalty-scheme manipulation if the tone and consent design are not right.

candidates.title: Open Seat
candidates.core_idea: Restaurants and cafés designate a seat at a bar or shared table as the 'Open Seat', a standing invitation to solo diners to sit beside someone and talk if they want. Paying at the Open Seat includes a conversation prompt printed on the receipt.
candidates.brand_connection: Dining is a core Priceless territory and Mastercard has long run curated experiences and city programmes. The idea turns a payment moment into a social opening.
expected_strengths: Visual and easy to understand: a chair with a mark that people can photograph and share.
Fits existing Priceless Cities and dining partnerships.
Low-tech and quick to prototype in a single city.
main_concerns: Forced sociability can make lonely people feel more exposed.
Relies on restaurant staff and settings that may not exist where isolation is greatest.
Close to existing communal-table and supper-club concepts, so less ownable.

candidates.title: Reconnect Rewards
candidates.core_idea: A rewards mechanic that unlocks a shared experience when two cardholders who haven't spent time together in six months or more tap at the same venue. Dormant friendships get a reason and a small financial nudge to restart.
candidates.brand_connection: It uses Mastercard's loyalty and offers capabilities and the Priceless experience catalogue, and positions the card as a tool for relationships, not only purchases.
expected_strengths: Clear, shareable mechanic that gives people a low-pressure excuse to get in touch.
Measurable through redemptions and venue partners.
Strong partner appeal for hospitality and entertainment brands.
main_concerns: Puts a price on friendship, which can feel transactional or contradict 'money can't buy'.
Helps people who already have connections more than people who are truly isolated.
Needs cross-cardholder data matching, which raises privacy and technical hurdles.

reasons_for_selection: It has the sharpest insight: loneliness often lives in routines, and silent payment has made those routines anonymous.
It is the most ownable for Mastercard, since it sits at the tap, builds on True Name and supports local merchants.
It gives Priceless a fresh and honest meaning: being known is the thing money can't buy, but a payment can open the door to it.
It scales from a modest neighbourhood pilot into a broader cultural platform with real people's stories, merchant tools and in-store symbols.
It reaches people who are isolated but still have daily routines, and does not require them to join anything or perform sociability.

rejected.reason: Strong stance, but it works against the speed and convenience that merchants and consumers value from Mastercard, and slowing a lane does not create recognition. Its best element, admitting that frictionless payment has a human cost, is folded into the narrative of the selected idea.
Pleasant and visual, but it puts pressure on lonely people to be social in public and is similar to existing communal dining concepts, so it is less ownable and less tied to the payment moment.

Neat mechanic, but it risks monetising friendship, favours people who already have connections, and depends on complex data matching between cardholders. It conflicts with the core Priceless belief rather than expressing it.

revisions_after_selection.change: Made the name cardholder-chosen, per-merchant and revocable, using the same philosophy as True Name, and stated that no spending or personal data is shared with merchants.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Privacy is the biggest risk for a financial brand. Consent and control must be the visible design principle so that recognition does not feel like surveillance.

revisions_after_selection.change: Defined a 'Regular' by showing up, not by spend, and removed any discount or loyalty-points mechanic from the core idea.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Tying recognition to spend would turn belonging into a transaction and contradict 'priceless'. It also keeps the idea about people rather than promotions.

revisions_after_selection.change: Staged the rollout: a low-tech first phase (a name card shown at tap and a staff greeting kit) in one neighbourhood, with terminal display as a later phase.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This avoids dependence on acquirer and terminal changes at launch, makes a pilot feasible and lets real stories be gathered early.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added the Slow Lane admission as the campaign's opening line of truth: payments got faster and quieter, and something small got lost.
revisions_after_selection.reason: A candid acknowledgement makes the brand more credible on loneliness and gives the campaign a tension to resolve, rather than a general message about connection.

final_proposal.title: Known By Name
final_proposal.idea: Loneliness often hides in the smallest ritual: the café where someone is the 8:10 flat white. Payments have made that ritual silent: tap, beep, gone. Mastercard turns the beep into belonging. Cardholders opt in to share the name they like to be called with places they choose. At tap, the terminal shows it and the person behind the counter says, 'Morning, Ana.' No spend data is shared, and anyone can withdraw at any time. Small businesses receive a 'Regulars' window mark and a greeting kit. The campaign films real regulars (retirees, night-shift workers, new arrivals) and the people who know them. It extends True Name's belief that a name is identity: some things money can't buy, like being known. Start with a single neighbourhood pilot.
follow_up_questions: Which everyday places (the pharmacy, the laundromat, the bus kiosk) are the most overlooked sources of recognition, and how would the idea change in each?
How could recognition be offered to people who don't want to be noticed, so that it stays an invitation and never becomes pressure?
What would a brand have to give up or admit about its own convenience-driven products to be believable on the topic of loneliness?
