task_understanding.focus: Loneliness is partly built into modern life, and payments helped build it. Tap-and-go, self-checkout and apps have removed the small, repeated exchanges with baristas, cashiers and shopkeepers that research on 'weak ties' links to belonging. Mastercard sits inside nearly every one of these moments. The opportunity is to put a little humanity back into the transaction without adding friction, in a way only a payments brand can.
assumptions: Mastercard's Priceless platform ('there are some things money can't buy') is a natural home for a loneliness idea, but it needs a fresh, concrete expression rather than another sentimental film.

The brand has credible precedents to build on: True Name (a chosen name on the card), accessibility innovations such as the Touch Card, small-business programmes and the Mastercard Economics Institute.
The client wants a campaign with real product or behavioural substance. A purely awareness message about loneliness would feel opportunistic from a financial brand.
The audience is broad. Lonely people include young city-movers, remote workers, older adults and newcomers, and many of them would resist being labelled 'lonely'. The idea must not stigmatise.
Privacy and trust are non-negotiable in finance. Any use of transaction data or personal information must be opt-in, transparent and clearly beneficial.
A pilot-then-scale model (one city, a small number of merchants) is more credible and cheaper than a global launch on day one.

candidates.title: Known Here
candidates.core_idea: An opt-in setting that lets you choose a name or nickname to show at the till of the local places you choose, such as your café, bakery or corner shop. When you tap, the person behind the counter sees 'Thanks, Dani' and can greet you the way a neighbour would. Being known by name is the smallest unit of belonging, and the checkout is often the only place a lonely person still gets it. The campaign is built around the 'regular': the small business that knows you and the customer who finally feels recognised.
candidates.brand_connection: Extends True Name (identity on the card) from the card face to the moment of payment. It makes Mastercard the brand that reverses the anonymity its own industry's convenience created. It supports small businesses and gives Priceless a daily, tangible meaning: being recognised can't be bought, but it can be enabled.
expected_strengths: Starts from a sharp, original insight: the till is the last place some people are still known.
Is a real product behaviour, not an ad claim, so it earns media and cultural conversation.
Is tiny, intimate and emotional, yet scalable through merchant terminals and a visible decal.
Platformable: 'Regulars' stories, a Regular of the Year, a street-level takeover of one neighbourhood.
Does not label anyone lonely. It simply offers recognition.
main_concerns: Privacy and safety worries about a name appearing on merchant screens.
Technical and merchant-adoption complexity across terminals.
Some people want anonymity; the idea must not pressure anyone to chat.
Risk of feeling gimmicky if the first pilot is thin.

candidates.title: Overdue
candidates.core_idea: Reframe friendship in payment language. An opt-in feature or campaign gives you a gentle 'statement' of the people you haven't spent time with in a while and lets you send a 'payment' that is an invitation, such as a pre-paid coffee or a shared-ticket voucher, instead of money. The tagline logic is 'Some debts you're glad to owe.'
candidates.brand_connection: Plays with Mastercard's native vocabulary (balance, statement, overdue, payment) and turns it toward relationships. It also gives the brand a reason to fund shared experiences, which fits Priceless.
expected_strengths: Witty, shareable and instantly understandable.
Lets people act on an intention they already have, to reconnect.
Easy to prototype as a digital tool or a social activation.
main_concerns: Could create guilt or a feeling of friendship as obligation.
Implies analysis of personal behaviour, which raises data-trust issues.
Mostly helps people who already have friends to reconnect with, not the most isolated.
Similar reminder and gifting apps exist.

candidates.title: First Friend
candidates.core_idea: Target the moments when loneliness spikes: moving to a new city or country. International students, relocators and newcomers get a Mastercard-backed 'First Friend' programme that pairs them with a local who shares an interest. Mastercard pays for the first meal or activity, and the local's side is covered too, so no one hosts at their own expense.
candidates.brand_connection: Draws on Mastercard's global, cross-border identity and its role in helping people settle into new places. It also fits the Priceless Cities model of unlocking local experiences.
expected_strengths: Addresses a real, high-intensity loneliness moment.
Emotional, story-rich, easy to film and to partner on with universities and cities.
Strong global-citizen alignment with the brand.
main_concerns: Operationally heavy: matching, safety and vetting are costly.
Narrow audience compared with the wider loneliness problem.
Resembles existing buddy and expat-network programmes.

candidates.title: The Third Place Index
candidates.core_idea: Use aggregated, anonymised Mastercard Economics Institute data to map where neighbourhoods have lost the 'third places' (cafés, barbers, pubs, community spaces) where people gather, and publish it as a loneliness-risk lens for cities. Pair it with micro-grants and cardholder offers that help local gathering places reopen or survive.
candidates.brand_connection: Uses Mastercard's unique data authority and its small-business commitments to turn an abstract social issue into a civic, solvable one.
expected_strengths: Credible, newsworthy and attractive to governments, NGOs and media.
Makes the brand a serious participant in the loneliness debate.
Gives a long-term platform with a yearly report and city partnerships.
main_concerns: Cold and analytical for a consumer campaign; weak emotional pull.
Spending data is an imperfect proxy for loneliness and could be misread.
Cardholders see the effect only indirectly.

reasons_for_selection: It has the sharpest insight of the four, and it is one only a payments brand could own: the moment of payment is where anonymity and recognition are decided.
It is a behaviour, not a message. It would exist in the world every day and could not be dismissed as cause-washing.
It builds directly on a real brand asset (True Name), so it feels like a natural next step rather than a stretch.
It is inclusive. It helps older people, remote workers and newcomers alike without calling anyone lonely.
It is cheap to pilot in one neighbourhood and has an obvious scaling path through merchants and decals.
It offers a rich campaign platform: regulars' stories, local takeovers, and a yearly 'Regular of the Year'.

rejected.reason: Witty, but it risks guilt, depends on personal-behaviour data that is sensitive for a finance brand, and mostly serves people who already have connections. It is better kept as a possible social extension than as the core idea.
Emotionally strong, but operationally heavy, narrow in audience and close to existing buddy programmes. Matching strangers also brings safety obligations that dilute the brand focus.

Credible and good for PR and policy, but too analytical to build an emotional consumer campaign, and spending data is a shaky proxy for loneliness. It could work later as a supporting proof point, with the data showing where Known Here matters most.

revisions_after_selection.change: Made the feature opt-in per merchant. Cardholders choose which places can see their chosen name, and the name is only ever a nickname they supply.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Addresses the biggest risk: privacy and safety concerns about a name appearing on a screen. It also keeps control with the customer and protects trust.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added an explicit 'quiet regular' option, so the merchant sees a warm greeting prompt but the customer signals whether they want conversation or just recognition.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Prevents the idea from pressuring shy or private people into chatting, and keeps the benefit as recognition, not forced social contact.

revisions_after_selection.change: Changed the launch from a broad rollout to a single-neighbourhood pilot with a small group of independent merchants, using street-level activations as the campaign's first proof.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Reduces technical and merchant-adoption risk, lets the story be told through real regulars, and avoids a thin, gimmicky first impression.

revisions_after_selection.change: Positioned the campaign around the regular and the shopkeeper rather than around 'loneliness', and kept loneliness data from C4 as supporting evidence only.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Avoids stigmatising people and keeps the tone warm and human, while still giving the issue credibility.

final_proposal.title: Known Here
final_proposal.idea: Convenience took the small human moments out of paying, and for many people the till was the only place left where anyone knew them. Known Here is an opt-in Mastercard setting. You choose a name or nickname and the local places where it appears, and when you tap, your barista sees 'Thanks, Dani'. A 'quiet regular' option means recognition never turns into pressure. It builds on True Name, giving a chosen identity a daily home. We launch in one neighbourhood with independent shops, a window decal, and stories of the regulars and the people who know them. Priceless has always been about what money can't buy. Known Here lets a payment carry a little of it.
follow_up_questions: Where else in daily life do payments or transactions strip out human recognition, and could the same principle of being known apply there?
How could the idea reach people who rarely visit shops, such as remote workers or housebound older adults, without losing its simplicity?
What would make a shopkeeper feel the benefit as much as the customer, and how could that become part of the story?

task_understanding.focus: Luxury's sustainability story is dominated by materials and promises about the future, while the strongest proof of luxury, that it lasts and can be mended, is hidden. The opportunity for Dior is to make repair and reuse a visible, desirable act of craftsmanship rather than a defensive 'responsible' gesture. This means turning the atelier's savoir-faire into a lifelong relationship with the owner, and reframing a worn Dior piece as a story of value, not a sign of decline.
assumptions: Dior's equity rests on couture heritage, the atelier at 30 Avenue Montaigne, and the idea of the 'hand'. Repair is a natural extension of that craft, not a new behaviour to bolt on.
Luxury buyers increasingly doubt vague sustainability claims and respond better to tangible proof, provenance and craft than to eco-messaging.
Younger affluent audiences already engage with resale, vintage and archive culture, and they treat a pre-owned Dior piece as a status signal when its history is known.
Dior owners hold emotional attachments to specific pieces (a Bar jacket, a Saddle bag, a mother's scarf), so repair is about memory and identity as much as function.
Dior must protect exclusivity and brand desirability, so repair cannot feel discounted, utilitarian or like an admission of poor durability.
The client wants a platformable idea that can scale across services, content, retail and social, not a one-off activation.

candidate.title: The Visible Mend: Every Dior Has a Second Signature
candidate.core_idea: Dior turns repair into a couture act of authorship. When a piece comes back to the atelier, the artisan who restores it leaves a discreet, designed 'second signature': a tiny hand-stitched mark, a gold thread, a embroidered date or initial inside the lining or along the seam. Like kintsugi, the mend is not hidden but celebrated, and it records that the piece has lived. Each mended piece also receives a digital 'life record' (owner chapters, restorations, resale passage) that travels with it, so a repaired Dior becomes more valuable, not less, in the resale market. The platform line of thought: 'A Dior is never finished.' Campaign expressions include a film following one jacket across three decades and three owners, a limited 'Atelier Mend' capsule where Dior designers reimagine damaged archive pieces, pop-up repair salons where clients watch their piece restored by hand, and a social mechanic where owners share the story behind the piece they have kept, mended or passed on.
candidate.brand_connection: It roots sustainability in what Dior already owns: the atelier, the petites mains, the notion of couture as bespoke, ongoing craft. Monsieur Dior's belief in the dress as a lasting architecture of the body makes it natural to say the garment continues to be tended. It also echoes the house's tradition of signed, numbered, documented couture pieces. Repair becomes the most intimate form of client service, extending the couture relationship past the point of sale.
expected_strengths: Reframes repair from a cost or flaw into a status marker and collectible detail, which fits luxury desirability.
Makes durability visible and credible without greenwashing language; the proof is in the stitching.
Strengthens resale value and pre-owned trust, supporting circularity while protecting brand control over secondary markets.
Highly visual and filmable, with a clear craft-led story that generates PR, social content and editorial interest.
Platformable across service, product, content and retail, and it can flex to leather goods, ready-to-wear, jewellery and shoes.
Deepens client loyalty by creating a lifelong relationship and reasons to return to the maison.
main_concerns: Operational capacity: atelier time is scarce, so the service may need to be tiered, limited or ticketed to avoid disappointing clients.
Risk of seeming to normalise damage or encourage lower-quality perception if the narrative is not handled with confidence.
Authenticity and exclusivity tension: needs care so repair does not feel like a marketing gimmick or become accessible only to the very top clients.
Digital life records require data, privacy and authentication infrastructure, and must integrate with existing resale and counterfeit protection efforts.
Some clients may not want visible marks on their pieces, so the signature must be optional and designed with sensitivity.

final_proposal.title: The Visible Mend
final_proposal.idea: What if repairing a Dior became the most luxurious thing you could do to it? When a piece returns to the atelier, the artisan who restores it adds a discreet second signature: a gold thread, a tiny embroidered date, an initial inside the lining. Like kintsugi, the mend is celebrated, not hidden. Each restored piece carries a life record of its owners and repairs, so its story raises its value. Dior designers reimagine damaged archive pieces in an 'Atelier Mend' capsule, while repair salons let clients watch their jacket or bag restored by hand. A film follows one Bar jacket across three decades and three owners. The line: a Dior is never finished. Durability stops being a claim and becomes something you can see, touch and inherit.
follow_up_questions: What would make a mend feel like a badge of honour rather than a flaw for different types of clients, from a first-time buyer to a lifelong collector?
How could the second signature be designed so each artisan's hand becomes recognisable, and could the artisans themselves become the stars of the campaign?
Where does the idea stretch next: could clients commission a mend as a gift, or could pieces move between owners with their stories attached, like a passport?

task_understanding.focus: The first paycheck is a big emotional milestone that usually arrives as a confusing, badly designed document. The gross-to-net gap, unfamiliar tax lines and cryptic codes turn pride into a quiet 'wait, what?'. The opportunity is to show that clear visual communication matters at work, starting with the first document that has your name and your worth on it. This lets Canva's work and teams offer speak to employers and managers as well as to first-time earners.
assumptions: Canva is seen as a friendly, democratizing design tool. Its B2B growth depends on proving it is useful for everyday business communication, not only marketing and presentations.
Most first-time earners (Gen Z, school leavers, part-time and gig workers) do not fully understand their payslip, and many feel a mix of pride and confusion.
The buyers and influencers in B2B (HR, people ops, small business owners, team managers) care about onboarding, retention and employer brand, and they send many badly designed documents.
The campaign should celebrate the milestone without giving financial advice, which is outside Canva's credibility and carries compliance risk.
Payslip formats and tax rules differ by country, so the idea must work as a flexible, customizable framework and not as one fixed template.

candidates.title: Frame It
candidates.core_idea: Turn the first paycheck into a keepsake. Canva offers templates to restyle a payslip or bank screenshot into a framed print, social post or card, so people can celebrate 'my first real money' the way they would a graduation.
candidates.brand_connection: It positions Canva as the tool for marking life's moments, using its existing template and sharing strengths.
expected_strengths: Emotional and highly shareable
Simple to produce and easy for consumers to understand
Fits Canva's friendly personality
main_concerns: Weak B2B relevance, so it does little for work and teams products
Privacy and oversharing of pay details
Risk of looking like a trivial template promotion that other brands could also run

candidates.title: Paycheck, Explained
candidates.core_idea: Redesign the confusing first payslip experience. Canva gives employers and managers a kit of plain-language, visual 'first pay pages' that show where gross pay went, what each deduction means and what the person actually takes home, together with a personal welcome note. The campaign makes the case that a clear document is a form of respect.
candidates.brand_connection: It shows Canva solving a real business communication problem. Clear visual explanation of complex information is what Canva does best, and it is aimed squarely at HR, small business and manager audiences.
expected_strengths: Rooted in a real, widely felt tension (first-paycheck shock)
Gives B2B buyers a concrete use case tied to onboarding and retention
Platformable across film, templates, HR partnerships and employee-shared content
Gives the topic a clear, ownable angle, which is clarity
main_concerns: Payroll is regulated and varies by country, so the content must stay explanatory and not advisory
Could feel dry if the emotional side is not built in
Needs employers to adopt it, which takes distribution effort

candidates.title: First Thank-You
candidates.core_idea: Encourage people to spend part of their first paycheck on a thank-you to whoever helped them get there (a parent, teacher or mentor) and design it in Canva: cards, videos, mini-books.
candidates.brand_connection: It links Canva to heartfelt personal creation and gifting, and to the pride of a first earning moment.
expected_strengths: Very warm and likely to generate emotional content
Easy for people to join in
Works well as a seasonal or social moment
main_concerns: Strongly consumer-focused, so it weakens the B2B and productivity positioning
Resembles many existing gratitude and gifting campaigns, so it is not very surprising
Could feel like pressure to spend the money

candidates.title: The Raise Starts Here
candidates.core_idea: Position the first paycheck as the start of a career story. Canva gives young workers a 'brag page' kit (a one-page record of wins, skills and results) so that by the time of their first review, they can make the case for their next paycheck.
candidates.brand_connection: It connects to Canva's presentation, resume and documents tools and to the idea of design as a way to persuade.
expected_strengths: Ambitious, useful and aligned with productivity
Has a long-term product use beyond the first payday
Gives managers a reason to promote it
main_concerns: The link to the first paycheck itself is weaker, since the topic becomes about negotiation
Overlaps with existing resume and career tool territory
May feel premature to someone still on their first payslip

reasons_for_selection: It starts from a true, specific tension (pride mixed with confusion) and turns it into a product-led idea, which is stronger than celebrating the milestone generally.
It speaks to the B2B side directly by giving HR, managers and small business owners a reason to use Canva for something they already have to do.
It is a platform: the same idea can run as a film, a template kit, employer partnerships and employee-shared content.
It demonstrates Canva's core value (making complicated things clear and human) without needing to claim financial expertise.

rejected.reason: Charming but shallow. It has little B2B value, raises privacy concerns and is easy for others to copy, so it would not build the work and teams story.
Emotionally warm but familiar, aimed at consumers and unconnected to workplace productivity. It also risks encouraging spending.
Useful, but it moves the focus from the first paycheck to career negotiation and competes with crowded career-tool territory. It could work as a later phase.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a short personal welcome note and a 'first payday' moment to the kit, so the page celebrates the person as well as explaining the numbers.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Without the emotional layer the idea risked feeling like dry HR paperwork and would be less likely to spread.

revisions_after_selection.change: Framed the content strictly as plain-language explanation of what each line means, with no advice on saving, tax or spending, and with customizable fields by country.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Payroll rules differ by region and giving financial advice would create compliance risk and go beyond Canva's credibility.

revisions_after_selection.change: Made employers and managers the main distributors, with a simple, consumer-facing version that new hires can use to understand their own payslip.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This keeps the B2B focus while still giving the audience an immediate, shareable benefit.

revisions_after_selection.change: Changed the template examples to use dummy data only in all public content.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It avoids privacy issues and encourages people to share the design, not their real pay.

final_proposal.title: Paycheck, Explained
final_proposal.idea: Your first paycheck is the first document that says what you're worth, and it's usually unreadable. Canva rebuilds it as a clear, human 'first pay page': where the gross went, what each deduction means in plain words, what's yours, and a welcome note from the team. A free kit lets employers, managers and small businesses send it with every new hire's first payday, customized by country and brand. The campaign opens with real first-timers reading their original payslips, then reveals the redesigned version. New hires can also use a simple version to decode their own slip, and share the dummy-data design, not their numbers. The message: clear communication is a form of respect, and good design makes work feel human from day one.
follow_up_questions: Which other 'first' documents at work (offer letter, contract, performance review) are just as confusing, and could Canva make a series out of them?
How could employers make first payday a small ritual so it feels like a celebration and not a transaction?
What would be the right partners (payroll providers, schools, youth organizations) to give the kit credibility without making it feel like financial advice?

task_understanding.focus: The first paycheck is a rite of passage everyone remembers, but it leaves nothing behind. It lands as a number, gets spent within days, and the only record is a payslip nobody wants to keep. The opportunity is for Canva to turn this moment into something people make, keep and share. That shows Canva as the tool for marking and communicating the moments that matter at work, not just for making slides and social posts.
assumptions: Canva's brand strength is making creation feel easy and personal for non-designers, so a campaign about a personal milestone fits better than a feature-led one.
Most people remember what their first paycheck became (shoes, rent, a dinner for their parents) far better than the amount.
The core audience is Gen Z and young millennials entering work, including interns, part-timers and graduates, plus the managers and HR teams who onboard them.
In B2B SaaS, workplace emotion is under-used. Employers rarely mark first payday, and Canva Teams buyers would value a low-cost way to make new hires feel welcomed.
Pay figures are sensitive, so the campaign should never ask people to publish how much they earn.
The campaign should show Canva's value through a shareable, repeatable template and keep financial advice out of it.

Canva offers a template that turns the first paycheck into a keepsake poster of what it became: the sneakers, the first rent, the dinner for Mum. expected_strengths: Highly shareable, because everyone has a first-paycheck story and no pay data is exposed.

candidates.core_idea: Own the shock of the gap between gross and net pay. Canva provides clear visual templates and infographics that show where a first paycheck goes (tax, pension, rent), so first-time earners can understand their money at a glance.
candidates.brand_connection: Canva already turns complex information into clear visuals, and this applies that strength to a real pain point.
expected_strengths: Genuinely useful and strong for search and PR.
Positions Canva as a clarity tool.
Easy to create content for.
main_concerns: Drifts into fintech or financial advice, which Canva has no credibility in.
Risks feeling preachy and dull.

candidates.brand_connection: Directly supports Canva for Teams by showing brand-consistent internal communication, and it is aimed at the actual B2B buyer.
expected_strengths: Clear commercial link to team plans.

main_concerns: Emotionally flat and mostly a templates play.

final_proposal.title: What It Became
final_proposal.idea: A first paycheck is gone in days, but everyone remembers what it turned into: the trainers, the first rent, the dinner for Mum. Canva makes that visible. task_understanding.focus: The first paycheck is a big emotional moment, but the document that marks it, the payslip, is one of the least readable and least human documents a person receives. The opportunity is for Canva to own the idea that clear, well-designed communication matters most when it matters personally, starting with the first paycheck, and to link that to Canva's workplace and team products.
assumptions: Canva is seen as a friendly, creative tool for everyone, and its B2B growth depends on being seen as a useful everyday work tool, not just a design tool.
The first paycheck is a rite of passage for school leavers, graduates, career changers and new freelancers. It combines pride with confusion about tax, deductions and 'where did the rest go?'.
Primary audience: 18-26-year-olds starting their first real job. Secondary audience: the HR, payroll and people-ops teams who onboard them and are Canva's B2B buyers.
Many people share or keep the moment (a photo, a screenshot, a story), but few feel the document itself is worth keeping.
Canva should not give financial or tax advice. It should make information clearer and leave the advice to others.
Payslip formats and tax rules differ by country, so the idea needs to work locally without being rebuilt each time.

candidates.title: Payslip, Decoded
candidates.core_idea: Redesign the first payslip so it is readable. Canva creates a set of visual payslip templates and a simple explainer layout that turns lines like gross, net, tax and pension into plain-language visuals. Employers can send it to new hires with their first pay, and individuals can rebuild their own as a clear one-page picture. The message: your first paycheck deserves better design.
candidates.brand_connection: Canva's core skill is making complicated information clear and good-looking. The idea shows that skill on a document everyone has seen and nobody has liked, and it gives HR and payroll teams a practical reason to use Canva for Teams.
expected_strengths: Delivers real utility, which suits a productivity and SaaS brand.
Gives a direct B2B route through onboarding kits for HR, payroll and people-ops teams.
Fits the topic: most first-paycheck content is about spending, and this one is about understanding.
Platformable: later chapters could cover offer letters, contracts and benefits guides.
Easy to demonstrate with before-and-after visuals.
main_concerns: Payslip rules and layouts vary by country, so it needs local adaptation.
Privacy: people may hesitate to upload their payslip, so templates must work without uploads.
It could drift into financial advice, so wording must be careful.
It is less emotional than the topic could support unless it is framed well.

candidates.title: Paid to Design
candidates.core_idea: A social campaign collecting people's first paycheck earned from something they made in Canva (a menu, a flyer, a pitch deck, a logo for a friend's business). People share the item and what they were paid. Canva turns the best stories into a public gallery and a starter kit for turning design skills into paid work.
candidates.brand_connection: It shows Canva as a tool that lets non-designers earn money, which supports the work and productivity side of the brand.
expected_strengths: Real stories of people who earned from Canva create credibility.
Strong user-generated content potential.
Aspirational for side-hustlers and freelancers.
main_concerns: Narrow audience: only people who have earned from design work.
Can feel like a typical creator-economy campaign.
Weak link to the B2B buyer.
Sharing pay amounts publicly can be awkward or invite comparison.

candidates.title: Dear First Paycheck
candidates.core_idea: Invite young people to interview a parent or grandparent about their first paycheck, then turn the answers into a short visual story or card. Canva templates compare what the first wage was, what it bought, and what it feels like today. The result is a shared family record of how work and money have changed.
candidates.brand_connection: Canva helps people turn memories and facts into shareable stories. This extends that into family storytelling, with the first paycheck as the prompt.
expected_strengths: Emotional and cross-generational, which is good for sharing.
Fits natural moments such as holidays and family gatherings.
Easy for people to join with simple templates.
main_concerns: Moves the focus from work to family nostalgia, which weakens the B2B and productivity link.
Wage comparisons can reopen painful topics around cost of living.
Likely to be a seasonal spike, not an ongoing platform.

candidates.title: The Framed Stub
candidates.core_idea: Make keeping the first paycheck a ritual. Canva offers keepsake templates (a framed payslip, a 'first earned' certificate, a desk-sized print) and a print partnership so people can display their first pay with the date and a note to their future self. The line: some documents are worth framing.
candidates.brand_connection: It uses Canva's design and print tools to turn an ordinary document into something people want to keep.
expected_strengths: Simple, visual and easy to understand.
Works well as a shareable photo moment.
Print extension adds a product opportunity.
main_concerns: Many first paychecks are digital with no physical stub.
Sentimental but with no real work utility.
Little connection to the B2B audience.
May feel like a one-off gift item, not a campaign.

reasons_for_selection: It offers the strongest link between the topic and what Canva does best: making complex information clear.
It is useful in a way people will notice, which fits a productivity brand better than a nostalgic one.

rejected.reason: The audience is too narrow and the link to the B2B buyer is weak. It also follows a familiar creator-economy pattern.
It is emotionally appealing, but it moves away from work and productivity, and it is likely to be seasonal. It also risks sensitive conversations about money.
It is pleasant and visual, but many paychecks are digital and the idea has little real utility or B2B relevance. It is better as a small extension than as the core.

revisions_after_selection.change: Reframed the headline from 'decoding deductions' to 'finally see what you earned', putting the amount earned first and the deductions second.

revisions_after_selection.change: Made the templates work without any upload: people type in their own numbers, or employers fill in a template.

revisions_after_selection.reason: Brings back the emotional, shareable side of the topic so the campaign is not just a utility.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added an employer route: a free 'First Paycheck Welcome Kit' for HR teams to send with a new hire's first pay.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Makes the B2B benefit concrete and gives Canva a way to reach teams at the moment of onboarding.

final_proposal.title: Your First Paycheck, Finally Readable
final_proposal.idea: The first paycheck is one of the proudest moments of working life, yet the payslip that comes with it looks like a tax form. Canva fixes it. We launch a set of free visual payslip templates that lead with what you earned and then show, in plain words, where the rest went. Nothing is uploaded and no advice is given; the templates simply make the information clear. Employers and payroll teams get a 'First Paycheck Welcome Kit' to send with a new hire's first pay. Individuals can also make a 'Share the win' card that hides the numbers and shows only 'My first paycheck'. The campaign shows Canva's core skill, making complicated things clear, on a document everyone has received and nobody has enjoyed, and it opens the door to other first-job documents.
follow_up_questions: Which other first-job documents (offer letters, contracts, benefits guides) are just as confusing, and which would make the strongest next chapter?
How could payroll providers or HR platforms work with Canva so the readable payslip arrives automatically with the first pay?
What would make someone proud to share a payslip card, and how can the campaign keep the amount private while keeping the moment public?

Platformable across film, retail, social, CRM, pre-owned and collaborations with artists and designers on repair signatures.

final_proposal.title: The Second Fitting
final_proposal.idea: At Dior, every piece is fitted once. We think it deserves a second. And a third. The Second Fitting invites anyone to bring a Dior piece back to the atelier for lifelong care, and makes the repair as beautiful as the original design. Topic from the client: repair and reuse

task_understanding.focus: Luxury's sustainability story is usually about what a house makes next. Dior's opportunity is to make repair and reuse feel like the highest form of luxury rather than a guilt-driven compromise: a Dior piece is built to be inherited, so it should be proudly mended, altered and passed on. The campaign must turn the 'second life' of Dior garments and objects into a desirable, culturally visible behaviour, and make the atelier's craft the hero of the aftercare story, not only of the first sale.
assumptions: Dior's core equity is couture craft, the atelier, the Bar jacket and the New Look, and a heritage of reinventing silhouettes. Repair and reuse should extend that equity rather than sit beside it as a CSR add-on.

Luxury buyers already own pieces they love but rarely use them, because they fear damaging them, think repair is a hassle, or assume repair is only for 'ordinary' clothes. The barrier is emotional and logistical, not just informational.

The audience spans heirloom-minded long-term clients and younger aspirational buyers who are active in resale and vintage culture and are skeptical of greenwashing. The campaign must speak to both without discounting the brand.
Dior wants to protect brand desirability and pricing power. Repair and reuse must read as exclusive craft and provenance, not as a discount route or a signal that the brand is less new.

Dior has the infrastructure (ateliers, client services, boutiques, archives) to offer repair, alteration and possibly certified resale or upcycling, though operational capacity and the specific offer will need to be confirmed with the client.
Claims must be specific and verifiable. Vague 'sustainable luxury' language would hurt credibility.

candidates.title: The Mended Dior
candidates.core_idea: Reframe visible repair as the new status mark. Dior's ateliers invite clients to bring in any Dior piece, however worn, and the house repairs it with a signature, deliberately visible 'Dior stitch' (a couture-grade mend in thread, embroidery or metalwork) that records the piece's history. Repairs become collectable, like the patina on a Bar jacket or a scuffed Lady Dior. Campaign: portraits of owners with their mended pieces and the story of the tear.
candidates.brand_connection: Draws on atelier craft and the idea that couture is made by hand and so can be remade by hand. Echoes the Dior tradition of transforming silhouettes and elevates the petites mains as protagonists.
expected_strengths: A highly visual, ownable signal (the visible mend) that people can show on social media and in street style.
Turns a perceived flaw into a status marker, which is a genuine cultural inversion.
Strongly tied to craft, the part of Dior no competitor can copy.
main_concerns: Visible mending is an established idea (kintsugi, sashiko, Visible Mending trends and some fashion brands), so the novelty must come from Dior's craft level.
Some traditional clients may not want visible repairs on investment pieces, so an invisible option is needed.
Risk of seeming to romanticise damage if not handled with elegance.

candidates.title: Dior Lineage
candidates.core_idea: Make every Dior piece a documented heirloom. Each repaired or resold piece receives a 'lineage' record (a digital and physical passport) listing its owners, alterations and the stories attached. Clients can pass pieces on within the Dior ecosystem, with the atelier re-fitting them to the next owner. Campaign: 'Who wore it before you' stories, with the house reuniting generations or strangers via a single garment.
candidates.brand_connection: Builds on the house's heritage, archives and the mother-to-daughter, muse-to-muse tradition around Christian Dior's own history. Positions the brand as custodian of a long relationship, not a one-off transaction.
expected_strengths: Makes reuse emotionally rich and exclusive (provenance adds value rather than lowering it).
Creates a CRM and retention mechanism, keeping resale within the house and protecting brand control.
Rich storytelling territory with strong emotional pull.
main_concerns: Requires substantial operational build (authentication, tracking, resale), which is costly and slow.
Passport and traceability concepts are well covered by luxury groups and blockchain pilots, so differentiation is needed.
Could feel more like a service programme than a campaign without a bold cultural hook.

candidates.title: The Dior Wardrobe Swap Atelier
candidates.core_idea: Open pop-up 'second-life ateliers' in key cities where people bring a beloved Dior piece they no longer wear and, working with Dior's artisans and young designers, co-create a reworked version: a coat becomes a bag, a gown becomes a jacket. The newly created pieces are shown in a mini-collection, with the original owner credited. The campaign makes reinvention, the house's founding act (the New Look reinvented a post-war silhouette), a participatory ritual.
candidates.brand_connection: Dior's history is one of radical reinvention through silhouette, and the Dior codes (Bar jacket, cannage, toile de Jouy) are modular and recognisable, so they transform well.
expected_strengths: Experiential, press-worthy and highly shareable, with strong content value for both Dior and the participants.
Appeals to younger, creative audiences while giving clients a new kind of exclusivity.
Positions upcycling as creative expression, not sacrifice.
main_concerns: Hard to scale beyond select cities and clients, and high touch per piece.
Upcycling can dilute the integrity of archival or iconic pieces if not curated.
May be perceived as a one-off event rather than a lasting behaviour change.

candidates.title: Never Finished
candidates.core_idea: Position Dior pieces as 'unfinished by design': each purchase is only the first chapter, and Dior commits to a lifelong 'chapter service' where pieces are refreshed, re-cut and updated as bodies, tastes and lives change (hemlines, a new lining, resized for a daughter). The campaign dramatises life events (a first job, a pregnancy, a divorce, a reinvention) with a Dior piece that is altered each time. It reframes ownership as a long relationship with the atelier and reframes 'newness' as something you can have without buying new.
candidates.brand_connection: Echoes Christian Dior's belief that clothes should follow a woman's transformations, and the house's focus on fit and tailoring, the very skill that makes alteration possible.
expected_strengths: Directly counters the 'only new is luxurious' assumption with a clear human insight: our lives change, so our clothes should be able to change too.
A platformable idea that can flex across ready-to-wear, accessories, men's and beauty-adjacent items.
Lower operational lift than a full resale ecosystem, as it builds on existing alteration services.
main_concerns: Could be read as a commercial excuse to keep selling services without bold behavioural hooks.
Emotional life-event storytelling is a familiar genre and risks sentimentality.
Needs a sharp visual and cultural device to avoid being merely a service announcement.

reasons_for_selection: It offers the sharpest cultural inversion: what the world treats as damage becomes the mark of the most desirable Dior piece. That gives a campaign a clear, discussable point of view.
It is the most distinctly Dior because it rests on atelier craft, which competitors cannot easily replicate, and it makes the artisans visible heroes.
It creates a visual, ownable asset (the Dior stitch) that works across film, print, social, boutique and street style, and that clients can wear and show.
It can launch with the existing repair and alteration capability and then scale, and it can later absorb elements of C2 (records of history) and C4 (long-term care) as a platform.

It speaks to both heirloom clients (craft and care) and younger audiences familiar with vintage and visible mending, while keeping the brand's pricing power intact because the mend is couture-level work.

rejected.reason: Emotionally strong and strategically smart for retention, but it depends on heavy infrastructure (authentication, tracking, resale) and lacks a bold, immediate cultural hook. It is better as a later layer of the platform than as the lead idea.

Creative and highly shareable, but limited in scale and reach, and it risks altering iconic pieces in ways that could dilute them. It is a strong activation to run inside the chosen platform rather than the platform itself.

A sound human insight and relatively easy to deliver, but it is closer to a service proposition and the life-event storytelling is a familiar genre. It lacks the single striking visual device of the mended signature and is better folded into the aftercare offer.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added an 'invisible mend' option alongside the visible Dior stitch, so clients choose how their repair shows.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Many long-term clients will not want visible marks on investment pieces, and forcing visibility would feel dictatorial and could alienate core customers. Choice keeps the idea inclusive while the visible option remains the hero.

revisions_after_selection.change: Shifted the creative hook from romanticising damage to honouring the wearer's life: each mend is signed and dated by the artisan who made it, and the owner's story is told, not the flaw.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This avoids the risk of glamorising damage and sidesteps the 'visible mending' trend cliché by making the artisan and the owner the stars, which is more distinctly Dior.

revisions_after_selection.change: Planned the mend design as a limited vocabulary of Dior codes (cannage stitch, toile de Jouy thread, the bee, the star) rather than free-form patches.
revisions_after_selection.reason: A consistent, recognisable language makes the repair instantly identifiable as Dior and collectable, and protects brand consistency.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a scalability and honesty layer: clear, verifiable commitments on repair capacity, turnaround times and what is covered, with a phased rollout from flagship cities.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Overpromising repair services to a luxury clientele would damage trust, and vague sustainability claims invite accusations of greenwashing.

final_proposal.title: Dior Mended
final_proposal.idea: Dior turns repair into the new status symbol. Clients bring any Dior piece, however worn, to the atelier, where the petites mains mend it with a signature stitch drawn from Dior's codes (cannage, toile de Jouy, the bee) or, if preferred, invisibly. Every mend is signed and dated by its artisan. The campaign portrays owners and artisans together, telling the story behind each tear: the dance, the dash for a taxi, the daughter who borrowed it. A scuffed Lady Dior or a darned Bar jacket becomes proof of a life fully lived, and the mend becomes the most desirable detail in the wardrobe. Launch with films and portraits, boutique repair salons and a small exhibition of mended icons, then scale city by city.
follow_up_questions: What would make a mend something people want to be seen with, and how can a repair become collectable rather than just functional?
Which other Dior codes, rituals or craft moments could carry the repair story to audiences who would never visit an atelier?
How might the platform expand over time into lineage, passing pieces on, and long-term care without losing the simple power of the mend?

task_understanding.focus: The first paycheck is a rare moment when a person is, for the first time, officially paid for their work, and it is also the first time many people feel like a professional. Canva can own the neglected part of that moment: the identity and the paperwork around it. Almost nobody is ready for the 'I am now a working person' role, and the things that prove it (a CV, a portfolio, a LinkedIn banner, a freelance invoice, a pitch deck, a budget) are often made in a panic and look amateur. The opportunity is to move Canva from 'design tool' to 'the tool you use to become the professional you just got paid to be', and to seed lifelong workplace habits in Gen Z and early-career people who will later bring Canva into their teams and buy for them.
assumptions: The core audience is 18-27-year-olds starting their first job, internship, side hustle or freelance gig, plus the Gen Z workers who will later influence B2B and team-plan purchases.
Canva is already known and loved in education and personal use. The gap is being seen as a serious professional tool at the start of a career, not only for school projects and social posts.
The first paycheck is emotionally loaded: pride, disbelief, anxiety about money, impostor feeling, and a wish to mark it. It is more about identity than about finance.
Canva should not pretend to be a bank or a finance app. Its credible territory is making, presenting, organising and sharing, so the idea should create things rather than give money advice.
Social platforms (TikTok, Instagram, LinkedIn) are where first-paycheck stories are already shared, so the idea needs a shareable artefact and a native behaviour to ride.
The brief is cross-market, so the idea should work without depending on a specific currency, pay cycle or tax system.
Canva's freemium model means the campaign should lead to free usage and templates first, with Pro and Teams upgrades coming through habit rather than hard selling.
task_understanding.approach_note: Candidates deliberately differ in mechanism: a ritual object, a content trend, a product-led utility, and a cultural provocation.

candidates.title: The Pay Stub Portrait
candidates.core_idea: Turn the first paycheck into a keepsake. Users drop in the first pay amount (hidden if they wish), job title and a single 'what I did to earn this' line, and Canva generates a beautifully designed commemorative card, like a first-day-of-school photo for adulthood. Templates range from framed-certificate to receipt-style to tiny-poster. They are shared with the people who helped, such as parents, mentors and friends. The campaign positions the first paycheck as a milestone that deserves a designed marker.
candidates.brand_connection: Canva makes celebration and personal milestones easy to design (birthdays, graduations, invitations). This extends that muscle to a milestone nobody has designed for yet, and puts Canva at the moment someone first sees themselves as a professional.
expected_strengths: Emotionally warm and instantly understood.
Highly shareable artefact that works on any social platform.
Low production barrier and easy to localise.
Creates a natural reason to thank parents or mentors, which adds PR and family-audience warmth.
main_concerns: Could feel sweet but lightweight, with limited link to professional use and B2B value.
Sharing pay amounts is sensitive, so privacy design is essential.
One-off moment with no ongoing habit.

candidates.title: Make It Look Like You Belong
candidates.core_idea: Attack the real first-job fear: looking like you don't know what you're doing. Canva creates the 'First Paycheck Starter Kit': a set of templates for the things a new worker is suddenly expected to produce (a polished one-page CV refresh, a team intro slide, a 30-60-90 day plan, a simple freelance invoice, a 'what I did this week' update for the boss). The campaign frames the paycheck as a receipt for the professional you have already become, and the kit is the wardrobe that helps you dress the part. Content features real first-jobbers revealing the small things they faked until they could do.
candidates.brand_connection: Directly rooted in Canva's product truth: professional-looking output with no design skills. It shows Canva as the confidence layer between 'I got the job' and 'I look like I deserve it', and plants workplace habits that scale into Teams and Enterprise.
expected_strengths: Strongest link to business value: workplace use, templates and team adoption.
Insight is real and widely felt (impostor feeling).
Creates tangible, ongoing utility rather than a single moment.
Easy to extend with creators, universities and employers' onboarding programmes.
main_concerns: Utility can feel like standard template marketing unless the emotional tension is sharply expressed.
Less inherently viral than a ritual or trend.
Risk of sounding patronising if it implies new workers are unqualified.

candidates.title: Paycheck Remix
candidates.core_idea: A user-generated trend where people show what their first paycheck actually became, designed as a tiny visual breakdown: 40% rent, 25% the thing they swore they'd buy, 5% mum's gift, 30% 'disappeared'. Canva supplies editable, funny, honest pie-chart and receipt-style templates ('My first paycheck, honestly'). Creators and everyday people fill them in and remix each other's, turning private money anxiety into a warm, comparative and funny format. Data from the trend becomes a cultural report on how a generation really starts earning.
candidates.brand_connection: Canva already powers trend templates people remix and share. This makes data visualisation personal, playful and easy, showing that design is how people make sense of their own lives. It gives Canva a credible voice on early-career culture without giving financial advice.
expected_strengths: Native to social behaviour and built for remixing.
Funny, relatable and honest, which suits Gen Z tone.
Generates real insight data for PR (a 'first paycheck report').
Template-driven so Canva's product is the engine of the trend.
main_concerns: Money talk can embarrass or exclude lower earners and invite comparison or judgment.
Trend adoption depends on seeding with the right creators.
Weaker link to professional identity and B2B.

candidates.title: The Unpaid Portfolio Tax
candidates.core_idea: A provocative cultural stance. Many creative and early-career people are asked to work for 'exposure', or do unpaid trials, before ever seeing a first paycheck. Canva launches a campaign that names this directly, with the line that the first paycheck is where you stop paying to be seen. It gives freelancers and juniors free tools to price, pitch and invoice professionally (rate card, proposal and invoice templates), and publicly calls out companies by creating a 'Pay Day One' pledge for employers who commit to paying for all trial work. The campaign ends when the first paid invoice is sent.
candidates.brand_connection: Canva has a large creator and freelancer community and has long argued that design is for everyone. Taking a position on fair pay for creative work would give the brand a stronger point of view and tie it to the economic reality of its core users.
expected_strengths: Bold, provocative and PR-worthy, with a clear cultural stance.
Taps real frustration among creatives and freelancers.
Builds employer and agency conversation, which has B2B reach.
Differentiates from typical tool-led SaaS advertising.
main_concerns: Calling out employers risks backlash from Canva's own B2B customers.
Needs credible Canva action to avoid being accused of performative activism.
Narrows the audience to creative or freelance workers and misses most first-job holders.

reasons_for_selection: It is the only direction that combines a true emotional insight (the fear of not looking like a real professional) with Canva's core product truth (professional-quality output without expertise).
It has real B2B value: habits formed at the first job are brought into teams, and Canva becomes familiar to the next generation of buyers and influencers.
It produces ongoing utility and repeated use, not a single-share moment, so it supports retention and conversion on free-to-paid and Teams.
It can borrow the strengths of other ideas, such as a shareable celebration artefact and honest creator stories, without inheriting their weaknesses.
It sits safely within Canva's credible territory and avoids financial advice, privacy risk and employer backlash.

rejected.reason: Charming and shareable, but it is a one-off keepsake with weak ties to professional use and B2B growth, and it carries privacy sensitivity around pay. Its best element, the celebratory moment, is borrowed as a small feature inside the chosen idea.

Strong for social reach and PR data, but money comparison can exclude or embarrass people and the trend depends on creator seeding. It builds cultural buzz more than professional confidence or workplace adoption.

Bold and distinctive, but it risks alienating Canva's business customers, requires credible follow-through to avoid looking performative, and speaks mainly to creative freelancers rather than the broader first-job audience.

revisions_after_selection.change: Reframed the emotional tone from 'fake it until you make it' to 'you already earned your seat', with the paycheck as proof.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The original framing could sound patronising or imply new workers are unqualified. Positioning the paycheck as evidence of belonging turns impostor feeling into confidence.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a small 'first paycheck' moment inside the kit: a one-tap celebratory card to mark the day and share with whoever helped, without showing any amounts.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The idea needed an emotional and shareable hook to compete for attention on social platforms, and leaving out amounts avoids the privacy and comparison issues seen in C1 and C3.

revisions_after_selection.change: Built the campaign around real first-jobbers revealing the small thing they were secretly unsure how to make, rather than leading with the template list.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Starting from honest human stories avoids generic template marketing and gives creators and employers a clear role.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added an employer and university onboarding route in which the kit is offered as a free pack for new hires and graduates.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This creates a direct path from individual habit to team and organisational adoption, strengthening the B2B objective.

final_proposal.title: Day One, Looking Like You Belong
final_proposal.idea: The first paycheck is proof you belong, yet most people spend their first weeks feeling like they're faking it. Canva launches the First Paycheck Kit: templates for the things new workers are suddenly asked to make, such as a team intro slide, a 30-60-90 day plan, a weekly update, a freelance invoice and a refreshed CV. The campaign is told through real first-jobbers confessing the small thing they secretly didn't know how to make, and how it turned out fine. Payday unlocks a one-tap thank-you card to share with whoever helped you get there, with no amounts shown. Employers and universities can hand the kit to new hires, turning a personal confidence boost into a habit that follows people into their teams.
follow_up_questions: Which first-job moment (the intro slide, the first invoice, the first update to a boss) is the most universally nerve-racking, and could it become the single hero story of the campaign?
How could the kit work for people whose first paycheck looks very different, such as gig workers, apprentices, family business staff or people in markets with other pay rhythms?
What would make an employer proudly share the kit with every new hire, and how would Canva know that this habit is carrying into team use?

The opportunity is to make repair and reuse a prestige act at Dior by treating mending as an extension of couture craft, which has always been about fitting, refitting and perfecting. Dior's strongest assets for this topic are its ateliers and 'petites mains', its archive and heritage (Galerie Dior, the New Look), and iconic objects like the Lady Dior and Book Tote that are designed to outlive trends.
Dior cannot adopt a thrifty or eco-activist tone. Any sustainability message must feel like desire, craft and exclusivity, not guilt or discount culture.
The core audience is aspirational and established luxury buyers, plus Gen Z and Millennials who buy vintage, follow craft content and judge brands on durability and honesty.
Brand-owned resale is risky for a house that guards scarcity and image, so the strongest ideas keep objects in Dior's care and authorship rather than in open marketplaces.
Claims must be concrete and verifiable (what is repaired, by whom, how long it takes) to avoid greenwashing accusations.

candidates.title: The Second Signature
candidates.core_idea: Every Dior piece repaired in the ateliers returns with a second signature: a small tape or embroidered mark carrying the initials of the atelier hand who mended it and the date. Repair becomes co-authorship between the original designer, the maker and the owner, so a mended piece is worth more, not less. The campaign shows these hands and the objects they have revived.
candidates.brand_connection: It uses Dior's most distinctive asset, the anonymous 'petites mains' of the ateliers, and gives them a name. It extends the couture logic of the signed, numbered, individually fitted piece to the whole life of a garment.
expected_strengths: Reframes repair from flaw to value-adding authorship, which is a genuine, surprising insight for luxury.
Highly platformable: films, portraits of makers, owner stories, an exhibition, a visible mark that circulates on social media.
Fits the existing service and needs no new product or resale model.
Celebrates craftspeople, which supports employer brand and savoir-faire storytelling.
main_concerns: Some clients want repairs to be invisible and may not want a mark.
Requires atelier capacity and consistent quality across boutiques.
Could be read as marketing sentiment unless repair access and pricing are transparent.

candidates.title: Passed On
candidates.core_idea: A Dior 'passport' follows an object across owners. When a Lady Dior or a jacket is gifted or inherited, the atelier refreshes it, records the chain of owners and stories in a digital and paper provenance book, and re-certifies it. Reuse becomes lineage and inheritance rather than secondhand.
candidates.brand_connection: It draws on Dior's heritage, family-like lineage and the emotional status of iconic bags as heirlooms.
expected_strengths: Emotionally powerful: appeals to generational storytelling and gift culture.
Strengthens authenticity and combats counterfeits through provenance.
Builds a long-term relationship data asset with clients.
main_concerns: Edges toward resale, which could dilute exclusivity and complicate pricing.
Needs complex tracking infrastructure and privacy handling.
Less distinctive, since other luxury houses have launched authentication and certification schemes.

candidates.title: Open Atelier Hours
candidates.core_idea: Dior couturiers run pop-up repair clinics where anyone can bring any beloved garment, from any brand or none, and have it mended by a Dior hand. The offer is free and the queue is the content. Dior positions savoir-faire as a gift to culture, not just to customers.
candidates.brand_connection: It opens the door to the atelier and spreads couture knowledge beyond clients, echoing Dior's role as a cultural institution.
expected_strengths: Generates strong earned media, human stories and an unexpected act of generosity.
Reaches younger people who may never enter a Dior boutique.
Reinforces the idea that care for clothes is a universal value.
main_concerns: Costly and hard to scale, so risks looking like a one-off stunt.
Mending non-Dior pieces may blur the product link and brand exclusivity.
Long queues and mixed outcomes could produce negative experiences.

candidates.title: Built to Be Reopened
candidates.core_idea: A capsule collection designed explicitly for lifelong modification: hidden seam allowances, swappable straps and hardware, linings that can be re-embroidered, and a lifetime 'reopening' of the piece to re-cut or restyle it as the owner's life changes. The product is the message: Dior pieces are never finished.
candidates.brand_connection: It builds on the couture principle of the made-to-measure, evolving garment and Dior's strength in design innovation.
expected_strengths: Product-led proof, not just storytelling, which makes the claim credible.
Creates new reasons for repeat visits and ongoing client relationships.
Can attract design press and fashion-critic attention.
main_concerns: Needs product development time and a design shift, so it is slow to launch.
Risks being seen as a limited capsule rather than a house-wide stance.
Modular elements may conflict with the iconic, fixed silhouettes of Dior pieces.

reasons_for_selection: It offers the sharpest strategic insight: the mend is the one part of a garment's life that luxury hides, and Dior is uniquely placed to turn it into the part that is signed.
It rests entirely on what Dior already owns (the ateliers, the petites mains, an existing repair service), so it is credible, deliverable and not greenwash.
It is a true platform: a mark that can appear on products, in films, in exhibitions and on social media, and that scales from one client story to a global movement.
It keeps reuse within Dior's control and exclusivity, avoiding the brand risks of resale and the cost and scale problems of public clinics.

rejected.reason: Emotionally strong but drifts toward resale and requires heavy tracking infrastructure. Provenance schemes are also already common in luxury, so it is less distinctive. Its best element, the story of owners, can be folded into C1.

Generous and press-friendly, but costly, hard to scale and weakly tied to Dior products. It risks being a one-off stunt and could dilute exclusivity. It could return later as an occasional activation within C1.

Credible product proof, but it has a long development timeline and may be seen as a limited capsule. It also conflicts with the fixed iconic silhouettes. It is better treated as a future product extension once the mindset is established.

revisions_after_selection.change: Let the client choose between an invisible mend and a signed mend, and place the default signature inside the lining or on the care tape rather than on the outside.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Dior clients value polish and discretion. Choice protects the aesthetic and makes the mark an act of pride, not an obligation.

revisions_after_selection.change: Frame repair as 'the next chapter' of a piece, never as damage, and avoid showing broken product in the creative.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Prevents any implication that Dior products fail and keeps the tone aspirational rather than apologetic.

revisions_after_selection.change: Publish simple facts: how many pieces are mended, typical turnaround, and access for older pieces, and name the makers with their consent.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Specific, verifiable proof guards against greenwashing accusations and gives the makers real recognition.

revisions_after_selection.change: Add an annual showcase of mended pieces and their owners at Galerie Dior, and feature selected stories from the owners in the campaign.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Gives the campaign a cultural peak and brings in C2's emotional lineage idea without the resale risk.

final_proposal.title: The Second Signature
final_proposal.idea: Couture has always been the art of fitting and refitting, yet luxury hides the mend as if it were shame. Dior turns it into authorship. Every piece repaired in the ateliers returns with a second signature, the initials of the petite main who mended it and the date, stitched into the lining. Owners can choose an invisible mend or a visible one, but the maker is always named. The campaign introduces these hands through short portrait films, follows mended pieces and their owners, and culminates in a Galerie Dior exhibition of objects whose value grew because they were repaired. The message is simple and unmistakably Dior: a piece is never finished, only passed to the next pair of hands.
follow_up_questions: Which Dior object, such as a Lady Dior, a Bar jacket or a pair of shoes, would tell the most moving 'second signature' story, and who should be its owner?
How could the mark of the maker appear beyond the lining, for example in a digital tag, a sound or a ritual at handover, without cheapening the luxury?
What would make a younger customer who has never bought Dior want to bring something in for a mend, and what is Dior's honest answer to the price barrier?

task_understanding.focus: The first paycheck is a rite of passage: the first time the world pays you for something you can do. Canva is usually seen as a free-ish tool for making things, not a place where careers start. The opportunity is to own the moment when 'I made this' becomes 'someone paid me for this', and to show Canva as the starting line of working life for students, side-hustlers, career-changers and the small businesses that hire them.
assumptions: The primary audience is 18-28-year-olds entering work or monetising a skill for the first time, plus first-time freelancers of any age. Small business owners are a secondary audience, as buyers of design.
Many Canva users already earn from it (social content, menus, decks, Etsy assets), so for them the first paycheck often is a Canva project.

Emotionally, the first paycheck mixes pride, disbelief, tax-deduction shock, and uncertainty about worth. Culturally it is already documented (screenshots, 'first paycheck' TikToks, framed first dollars in shops).
As a B2B/SaaS brand, Canva needs the idea to ladder to real product use (templates, Canva for Work/Teams, invoices, decks) and not become a sentimental ad with no behaviour change.
Canva's brand voice is optimistic, inclusive and democratising ('empower the world to design'), so the idea should widen access and not signal elitism.
Professional designers are a sensitive stakeholder group. Any idea that implies design is trivial or cheap could draw backlash.
Budget and operational complexity are real constraints, so the idea should be pilot-able in one market before scaling.

candidates.title: Frame the First
candidates.core_idea: Revive the tradition of shop owners framing their first dollar, and give it to individuals. Canva offers beautifully designed, personalisable 'First Paycheck' keepsakes (frame-ready prints, share cards, and a custom wall piece) that turn a dull pay stub or a bank notification into a celebrated object. People post them with a shared tag.
candidates.brand_connection: Canva turns raw material into something worth showing off. It is the tool for commemorating and sharing, and the keepsake is made with the product.
expected_strengths: Emotionally simple and highly shareable
Low production cost and easy to localise
Taps an existing behaviour (screenshotting the first paycheck)
main_concerns: Celebratory but light on strategic substance, and it could read as a template promotion
Weak tie to B2B or Work use cases
Easy for other brands (banks, payroll apps) to copy

candidates.title: Where Did It Go? (The Paycheck Explained)
candidates.core_idea: Gen Z's first paycheck shock is the gap between the number they were promised and the number they receive. Canva launches a visual explainer toolkit that turns a pay stub's confusing lines (tax, benefits, deductions) into clear, customisable, shareable infographics, co-created with finance educators and creators.
candidates.brand_connection: Canva's core skill is making complex information visual and understandable, which is the same job it does for decks and reports.
expected_strengths: Real utility and a strong, relatable cultural insight
Showcases data-visualisation and infographic features
Good fit for educator and creator partnerships
main_concerns: Risk of seeming to give financial advice, with legal and accuracy exposure
Privacy concerns about uploading pay data
Less emotional, and a crowded space of finance influencers

candidates.title: Canva Firsts
candidates.core_idea: Instead of celebrating the first paycheck after it happens, Canva makes it happen. It matches first-time earners with real small businesses that need a menu, flyer, or pitch deck, and funds fair fees so the first paycheck comes from something designed in Canva. The paycheck itself becomes a frameable keepsake and a public story.
candidates.brand_connection: It makes Canva the origin of careers and not just a tool, and it serves both sides of its audience: newcomers who want to earn, and small businesses who need design. It delivers on 'empowering the world to design' with money behind it.
expected_strengths: Action over advertising, with strong earned-media and PR potential
Real stories and portfolio pieces make the content authentic and repeatable
Ladders to B2B use: small businesses experience Canva Teams and brand kits
Can start as a one-market pilot and scale as a recurring platform
main_concerns: Operational complexity: matching, quality control, payments, legal setup
Designers might see it as undercutting the profession
Impact is limited to the number of participants unless the content scales it

candidates.title: Price Yourself
candidates.core_idea: The hardest part of a first paycheck is deciding what you are worth. Canva launches a rate-card and quote toolkit (rate cards, proposals, invoices) plus real stories of first-timers who undercharged and learned. The campaign encourages people to ask for the number they deserve before the first job.
candidates.brand_connection: Proposals, invoices and rate cards are business documents that Canva already supports. It positions Canva as a quiet ally in professional confidence.
expected_strengths: Sharp, revealing insight about worth and undercharging
Strong link to Canva's business and freelancer tools
Resonates with underrepresented groups who undercharge most
main_concerns: Risk of preachy or advice-heavy tone
Less tied to the actual first-paycheck moment
Needs credible data and experts to avoid sounding generic

reasons_for_selection: It is the only direction where Canva creates the moment and not just comments on it, which gives it a bold, ownable role: the place where careers begin.
It serves both audiences in the B2B context, newcomers who earn and small businesses who buy design, and gives a path to Teams and brand-kit adoption.
It is platformable: each cohort, city or industry gives new stories, and the #MyFirstMade keepsake adds the ritual from C1.
It generates real proof (paid work, portfolio pieces) instead of claims, which suits a skeptical, cynical Gen Z audience.
It can be piloted in one market with a small cohort, which limits risk.

rejected.reason: Charming and shareable but it only decorates the moment. It lacks a strategic role for Canva and is easy for others to copy. Its best element, the frameable keepsake, is folded into C3.
Useful insight but it moves Canva into financial education, with accuracy, legal and privacy risks, and it is less ownable than design-led ideas.
A sharp insight, but it is further from the first-paycheck moment and risks sounding like career advice. It works better as a later chapter or supporting content for C3.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added professional designers as paid mentors and reviewers for each match, and set fees at fair market rates.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Reduces the risk of backlash from the design community and ensures the program raises the craft instead of undercutting it.

revisions_after_selection.change: Folded the C1 idea in: every first paycheck becomes a designed, frameable 'First Paycheck' template that winners personalise and share as #MyFirstMade.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Gives the program a ritual and a social asset, so reach is not limited to the number of participants.

revisions_after_selection.change: Scoped as a one-market pilot with a defined cohort and local small businesses, with the 'Firsts' format designed to repeat by city, industry or school.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Controls operational and legal complexity while proving the model and building a platform that can grow.

revisions_after_selection.change: Included small businesses as named partners and made their brand kits and Teams workspace part of the experience.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Ties the idea to B2B outcomes so it drives product adoption and not just goodwill.

final_proposal.title: Canva Firsts: Make the First Paycheck Happen
final_proposal.idea: The first paycheck is rarely about money. It's proof that something you made was worth someone else's money. Canva Firsts makes that proof possible. Canva matches first-time earners (students, career-changers, side-hustlers) with real small businesses needing a menu, flyer or pitch deck, and funds fair fees, so the first paycheck comes from something designed in Canva. Winners also get their pay as a frameable 'First Paycheck' template, echoing the shop-owner tradition of framing the first dollar, and share it as #MyFirstMade. Small businesses get design help, newcomers get a story and a portfolio piece, and pro designers join as paid mentors so the craft is lifted, not undercut. Canva shifts from the tool you use to the place where careers begin.
follow_up_questions: Which first-time earners are most underserved today, and how could the program reach them first rather than the people who would have found a way anyway?
What would make the framed 'First Paycheck' feel like a cultural object people want, not just a branded template?
How could the program grow beyond one cohort, through schools, local business associations or creators, without losing quality or fairness to professional designers?

task_understanding.focus: The first paycheck is a milestone people expect to feel triumphant. candidates.title: Read Your Pay

candidates.brand_connection: It is Canva's purpose applied to a real piece of life admin: making complicated information understandable and good-looking. It also gives work-focused teams a practical onboarding use case.

main_concerns: Risk of drifting into financial advice or inaccuracy across countries and tax systems.

candidates.title: Frame It
candidates.core_idea: Revive the old ritual of framing your first dollar or paycheck. Canva offers templates to design a keepsake of your first pay, with the numbers blurred or replaced by what it meant: 'First pay: paid for Mum's birthday dinner'. People share and print them.
candidates.brand_connection: Canva as the tool for making personal milestones look as good as they feel, with print and social sharing built in.
expected_strengths: Warm, emotional and highly shareable.

candidates.title: First Invoice
candidates.core_idea: For first-time freelancers and side-hustlers there is no paycheck. You have to ask to be paid. candidates.brand_connection: Directly serves small-business and creator users, positioning Canva as the place where a side-hustle becomes a business with a name, logo and invoice.
expected_strengths: Strong B2B and SMB fit, with a clear product link (documents, brand kits, invoicing).

revisions_after_selection.change: Limited scope to explaining and visualising what a payslip says, with no advice on tax or money management, and added 'check with your payroll provider' guidance in every template.

final_proposal.title: Read Your Pay
